The scenario architecture, the verdict, the Brent bands, the signed-MoU reference and the Murrin due-diligence tiers carry from v15 unmarked.

Bottom line · the strike is canceled; a corridor design is tabled

The scenario set stays bifurcated: Stalemate (modal) and Resolution (US-Qatari corridor tabled), with the apex tail held in the long-term allocation below the scenario-modelling threshold. Trump ordered a new attack on Iran for the 1–2 Aug weekend (WSJ), with energy infrastructure under consideration (CBS), then canceled it on 1 Aug saying deal parameters had been agreed — Axios reports Saudi pushback via MBS and the Washington Post a Pentagon force-availability warning — and on 2 Aug announced that US and Iranian officials will soon meet on the strait and the nuclear file. The design on the table is a US-Qatari two-corridor scheme: inbound through Iranian waters, outbound through Omani waters, no tolls. Negotiators reportedly back it pending IRGC approval; Foreign Ministry spokesperson Baghaei says on the record it “has nothing to do with” opening the strait — the Iran-formal-response trigger fires a third time — and Iranian diplomats counter with monitoring rights, “service fees,” blockade relief and sanctions relief. The strait stayed kinetic through the diplomacy, and the Houthis likely sank a first vessel at Bab el-Mandeb (4 Aug). Equities rallied three straight sessions on the turn (S&P 7,737 by 4 Aug), crude falling through the 3–4 Aug sessions — the FT has oil easing below $80 on 4 Aug, with no desk-series settle yet. Stavridis's three-path piece — renewed negotiations at ~60%, a dual-key reopening the most likely outcome — is per David the starting position for the firm's scenario-stress work. Murrin’s Article 2 nuclear scenario remains the analytical foundation under structural tail protection. Full scenario stances, drivers, equity and Brent views are in section 03.

01 · Due Diligence on Murrin

Verdict unchanged — cannot rule it out. WW3 117's call for total war is his own advocacy; his checkable claims hold.

Capabilities corroborated (Tier 1); interpretive layers held as hypotheses (Tier 2); the policy conclusion treated as advocacy (Tier 3). The full claim-by-claim verifiability table sits in the v1 tab.

Murrin’s capabilities case is sound and OSINT-sourced. Timeline sits at the aggressive end of a 6–12 month band that overlaps Roaring Lion’s own assessment. The preemptive-nuclear-use conclusion is his advocacy. The Gallant “440 Kilograms” piece restates the ~440kg 60% HEU stockpile that anchors the capabilities case, and ISW, citing five US-intelligence sources via CNN, reports Iran is physically hardening that stockpile — collapsing tunnels and mining storage entrances to defeat any seizure — so the fissile core is intact, deferred, and being entrenched. Iran agreed to readmit IAEA inspectors, the first forward step on the nuclear file; it is not down-blending. That step has stalled: the inspection access is unresolved, with Grossi expecting entry while Iran ties it to a final deal and sanctions relief, and Tehran then suspended the MoU outright on 18 Jul — the US-Iran meeting announced on 2 Aug is the first prospective nuclear-file table since. The ~440kg core stays inside Iran behind the entrenched tunnels. “Cannot rule out the nuclear scenario” holds as the analytical foundation; the apex is handled via the long-term allocation rather than modelled scenarios.

WW3 117 — the total-war call, graded

“WW3 117: Trump's Watershed Moment in Recognising a Common Autocratic Enemy” (28 Jul; reached the desk an hour after the v14 send) is Murrin's escalation call. The frame is a single integrated struggle — Ukraine, the Middle East and a coming Indo-Pacific theatre against one autocratic axis — hung on Senator Graham's funeral as the catalyst, and it concludes that Trump “has only one choice” — total war with Iran alongside Israel. It moves nothing in the architecture, the bands or the verdict.

ClaimTierChecked againstOur read
One integrated war. The regional wars are a single struggle against a shared autocratic axis; the fires merge. Interpretive BCA's Gertken (29 Jul, same intake) models the opposite as his base case: the wars stay separate on US political-will limits, Russia's two-front aversion and China's external constraints — with a Hormuz oil shock the tail that merges them. Pape frames the same linkages as read-through. The couplings themselves are documented on this desk: shared munitions strain, chokepoint tactics, Russian satellite targeting support. A live dispute between tracked sources. The file carries the wars as coupled through observable channels without adopting the single-war frame; the Graham-funeral catalyst is narrative. Gertken's own tail condition — an oil shock that kills demand — is the same transmission this file holds in the escalation legs.
“Iran's control of the strait remains unchallenged” after ~1,000 US strikes. Corroborated ISW's 26 Jul key assessment: the strikes have “likely failed to meaningfully affect” Iran's pursuit of strait control. Barclays (28 Jul): degradation achieved, “nothing that will meaningfully impact the IRGC's strategic calculus”; transits 3–6/day. Corroborated by both primary trackers — the third consecutive piece whose checkable core lands on ISW's own assessment. His ~1,000-strike figure matches ISW's count for the phase.
Axis logistics. The Caspian vessel strike, Russian satellite targeting for Iran, and Geran drones refitted with Chinese jet engines flowing back to Iran. Interpretive Ukraine's Caspian strikes on sanctioned vessels and Zelensky's satellite-imagery statements are already on this file (ISW, 25–26 Jul). The Chinese-engine transfer leg is his “believed to be,” unsourced; ISW separately reports Iran seeking PRC air-defence assistance. The component facts are carried from primary sources; the engine-transfer leg is uncorroborated; assembling them into one axis supply system is his frame. Held as a hypothesis, consistent with the WW3 116 treatment of the China-Russia claim.
Trump's “only one choice” — total war with Iran alongside Israel. Advocacy A prescription. The observable record at the cutoff is narrower: no US military response to the Jordan attack had followed, the day's joint US-Saudi strikes in Iraq retaliated for militia attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure and US interests, and Trump's promise to hit Iran hard is unexecuted against Iran itself; Israel remains out of the campaign. His conviction, kept in quotation — the same total-war advocacy graded at WW3 116 and Essential Lessons. The durable adjacent question is his interceptor-depletion cross-reference, already CSIS-corroborated in this file.

WW3 116, “The Battle for the Strait is On, so Prepare for Escalation” (17 Jul), is the tracked author's read of the current exchange. Murrin declares “Chapter Two” of the war — an existential contest for the strait and the Red Sea sea lanes that in his framing ends only with a victor and a vanquished. It is commentary rather than reporting: twenty-four distinct claims with no primary text of his own behind them, and the two that carry real weight are corroborated from outside the piece. Four of his headline claims have nothing on this desk that tests them either way.

ClaimTierChecked againstOur read
The MoU. An appeasement dwarfing Chamberlain's, and in full form it would have destroyed US maritime hegemony at a stroke. Interpretive The signed 14-point text is on file. ISW (18 Jul) attributes the collapse to divergent readings of Clause 5 — Iran reading it as affirming Iranian authority over the strait, Washington expecting pre-war traffic conditions. Corroborated at the level of mechanism: Clause 5 is where the deal failed, the leg he identified on signing day from the published clauses. The Chamberlain scaling and the hegemony conclusion are his register and carry no checkable content.

The imminence claim is his third dated one and carries no enrichment figure, no breakout estimate and no date, so it cannot be tested on its own terms. Advocacy A prescription. No source is offered and nothing on the desk bears on it. Reported as his conviction and kept in quotation. The escalation direction is consistent with the 6–19 Jul record. The grand-strategy prescription carries no falsifiable content.

Interpretive The “scum” remark is on the record from the Ankara NATO summit and already carried here. Tehran suspended the MoU on 18 Jul. No polling has reached the desk. The hardening direction is consistent with the observable sequence. The popularity leg is asserted without a pollster and is not carried. His own oil call runs against it — a print above $150 would restore the gas-price motive he argues is dead.
Assassination plot. A reported IRGC plot against Trump, passed via Israeli intelligence, corroborated by the Secret Service switching him back to the older Air Force One, and possibly the decisive factor driving him to destroy the IRGC. Interpretive A single unnamed Israeli-intelligence channel, hedged by Murrin himself. The aircraft switch is asserted without source and is unverified here, including the donor state of the aircraft he names. Uncorroborated on this desk. That the switch evidences the plot is his inference rather than anyone's report. The escalation-driver conclusion rests on that unverified chain plus a psychological read of Trump.
China and Russia. Iran fights on with their approval, confirmed by supplies flowing into its replenishment; US strikes on supply-route bridges acknowledge it. Interpretive ISW (17–18 Jul) confirms strikes on bridges, roads, a tunnel and telecoms around Bandar Abbas, a senior US official (WSJ, 17 Jul) describing the aim as disrupting supply routes to the city — routes ISW describes as Iran's own interior-to-coast logistics. ISW separately assesses the PRC and Russia are likely supporting Iranian targeting, citing a PRC reconnaissance satellite, Russian geolocation of US warships and aircraft, and Russian drone tactics. Both component facts are corroborated; joining them is his. What ISW documents is targeting intelligence, and no source on the desk reports Chinese or Russian materiel entering Iran. Held as a hypothesis.
Interceptor stocks. Every month of war consumes US holdings of PAC-3, THAAD and SM-3. Corroborated CSIS (Cancian and Park, 30 May 2026): PAC-3 MSE runs at roughly 650 a year with half going to allies, against a US decade-average buy of 225; the 3,203 Patriots requested for FY2027 first deliver May 2029. THAAD runs at 96 a year against an 857-interceptor request first delivering mid-2029. Both sit in the slowest three-plus-year replacement tier. Corroborated for two of his three named systems, from a defence-budget source rather than a strategic commentator. SM-3 is excluded: CSIS records less use than ground-launched systems and attributes the lag to small past orders and 36–39 month lead times. The monthly-burn framing is not how CSIS measures it, and the piece predates three further escalation rounds.
Who gains. Depletion benefits Moscow, leaving Ukraine exposed as PAC-3 stocks fall, and benefits Beijing more still by raising first-strike confidence before US stocks recover. Interpretive CSIS documents the allocation friction — THAAD deliveries re-sequenced away from allies, Japan's Tomahawks possibly delayed, Ukraine Patriots pushed back in the queue — and states the depleted inventories created a window of vulnerability in the Western Pacific. It contests the conclusion: demonstrated US combat experience against a PLA with none may preserve deterrence until inventories are restored. It says nothing about Russia benefiting. The queue and the Western Pacific window are corroborated in the source's own words, stronger support than he offers himself. The further step — that Moscow and Beijing are prolonging the conflict for this reason — has no support on the desk.
Mobile launchers. The hard target, rather than the underground missile cities; the fix is compressing the kill chain with persistent armed ISR striking within minutes. Advocacy Self-labelled house conjecture. The only adjacent datum is one unelaborated Reuters line (three US officials, 16 Jul) describing recent strikes as “shaping operations.” Every missile-related strike ISW reports in the window is a fixed site — the Lar launch site, the Yazd Missile Base, Konarak airbase. No in-window evidence of the shift in either direction. One detail runs the other way: the 116 downed telecom towers and the strike on the Radio and Communications Regulatory Authority degrade Iran's control of its own Shahed drones, which is fixed-infrastructure suppression.
Order of battle. 135 MQ-9s, 18 RQ-4s, roughly 50 MQ-4C Tritons and an operational RQ-180 for that mission, with the binding constraint numerical — “not dozens but hundreds” of platforms. Interpretive No independent check on the desk. Every figure is asserted without source, and no coverage modelling sits behind the hundreds. Not carried, consistent with the numeric record in his work — 300kg and 460kg for the same HEU stock inside one article, “Fatyie Ii” for the Fattah-2, a moving SPR figure. The RQ-180 entry is the exception and is credited: he hedges it as classified and unconfirmed. The mass-over-sophistication constraint is sound in kind; the figure is illustrative.
The Ukraine model. The 250km strike-drone campaign that largely isolated Crimea by land transfers to Hormuz — drones from the Omani Peninsula interdicting Iran's coastal batteries. Advocacy The Crimea-isolation premise is stated flatly and unsourced. Nothing on the desk tests the 250km radius or the Omani basing proposition. Prescription. ISW's own Hormuz mechanic cuts against the payoff — a single successful attack, or the persistent threat of one, deters transits — so suppressing launchers need not restore traffic. Logged, not carried.
Bab el-Mandeb. Yemeni sources report the Houthis preparing to close it with al-Shabaab, holding closure in reserve as their own asset; the strait carries 10–12% of seaborne trade, and simultaneous disruption with Hormuz would exceed any modern maritime crisis. Interpretive A closure vector is independently reported (Reuters, 16 Jul), reaching this desk inside the Capital Economics note rather than read directly, and on a different causal account: Iran instructing the Houthis conditional on US strikes against Iranian power plants. ISW's 17 Jul edition carries no Yemen, Houthi, Bab el-Mandeb or al-Shabaab content at all. Bremmer and Barclays both attribute Houthi behaviour to a payments dispute with Riyadh. The trade share is asserted without source; Capital Economics instead quantifies the consequence at roughly 4mn bpd rerouted via Yanbu and +$15–20/bbl on a dual closure. The vector is live and the Sanaa-airport leg is already on this file. His account of agency — a Houthi-owned asset held in reserve, largely independent of Tehran — is not the account our sources give. The al-Shabaab coordination and drone-transfer legs are uncorroborated rather than contradicted, resting on unnamed sourcing alone. The consequence arithmetic is usable; the trade share is not carried. v13: the blockade landed 20 Jul on the Houthis' own Sana'a-siege grievance — a datum for his agency read — but Reuters and ISW report a 13 Jul flight carrying IRGC commanders, missile equipment and gold into Yemen, and ISW's read (“their own agenda… a key Iranian partner”) lands between his account and the instruction account; the scope, Saudi-flagged vessels and Saudi port calls, is narrower than the full closure he sketches. v14: Houthi negotiator Abdul Salam states the blockade applies to Saudi Arabia alone (24 Jul), and ISW records the Houthis resisting Iran's request to close the strait fully for several months — both closer to his reserve-asset read — while NYT-cited officials say Iran would seek full closure if Trump strikes Tehran or critical infrastructure.
Oil above $150. A surge in the weeks ahead as risk premia rise, with significant pressure on government bond markets. Advocacy $150 sits inside the $130–160+ escalation band this file already holds. Brent settled around $88 on 17 Jul. Barclays' $65–80 range is the genuine out-of-band divergence. The bond call names no market, tenor, level or horizon. The level is inside our own range. He carries $150 as a base expectation within weeks; this file holds it as a tail. No supply-outage volume or trigger level is given and the horizon has not elapsed, so the call is logged unscored. His section heading asserting oil is set to rocket higher overstates his own hedged text. v14: the fortnight since has run a round trip — $100.69 settled 23 Jul, then the worst three-day fall since April 2020 to $84.09 on 28 Jul. No $150 print; the call tracks against, with his “weeks ahead” horizon not fully elapsed. Still unscored. v15: two weeks on, the peak is $100.69 on the AP settle and ~$94 on the desk series (23 Jul; divergence flagged at section 06), with Brent at ~$88 — the call tracks against on either series. v16: crude fell across the 3–4 Aug sessions on the cancellation and the talks announcement, the FT putting oil below $80 on 4 Aug — three weeks on from the piece, no print has approached $150 on either series.

Track record — prior calls against the 20 May to 20 Jul record

The capability, structure and chokepoint calls have held, and three of them are now working assumptions in this file. Timing and agency are where he fails, consistently and across every piece. The rows below are not independent trials — the Israel-trigger thesis recurs in four pieces and is entered once, and several draw on the same escalation sequence — so this reads as a map of where he is reliable rather than a hit rate. Unfalsifiable framing and advocacy carrying no forecast content are excluded, as is a 2024 Lebanon ground-campaign piece re-stamped 29 May 2026 and circulated as current with its body text never revised.

The measuring window is this desk's construction rather than his. Standing thesis
Across four pieces		 Israel is the uncontainable spoiler, and the IDF is the actor that moves on Iran's nuclear file. Not borne out Entered once though it recurs in four pieces. No Israeli unilateral strike on Iran occurred in the window. Hezbollah is absent from the escalation ledger; retaliation ran as direct Iranian state missile and drone fire against Gulf states and US bases; the nuclear-adjacent strike at Darkhovin was American; the Lebanon track moved toward a Rome-brokered pilot-zones structure on 14–15 Jul.
Trump 33 · Article 3 · IWI 13

Too early The 60-day track runs to roughly mid-August and has not elapsed. No Pacific escalation event has reached the desk in eight weeks, while the confrontation consuming US strike assets, munitions and diplomatic bandwidth was Hormuz. Khamenei was killed and Mojtaba succeeded him, but ISW assesses the strait attacks as chain-of-command decisions by senior IRGC officers, so the institution is functioning.

WW3 116 moves nothing in the scenario architecture, the Brent bands or the verdict. The two claims in it that carry weight are corroborated from outside the piece: CSIS puts PAC-3 and THAAD replenishment on a three-plus-year queue with FY2027 deliveries starting in 2029, supplying the numbers behind an interceptor mechanism he asserts without any, and ISW's Clause 5 finding vindicates the MoU read he made on signing day. The four claims nothing here tests are the assassination plot and the aircraft switch offered as its corroboration, the al-Shabaab coordination and drone transfer, the persistent-armed-ISR doctrine shift, and the Bear Island and Japan-Okinawa passages. The Bab el-Mandeb vector is the one genuinely new watch item, and the account of agency behind it is not his: Reuters has Iran instructing the Houthis conditional on US strikes against Iranian power plants, while Bremmer and Barclays both attribute Houthi behaviour to a payments dispute with Riyadh. The capability, structure and chokepoint reads are the durable part of his work, and three of them are now working assumptions in this file. His quantities do not travel into our text without independent confirmation. His timelines and his assignment of agency to Israel have failed repeatedly across the file.

Essential Lessons Part I — the retrospective, graded

“Essential Lessons from the Iran Conflict — Part I: Strategic Realities” (Murrinations, 21 Jul; reached the desk 26 Jul via Gary) is Murrin grading the war he has covered since WW3 112. It is doctrine — seven lessons and five predictions, one of them dated only as “inevitable.” The checkable lessons land close to sources this file already holds. It moves nothing in the architecture, the bands or the verdict. A Part II on operational lessons is flagged and will be read when it arrives.

ClaimTierChecked againstOur read
Air power cannot win alone. The campaign failed to force submission; Iran's hardened, dispersed depth defeated it. Corroborated ISW's own key assessment (26 Jul): the current level and type of US strikes have “likely failed to meaningfully affect” Iran's pursuit of strait control — ~1,000 targets since 12 Jul against ~13,000 in the war's first phase, with Iranian control consolidating via the mine threat. Corroborated by the primary source this file weights most, in the same week he published. The Vietnam and Kosovo parallels and the JCS air-power-bias counterfactual are his framing; the operative claim stands on ISW alone.
Time as a weapon. Iran survives the assault, uses pauses to repair and replenish, and emerges stronger. Corroborated ISW (27 Jul) assesses Iran is using the current pause to reconstitute, quoting a regime-linked analyst on rebuilding combat capacity, with the 8 Apr ceasefire as precedent. Corroborated in the v14 window — the pause v14 wrote into the file is the mechanism he describes. It cuts both ways for the diplomatic track: the pause that enables the table also lets Iran reconstitute (ISW, 27 Jul).
“Could hardly have been worse.” A mortal blow to US credibility; allies will question the security umbrella. Interpretive Pape (Foreign Affairs, same intake) argues the same direction: the 1991-dated unipolar era is over, with the Iran war as the demonstration. Mead (WSJ, 28 Jul) argues a tactical pause inside a longer campaign by a president “unlikely to give up.” Desk observables cut both ways — Japan's Tomahawk delays and Kuwait's reported Pakistan pact exploration against a blockade still enforced. A live dispute between tracked sources. The file's “exhausted America” leg already carries the credibility question as backdrop; the piece sharpens it without settling it. The “mortal blow” grading is his register.
Chokepoints are the US blind spot. The Houthi A2/AD episode is a test bed for Iranian and Chinese strategy. Interpretive ISW's standing assessment has the Red Sea expansion serving Iran's Hormuz objective; Pape extends the same logic to Taiwan (drone-armed denial of Chinese ports). Nothing on the desk addresses US Navy institutional posture. The chokepoint mechanism is a working assumption of this file. The institutional blind-spot claim and the sea-power-chairman counterfactual are untestable here; the Taiwan read-through is logged as backdrop alongside Pape's.
The next war. A future US-Iran confrontation is “inevitable” — economic pressure, cyber, proxies, drones — on Iran's timetable, from strength. Advocacy No horizon and no falsifiable content. ISW's reconstitution read is consistent in kind; nothing tests inevitability. His conviction, kept in quotation. The file's architecture already carries the substance — Stalemate modal, the apex re-timed and open-ended — without the inevitability claim.
02 · Scenario test

Live tail risk on a 6–12 month horizon — below the scenario-modelling threshold.

The conclusion is unchanged; the operational decision is to bear this tail in the long-term allocation rather than model it.

The apex first-use event is paradigm-break, so protection is structural rather than model-derived. As David noted, “in short, I probably don’t need to know what the damage would look like.” The deal does not lower the tail — it re-times it. The MOU defers the nuclear question to a 60-day negotiation while the HEU stays inside Iran, so the breakout clock moves from the battlefield to the talks table without resetting. The 25–28 Jun armed exchange was the test case for kinetic escalation short of first-use; the 6–8 Jul exchange a second instance; the 8–12 Jul continuation a third; the 13–16 Jul round a fourth — all conventional, with the apex below threshold throughout. The 17–19 Jul window is a fifth iteration, and it moves two markers the prior four did not: US service members were killed, and a strike reached a nuclear-file site — the Darkhovin plant in Khuzestan, per Iran's AEOI. Both stay inside the conventional channel: Darkhovin is a very-early-construction site with no nuclear material found at the IAEA's last inspection, and the ~440kg HEU core goes unmentioned in any of this window's exchanges. A second adjacency followed on 22 Jul: US strikes hit the Parchin complex in southeastern Tehran Province — the munitions site whose Taleghan 2 facility carries the pre-2003 weapons-test history — with no claim against the HEU itself. Washington chatter about striking Pickaxe Mountain, extending to unattributed tactical-nuclear talk (13D), is logged as apex texture and not carried. The sixth round (20–23 Jul) stayed conventional through the second-chokepoint window; the seventh (24–28 Jul) is a pause — the US flew no strike waves after 24 Jul, Iranian attacks ended with a single Bahrain strike, and the HEU went unmentioned. Two proliferation-adjacent items log without carrying: the NYT reports US intelligence assesses Mojtaba Khamenei more interested in a weapon than his father, favouring a miniaturised thermonuclear design, while Albright (24 Jul) assesses the programme too degraded for that pursuit now. ISW assesses Iran is using the pause to reconstitute, as after the 8 Apr ceasefire — the apex clock runs through the pause. An eighth window (28–31 Jul) ends the pause at Jordan and keeps the exchange conventional — the day's US-Saudi strikes hit militia sites in Iraq (retaliation for attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure and US interests), no US answer to the Jordan attack had landed by the 29 Jul cutoff, and the HEU is again unmentioned. Two nuclear-file signals log without carrying: 13D's “the nuclear issue is no longer viewed as taboo in Tehran” — the full text carries a debate on NPT withdrawal, with the North Korea precedent argued (WILTW, 30 Jul, on file) — and Barclays' framing of a strike on the Isfahan HEU stockpile or Pickaxe Mountain as Washington's “last option.” A ninth window (31 Jul–4 Aug) holds the pattern — a strike ordered for the weekend was canceled before flying, the exchange stayed conventional (UKMTO projectile incidents in the strait approaches; ISW records no US strike activity in the window), and the HEU is again unmentioned. The 2 Aug talks announcement names nuclear issues alongside the strait — the first prospective nuclear-file table since the 18 Jul suspension; the apex re-timing anchor would return if that table convenes, and Rubio's 4 Aug framing sequences it explicitly — denuclearisation “the ultimate deal,” the strait the immediate one (FT) — the nuclear question deferred behind the strait question a second time. One proliferation-adjacent item logs without carrying: the Mearsheimer panel reports a US-Saudi enrichment agreement signed around 22 Jul without fullest IAEA inspection rights — single-source, the signed execution of the greenlight WSJ reported at v13. The re-timing anchor itself has moved: with Tehran's 18 Jul suspension the 60-day track is no longer running, so the apex window is open-ended rather than deadline-bound. The placement is insensitive to that timing — the tail sits in the long-term allocation either way, which is what the structural-protection decision was for. What stays in the long-term allocation is the nightmare convergence — nuclear Iran + reinvigorated Russia + hedging China + exhausted America + isolated Israel arriving together around summer 2026 as oil buffers run dry; Murrin Article 3’s late-stage US-decline thesis sits on the “exhausted America” leg as backdrop conviction, with the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve at 307.6m barrels as of 24 Jul, the lowest since April 1983, with ~25m contracted barrels left and total US crude stocks at their lowest since 1984 — monitored daily at the tip-of-iceberg layer.

Verdict

Murrin Article 2 cannot be ruled out and remains a live tail risk on a 6–12 month horizon. The apex probability sits below the threshold where another modelled scenario would change the prescription. Israeli unilateral action remains the most plausible trigger — and the armed US-Iran exchanges under the MoU show the deal can turn kinetic through Hormuz directly; the strait and the Lebanon front are both live channels for an escalation that the long-term allocation is built to absorb. A fifth round — first US deaths, a formal Iranian suspension, retaliation across seven countries — extends the pattern at higher stakes without displacing Israeli unilateral action as the most plausible apex trigger. Israel is closer to the exchange than in any prior window: intercepting Iranian drones near its borders, detecting the Aqaba launch, and warning it will re-engage if attacked. The trigger has still not fired. A sixth round (20–23 Jul) adds the second chokepoint and the Parchin strike without displacing that read; WSJ (22 Jul) reports Israel deliberately sitting the campaign out while the IDF prepares options. A seventh window (24–28 Jul) is the first pause since the suspension and does not displace that read; Trump met Netanyahu in Washington (Bloomberg, 28 Jul) with Israel still out of the campaign. The eighth window's break does not displace the read: the Jordan attack and the Iraq strikes ran through bases and proxy sites, Israel stayed out, and Barclays flags an Israeli strike on Iranian sites as a live if unlikely risk ahead of the 27 Oct election. The trigger has still not fired.

03 · The scenario set

Stalemate / Resolution / BAU — stance, drivers, and market views.

Per the Eric/team binding decision (22 May): two scenarios modelled, plus the BAU baseline. The apex first-use scenario is held in the long-term allocation. Architecture held through v13 with the tier Suspended pending a convened table; v14 moved it to Hormuz track convened. v15: Iran rejected the proposal (a senior official to Reuters, 29 Jul) — the tier moves to Proposal rejected. v16: the US-Qatari corridor design is tabled with talks announced — the tier moves to US-Qatari corridor tabled.

The oil-to-equity beta has compressed to roughly 1.5% S&P downside per 10% oil rise, against ~4% in March. The 23 Jul session: S&P -1.2%, Nasdaq -2.2%, the 10Y at a one-year high — oil pressure compounded by earnings-day falls in Tesla (-14.5%) and Alphabet (-7.1%) (AP). The 23 Jul CTA selling was the largest since 10 Jun; by 27–28 Jul positioning was back to neutral and Treasuries rallied as oil fell (Vanda). The 29 Jul FOMC-day session sold off on the break and the hawkish hold (S&P -1.5% to 7,316, Dow -2.2%); the AI leg turned the 30 Jul session (Microsoft +16%, a record ~$450bn one-day gain), with the Kospi closing a record 18% higher on 31 Jul. The war leg and the AI leg are pulling equities in opposite directions. Three sessions then rallied on the turn: S&P 7,490 (31 Jul), 7,601 (3 Aug), 7,737 (4 Aug), the desk attributing each leg to de-escalation pricing plus AI earnings. Tight, elevated, drawing inventory. Settled prints reached the desk in the 16–17 Jul window: Brent closed $82.96 on 16 Jul (desk series) and settled ~$88 on 17 Jul per Bloomberg — up 4.6%, the biggest weekly advance since April — with the front month in backwardation (~-$1.3). Strait traffic: Kpler counted eight transits on 16 Jul. External calls now bracket this file's bands: Barclays $65–80 below the floor (carried watch item), Murrin above $150 (logged at section 01), CE +$15–20 on a dual-chokepoint closure. The 21–23 Jul window: settled $88.52 on 21 Jul, then $100.69 on 23 Jul (+7%, $102 intraday — AP) as the Red Sea attacks priced; the dual-chokepoint contingency is partially live at Bab el-Mandeb. Then the retreat: roughly 16% over three sessions to $84.09 settled 28 Jul (WTI $79.26), the worst run since April 2020, on de-escalation positioning — flow not normalised, dark transits continuing. The desk series puts the 23 Jul peak at ~$94 (the AP $100.69 divergence is flagged at section 06) and has ~$88 settled 30 Jul; the strait is kinetic again on the IRGC's three-tanker claim, transits under 10/day, and CE (30 Jul) flags a tipping point without a sustained flow recovery. v16: WTI traded above $86 post-settlement on 31 Jul on the CBS energy-infrastructure report, then crude fell across the 3–4 Aug sessions as the cancellation and the talks priced — the FT has international oil easing below $80 on the 4 Aug session, the first level on the desk since the ~$88 settle of 30 Jul (no desk-series settle yet), with US petrol above $4/gallon, ~35% over pre-war, and diesel above the Biden-era average. BCA logs two more external ranges below our floor — $70–100 behavioural (3 Aug) and Papic's $75–100 (4 Aug) — beside Barclays' $65–80; flagged, not adopted. CE (3 Aug) holds that the worst case can be avoided while flagging Bahrain's balance of payments at the brink under the closure, with Saudi or UAE support its base case.

US-Qatari corridor tabled
Eric/team + David · Good A		 Mearsheimer “humble pie”; JPOA 2.0 framework; Ferguson Hormuz Council; HEU export under Security Guarantee; post-war Gulf Treaty Organisation. Stage 1 signed; the first 60-day-track round convened (Switzerland, 21–22 Jun) with IAEA inspectors readmitted; the durable settlement stays gated on that track. The tier moved to Suspended at v12: Tehran formally suspended its MoU commitments on 18 Jul, the diplomatic channel went dead (ISW: “nothing significant to report”), and mediator Oman was itself a target of Iranian strikes and public hostility. ISW's structural read of the collapse: the two sides interpreted Clause 5 on Hormuz in fundamentally different ways — the US as a return to pre-war passage, Iran as affirmation of its authority — and the Gulf states rejected Iranian management and fees. The open question carried forward: whether a successor venue convenes (Qatar, Pakistan and Turkey are floated in intake reporting), and whether the regime split — Rezaei declaring diplomacy over against Ghalibaf and a Nour News op-ed still arguing for talks — resolves toward a reopened channel. v13: the venue question got its first concrete answer — Qatar, Egypt, Pakistan and Oman tabled a written 10-day framework (~20 Jul) with dual-lane reopening and a fee design (Malacca-style Iranian service fees, or an IMO-administered fund), and Iran confirmed receipt. No talks are scheduled; Trump is publicly skeptical while weighing a joint campaign with Israel (Axios). The tier stays Suspended until a table actually convenes. v14: it convened — Iranian and Omani delegations met in Tehran 24–25 Jul on restarting strait traffic, the lead proposal reopening the likely-mined middle passage, with UK/French demining offered once safe, Iran seeking joint management likely to include fees, and Qatar, Pakistan, Egypt and the Witkoff/Kushner channel involved (Bloomberg). A Hormuz agreement would gate resumed war-ending talks; Omani negotiators expected announceable progress within days. The contradictions ride along: Baghaei claims “progress” while saying traffic is unchanged, parliamentarians insist control is not returning to pre-war conditions, and the NYT-reported rejection via the Zaydi channel — denied by his office — is carried as contested. The tier moves to Hormuz track convened; the nuclear file has no table. ISW 28 Jul: the proposal's terms are a formal 10-day truce — Iran reopens the strait; the US lifts the blockade and considers unfreezing assets — with an Omani regional-consortium design for management; Iran is refusing to concede control, and ISW reads the refusal as showing Iran may calculate it can extract the blockade-lift, or further concessions, without giving up the strait. Three factions steer the Iranian side: the IRGC-Vahidi line likely guiding policy, the Pezeshkian/Araghchi/Ghalibaf camp differing over means and defining control less expansively, the Paydari Front against talks entirely. v15: the rejection landed — a senior Iranian official told Reuters (29 Jul) the Omani regional-management and voluntary-fee design is “unrealistic,” Gharibabadi having said (28 Jul, per ISW) Iran would go to war for strait sovereignty; the Jordan attack followed shortly after the refusal, and ISW assesses IRGC commander Vahidi almost certainly supported the strike decision. Both Omani fee designs are now refused — the early-July donations variant and this one — with Iran maintaining its demand to levy fees. The tier moves to Proposal rejected; the Pakistani-Qatari halt-attacks proposal stays under review by both sides (Barclays) as the surviving channel. v16: the surviving channel produced a design. US and Qatari mediators floated restoring pre-war traffic with inbound transit through Iranian waters and outbound through Omani waters, and no tolls (reported 3–4 Aug); Trump, having canceled the weekend's ordered strike on being told deal parameters were agreed (1 Aug), announced on 2 Aug that US and Iranian officials will soon meet on reopening the strait and on nuclear issues. The Iranian side split on the record: negotiators around Araghchi reportedly support the design awaiting IRGC approval (WSJ, 3 Aug); Baghaei says the proposal “has nothing to do with” opening the strait (2 Aug — the Foreign Ministry's formal response; the trigger fires a third time); IRGC-affiliated media deny any agreement; Rezaei rules out “a second corridor” “under any circumstances” (referent ambiguous per ISW); the Assembly of Experts brands “calls for surrender” an “unforgivable betrayal,” and Paydari parliamentarians prepare impeachment proceedings against Araghchi. By 4 Aug Iranian diplomats counter with maritime monitoring and intervention rights, “service fees,” blockade relief and sanctions relief — restoring the fee demand the no-toll design dropped. ISW's read: even the inbound leg alone preserves Iranian gatekeeping over entry to the Gulf. The FT (5 Aug) adds the mechanics from people briefed: approval still sits with Tehran's senior leadership; Iran would first send its own vessels, tankers included, through the waterway to prove it mine-free; no fees during the temporary arrangement, with Tehran insisting on eventual “service fees” that the Gulf states reject and Oman floating a Malacca-style voluntary-contribution design; a deal would bring the US blockade lifted and oil-sanctions relief. Rubio narrows the immediate US ask to the strait — “The denuclearisation of Iran is the ultimate deal… The immediate deal… is the strait” (4 Aug) — and Baghaei describes the arrangement as provisional, covering “inbound and outbound shipping routes” while final-settlement talks run, the vehicle Iran-Oman with the US providing input through Muscat (Vaez: “not really a deal between Iran and the US”). The tier moves to US-Qatari corridor tabled. Mid-single-digit upside. Declines toward $90–110 over months; market below the band until the 23 Jul spike — ~$73 at the pre-war anchor by 29 Jun, pushed back up by each escalation round since — now $82.96–~$88 on the first settled prints since v11, below the floor through v12, then into the band: $88.52 settled 21 Jul and $100.69 on 23 Jul, the entry escalation-driven — pricing a clean reopening the substance does not support; trust rebuild takes quarters. v14: three sessions took it back below the floor — $84.09 settled 28 Jul — this time on deal hopes running ahead of the table. v15: ~$88 settled 30 Jul after the rejection — still below the floor, the physical market dire (CE, 30 Jul) and the strait kinetic again. v16: crude fell across the 3–4 Aug sessions on the cancellation and the talks — again ahead of any agreed term.

External cross-check — Stavridis's three paths (4 Aug) · per David, the starting position for the scenario-stress work

Admiral Stavridis (Carlyle Compass, 4 Aug; via Gary, 5 Aug) weights three US paths: significant drawdown ~10%, major escalation ~30%, renewed negotiations backed by measured pressure ~60%. The 60% path lands where this file's Resolution track sits, and his predicted most-likely outcome — a dual-key reopening with Iran controlling northbound transit and Oman the southbound route — is structurally the US-Qatari corridor design now tabled; the fee and international-law frictions he flags as the residue are where Iran's 4 Aug counter-demands landed. His 30% escalation path — strikes on economic targets at 300–500+ per 24-hour cycle, an initial ~30,000 ground troops to secure the strait, an all-out Iranian response against Gulf energy — maps onto the escalation leg this file holds in the $130–160+ band; the 10% drawdown path is unmodelled here and sits nearest Mearsheimer's withdrawal expectation. His inputs run close to the file's own: Iran at ~65% combat-power loss yet retaining the missile, drone, small-craft and mine capability that threatens shipping; US and Israeli interceptor and precision-munitions depletion against substantial residual combat power (~60,000 troops, two carrier strike groups); Tehran having banked regime survival, $25bn in unfrozen assets and the proposed $300bn fund from the initial ceasefire — his figures for the Article 11 and Article 6 terms. He dates Trump's posture from 3 Aug: “holding off on a big strike” because “everyone in the region” is “begging for talks.” One structural read runs beyond the window: strait control as a depreciating asset for Tehran, the energy system adapting away from the chokepoint over several years — the corridors thesis David's 2 Aug piece argues from the infrastructure side. Per David (5 Aug), the piece is the starting position for the firm's scenario-stress work, to be incorporated across the 14-point-MoU, oil-shock, SPR and Murrin streams.

04 · The signed MoU

What the text says — the milestone, Article by Article.

The 14-point text Bloomberg published on 16 June and the version a senior US official read aloud on signing (17 Jun); the Article text below is verbatim from those primary publications. Tehran announced on 18 Jul it is suspending its commitments under this text; the table is carried as the reference for whatever track resumes, with the implementation boxes tracking how each obligation has executed and reversed.

ArticleText (close paraphrase)Our reading
1 · Ceasefire Immediate and permanent end to the war on all fronts including Lebanon; no hostile actions; refrain from the threat or use of force; the final agreement confirms this. Signed edit: a Lebanese-sovereignty guarantee was added. Contested — Iran reads it as obliging an Israeli withdrawal; Israel is not a signatory and keeps striking. The one clause advancing: the Lebanese Armed Forces began deploying into the Rome-brokered pilot zones on 16–17 Jul.
2 · Sovereignty Both parties respect each other’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and refrain from interfering in internal affairs. Implicitly constrains US regime-change; the IRGC structure survives. Iran also leans on this to frame “managing” Hormuz as an internal affair.
3 · 60-day window Negotiate and reach a final agreement within a maximum of 60 days, extendable by mutual consent. The clock for every deferred core. Suspended by Tehran on 18 Jul at roughly the window's halfway mark: Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei declared the signature “invalid” and Deputy FM Gharibabadi announced Iran is suspending its commitments. Neither side has formally withdrawn from the text itself.
4 · US obligations Immediate: lift the naval blockade, prevent interference against Iran, restore traffic within 30 days to pre-war capacity proportional to Iran’s pre-war volume. US withdraws forces from surrounding areas within 30 days after the final agreement. Asymmetry: the blockade lifts at once, but force withdrawal waits on the final agreement. Signed term tested and reversed: the US reinstated the blockade on 14 Jul, targeted at Iranian-flagged vessels and Iranian cargo. Enforcement turned kinetic in July — by 16 Jul three vessels redirected, one disabled, the Curacao-flagged M/T Wen Yao boarded by the 11th MEU off Duqm — and CENTCOM's first published tallies (4 Aug) put the totals since 14 Jul at 45 vessels redirected, two disabled and two boarded. The 30-day full-traffic-restoration deadline passed in breach on 17 Jul.
5 · Iran obligations (Hormuz) Immediate: resume merchant shipping in the Gulf / Sea of Oman within 30 days to pre-war volume, removing technical obstacles and neutralising mines. Signed edit: a joint Iranian-Omani administration and a 60-day toll bar were added. Iran’s win — the text does not bar Iran from “managing” the strait. Tested and unresolved: Oman’s own two-corridor proposal was rejected by Iran on 12 Jul, and shipping avoids the Omani route despite US escorts. The IRGC Navy now states the regime openly — “not a single drop of oil, gas, or chemical fertilizer” passes without its coordination and permission — and a Thai-flagged vessel was struck on the southern route on 17 Jul. Iran's Environmental Protection Agency floated UNCLOS-based “environmental services” fees on 18 Jul, a new variant of the fee ambition.
6 · $300bn development US and regional partners build a rehabilitation and development plan financing at least $300bn; the implementation mechanism is set within 60 days. External Gulf money, not a US outlay (Trump: “no money changes hands”; Reuters: no US government funds). Gulf-funded, routing the financing into the Gulf-state track.
7 · Sanctions US commits to ending all sanctions — UNSC resolutions, IAEA Board resolutions, all unilateral US primary and secondary sanctions — on a schedule set in the final agreement. Exceeds the JCPOA’s scope in principle, but the schedule is deferred to the final agreement. Signed term tested in the other direction: the US Treasury added over 50 sanctions targets on 14–15 Jul (the Shamkhani network, IRGC procurement) — new sanctions rather than the wind-down the Article commits to.
8 · Nuclear Iran reiterates it will never produce nuclear weapons; the fate of enriched material and all nuclear-related issues, including Iran’s “nuclear needs,” is “adequately addressed” in the final agreement. A restatement of Iran’s standing position. The version read aloud on signing adds on-site down-blending under IAEA supervision as the baseline method — gated to the final agreement and cutting against Iran’s simultaneous hardening of its HEU tunnels. The ~440kg core stays in Iran through the window. The file was touched kinetically for the first time in the 17–19 Jul window: Iran's AEOI says a 19 Jul US strike hit the Darkhovin plant in Khuzestan (IAEA: very early construction, no nuclear material found at its last inspection). Araghchi said on 19 Jul that some nuclear demands may remain “unresolvable.”
9 · Status quo Pending the final agreement, Iran holds the status quo on its nuclear programme and the US imposes no new sanctions and does not strengthen its forces in the region. The strategic freeze: Iran’s programme stays intact while US leverage is capped. The most consequential clause for the deferral read. Both halves are now in breach — new US sanctions landed 14–15 Jul, and more F-16s, F-35s and refuellers are moving to the region.
10 · Oil waivers US Treasury issues waivers immediately after signing for Iranian crude, petrochemicals and derivatives, and related services (banking, insurance, transport). Signed edit tested: the waiver was revoked on 8 Jul — the first rollback of a core MoU economic term. The wind-down completed on 17 Jul: General License X1 expired, revoking all Iranian-oil transaction authority.
11 · Frozen assets Frozen and restricted Iranian funds released and made fully available in line with negotiation progress, directed by the Central Bank of Iran. Sequenced to negotiation progress — Iran’s leverage-extraction path. Vance conditions release on “verified steps” on the HEU; Vahidi insists the funds are not barred from military spending.
12 · Implementation A mechanism to oversee implementation and the commitment to the final agreement. Compliance architecture with no specified membership, voting or enforcement — to be designed in 60 days.
13 · Sequencing gate Nuclear negotiations begin only after Iran receives assurances on the implementation of Articles 4, 5, 10 and 11 (blockade, Hormuz, oil waivers, frozen assets); talks then address only the remaining articles. Iran’s verification gate — it can delay the nuclear talks by contesting any of those four implementations. The Article 10 revocation and the blockade's 14 Jul return each gave Iran grounds to invoke it. The 18 Jul suspension goes past the gate: rather than invoking Article 13 to pause the nuclear talks, Tehran suspended its commitments across the text.
14 · UNSC ratification The final agreement is approved through a binding UN Security Council resolution. China and Russia become structural guarantors — neither the US nor Israel can unilaterally exit the final deal without a UNSC crisis. Iran’s durability anchor.
Implementation — weeks 1–5 (carried)

The week-by-week implementation record through 16 Jul — the two-way first week, the kinetic second, the tanker attacks and waiver revocation of the third, the central-Iran strikes and Muscat rejection of the fourth, and the blockade's return in the fifth — is carried in the v7–v11 tabs. The through-line: each week tested a different Article, and by week five a core term (Article 4) had formally reversed.

Implementation — week 6 · v12

The window (Art 3): Tehran suspended its MoU commitments on 18 Jul — Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei declared Trump's signature “invalid,” Deputy FM Gharibabadi announced the suspension, and Rezaei said diplomacy and negotiations “are over,” while Ghalibaf (16 Jul, state TV) and a Nour News op-ed (18 Jul) still argued for the talks track. ISW's negotiations section for the window: “nothing significant to report.” Casualties: two US service members killed at Muwaffaq Salti Airbase, Jordan (17 Jul, ascribed to the IRGC); a third killed in Iraqi Kurdistan (18 Jul); US toll 17 since 28 Feb. Blockade (Art 4): enforcement kinetic — three vessels redirected, one disabled, the M/T Wen Yao boarded; General License X1 expired 17 Jul, completing the Article 10 reversal; the 30-day full-lift deadline passed in breach the same day. Hormuz (Art 5): the IRGC Navy's permission regime stated openly; a Thai-flagged vessel struck 17 Jul; Kpler counted eight transits on 16 Jul; UNCLOS-based “environmental services” fees floated. Strikes: sixth, seventh and eighth consecutive US nights (16–18 Jul) — Bandar Abbas bridges, rail and telecoms severed, Chabahar, Oghab 44, and the IRGC launch infrastructure behind the Gulf-state attacks; three US officials call them “shaping operations.” Retaliation: seven countries — Kuwait (power, desalination and oil facilities struck three days running), Bahrain, Qatar, Oman (US radar assets on the Salamah Archipelago and Ghanem Island), Saudi Arabia (al Kharj missile, sirens at Yanbu), Syria (al Tanf) and Jordan (Muwaffaq Salti, then four missiles at Aqaba on 19 Jul). Nuclear (Art 8): the AEOI says a US strike hit the Darkhovin plant (19 Jul); Araghchi calls some nuclear demands possibly “unresolvable.” Leadership: Araghchi disclosed a six-person SNSC special committee making on-the-spot decisions while Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei — severely injured in the strikes that killed his father — is reportedly hard to reach; ISW assesses Vahidi very likely a member. Yemen: Reuters (16 Jul, single root source) reports Iran instructed the Houthis to prepare to close Bab el-Mandeb if the US strikes Iranian power plants; Houthi-Saudi cross-border attacks resumed for the first time since 2022. Lebanon (Art 1): the LAF began deploying into the pilot zones 16–17 Jul — the one obligation moving forward.

Implementation — week 7 · v13

The window (20–23 Jul): the suspension holds — ISW's negotiations section still reads “nothing significant to report” — while a four-party written framework (Qatar, Egypt, Pakistan, Oman, ~20 Jul) revives the June interim agreement's shape: a 10-day ceasefire, both Hormuz lanes reopened (southern free of Iranian attack, northern free of US blockade), and the fee question posed as Malacca-style Iranian service fees or an IMO-administered fund. Iran confirmed receipt; no talks are scheduled. Second chokepoint: the Houthis blockaded Saudi Red Sea port calls from 20 Jul, citing the Saudi siege of Sana'a, and struck the Encelia and Layla on 22 Jul (one hit UKMTO-confirmed); Bab el-Mandeb transits fell 64 to 30, recovering to 40 by 23 Jul, with at least seven diversions and an EU Naval Force warning. Strikes: the eleventh and twelfth consecutive US nights reached Bushehr Airport, Larak Island, Behbahan (the IRGC 15th Special Forces Brigade base), western and north-western Iran, and the Parchin complex near Tehran; Iran struck Dhahran's King Abdulaziz Air Base (a first), US early-warning radar in Kuwait (an AN/FPS-117), Jordanian bases and Aqaba. Workarounds: Iran-Pakistan trade to expand from $3bn toward $10bn with five-fold truck traffic — the land answer to the naval blockade. Posture (23 Jul): Trump threatened Iran and the Houthis with “major military punishment” and told Axios he may expand strikes (“They haven't received enough pain yet”); equities fell and the 10Y hit a one-year high; dozens of fighters and refuellers continue moving to the region. Axis widening: Iranian-backed Iraqi militias likely droned Kuwait's Abdali border crossing on 23 Jul — the first Axis attack on a regional border crossing since 11 Jul — with explosions reported on Bubiyan Island; the IRGC claims a southern-corridor tanker struck a naval mine, a claim ISW cannot observe and reads as deterrence messaging against the Omani route.

Implementation — week 8 · v14

The window (24–28 Jul): the suspension stands on paper while both sides stop shooting — no US strikes in Iran after 24 Jul (the first pause in 13 nights), Iranian attacks ending with a single Bahrain strike in the first window, and a senior Iranian official telling Reuters (26 Jul) the halt lasts as long as Washington's does, conveyed directly. ISW's 27 Jul edition had “nothing significant to report” on negotiations; its 28 Jul edition leads with them — the pause itself remains behaviour, with no agreed term behind it. Blockade (Art 4): maintained and enforced through the pause — the LPG carrier Lavine disabled in the Gulf of Oman on 24 Jul after repeated run attempts, two sailors reported killed per Iranian media; the tanker Charminar boarded 25 Jul and released. Hormuz (Art 5): the Tehran table works the strait directly — Iran-Oman delegations met 24–25 Jul on restarting strait traffic — the lead proposal reopening the likely-mined middle passage — with the UK and France offering demining once safe and Iran seeking joint management likely to include fees (Bloomberg); Baghaei claims “progress” while saying strait traffic is unchanged, and ISW records no vessel attacks in the strait since 20 Jul with traffic fallen and deterrence running on the mine threat. The proposal's reported terms (27 Jul): a formal 10-day truce — the strait reopened; the blockade lifted, asset-unfreezing considered — with an Omani regional-consortium design echoing the defunct Clause 5 consultation requirement; Iran is refusing to concede control. Lebanon (Art 1): Mojtaba Khamenei reaffirms Hezbollah's preservation and full Israeli capitulation in Lebanon as the “first condition” for resolving the war under the 17 Jun MoU; the LAF accuses the IDF of hindering the pilot zones (27 Jul) while making its first pilot-zone weapons-cache seizure the same day (undocumented by ISW); Rome expansion talks are set for 4–6 Aug. Contested: the NYT reports Iran rejected the US framework carried by Iraqi PM Zaydi on 23 Jul — no temporary deal leaving Hormuz unresolved — and Zaydi's office denies it on 24 Jul; Pakistani officials say both Washington and Tehran “have responded” to the joint Pakistani-Qatari proposal, content uncharacterised.

Implementation — week 9 · v15

The window (28–31 Jul): the pause ends on Iran's initiative — IRGC ballistic missiles at Muwaffaq Salti Airbase (28 Jul, five intercepted per Jordan; CENTCOM: an “attempted surprise attack”), launched shortly after Iran rejected compromise on strait control (ISW). Hormuz (Art 5): the Omani proposal — reopen the strait against a lifted blockade with asset-unfreezing considered, a regional consortium and voluntary fees — is rejected (a senior official to Reuters, 29 Jul, “unrealistic”); Gharibabadi said on 28 Jul that Iran would go to war for strait sovereignty (per ISW); the IRGC Navy claims three tanker strikes on the southern route, the first strait vessel attacks since 20 Jul; transits run under 10/day (desk series). Blockade (Art 4): stands; Iran's Khatam ol Anbia headquarters had already called it an escalation the armed forces “will respond accordingly” to — the Jordan strike appears to be that response. The proxy front: joint US-Saudi strikes on militia weapons and logistics sites across Iraq and the Iran-Iraq border (28 Jul; retaliation for militia attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure and US interests per ISW; at least four Quds Force officers reported killed in Diyala); Trump promises to hit Iran hard; through ISW's 29 Jul cutoff no resumed US strikes on Iran itself, and no US answer to the Jordan attack. Lebanon (Art 1): carried — the first pilot-zone cache seizure stands (undocumented by ISW); Rome expansion talks 4–6 Aug. Second front: the Houthis threaten expanded attacks on Saudi targets and float Red Sea transit fees; Global21 carries a single-source claim of a ~50-nation Saudi coalition to force Bab el-Mandeb open, announcement expected “next week”; an unattributed drone attack targets a US-owned tanker at Damietta, Egypt (29 Jul) — a Mediterranean first, logged as a vector.

Implementation — week 10 · v16

The window (31 Jul–4 Aug): the suspension stands while both capitals work the corridor design. Strikes: a new attack ordered for the 1–2 Aug weekend (WSJ, 31 Jul) with energy infrastructure under consideration (CBS), then canceled on 1 Aug — Trump citing agreed deal parameters; ISW records no US strike activity in the window. Iran's SNSC vowed to strengthen strait control and close other waterways — “the price will be paid by US citizens and the global economy” — and IRGC-affiliated outlets published a six-country energy-facility target list. Blockade (Art 4): first published enforcement tallies — 45 vessels redirected, two disabled, two boarded since 14 Jul (CENTCOM, 4 Aug). Hormuz (Art 5): Iran's Strait Authority announces no transit permits until US operations end (31 Jul); CENTCOM states the strait remains open; at least four southern-route transits counted in the 31 Jul–1 Aug window; UKMTO projectile incidents 31 Jul (the Gaslog Shanghai), 2 Aug (a failed attack ISW ties to the IRGC Navy) and 3 Aug (a cargo ship in Omani waters). The US-Qatari two-corridor design — inbound Iranian waters, outbound Omani waters, no tolls — is floated 3–4 Aug; Iran counters with monitoring and intervention rights, “service fees,” blockade relief and sanctions relief. Talks (Art 3): Trump announces on 2 Aug that US and Iranian officials will soon meet on the strait and nuclear issues — the first prospective nuclear-file table since the suspension; Baghaei's formal response lands the same day, and the negotiator/IRGC split runs open. Reconstitution (Art 9): Artesh spokesperson Akraminia states on the record that Iran “fully exploited” the MoU and ceasefire to import, repair and produce new systems — including drones already used against US Gulf bases — the reconstitution ISW has assessed since July, now stated by the regime itself; separately, two senior IRGC officers tell the NYT that Quds Force commanders coordinated with Hezbollah, the Houthis and Iraqi militias during the April ceasefire to raise the war's cost, with Reuters carrying eight Iraqi sources on IRGC covert cells in Iraq. Lebanon (Art 1): Rome talks resumed 4–6 Aug on pilot-zone disarmament verification; the LAF seized a Grad-rocket shipment near Aarsal (4 Aug); judiciary authorization for private-property searches is outstanding, which ISW assesses will stall disarmament if unresolved. Second front: the Houthis likely sank the Indian-flagged MSV Faize Noore Oliya near Bab el-Mandeb (4 Aug, one-way naval drone, per India's shipping minister) and hit Najran airport's main radar (4 Aug, Saudi-unconfirmed); the Houthi operations centre denies imposing transit fees (1 Aug); Saudi-Houthi indirect talks run via Omani mediation with the US privately discouraging Saudi retaliation (Bloomberg, 4 Aug); Saudi Red Sea exports run at 3.5mn bpd per the Economist (30 Jul) — the panel-claimed halt is contradicted and carried contested. Iraq: Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Kuwait reportedly warn Baghdad they will strike militias inside Iraq on further attacks (31 Jul); Zaydi orders a joint security committee (1 Aug); the US reportedly withholds ~$30bn of Saddam-era funds pending militia disarmament (2 Aug); the PMF reportedly evacuates its Ninewa headquarters anticipating strikes (2 Aug); Iraqi sources put the 28 Jul strike toll at 20+ PMF members — a wider count than the ≥4 Quds Force officers carried at v15, different reference classes.

05 · Stakeholder map

Actor positions through the Stalemate / Resolution lens.

The Roaring Lion A/B/C framework is the analytical reference: Stalemate ≈ persistent Bad B; Resolution ≈ Good A via JPOA 2.0 + Hormuz Council + Security Guarantee. v15: the US and Iran cells moved on the break and the rejection, the GCC cell on Riyadh's strikes into Iraq. v16: the US and Iran cells move on the cancellation and the talks; the Houthis cell moves on the first Bab el-Mandeb sinking; the GCC cell adds the Iraq warnings and the Saudi-Houthi Oman track.

United States
The US version of the terms — dismantle the nuclear programme, end Axis support — is far harder than Iran’s, so the signed ceasefire sat on an unreconciled core throughout. Trump chose the blockade track on 13–14 Jul, reinstating it against Iranian-flagged shipping, and strikes reached roughly 200km inland by 15 Jul. The campaign then widened past every prior round: three consecutive further strike nights (sixth through eighth) interdicting Iran's internal logistics — the bridges, rail junction and telecoms feeding Bandar Abbas, whose port handles ~85% of Iran's container traffic — plus the IRGC launch infrastructure behind the Gulf-state attacks, and, per Iran's AEOI, the Darkhovin nuclear plant on 19 Jul. Two US service members were killed at Muwaffaq Salti Airbase on 17 Jul and a third in Iraqi Kurdistan on 18 Jul — the first US deaths of the conflict, with no US stand-down following them. Three US officials characterise the strikes as “shaping operations” (Reuters); more F-16s, F-35s and refuelling aircraft are moving to the region, plus additional refuellers to Israel (Axios); WSJ reports a Trump threat against Pickaxe Mountain. US officials also told the WSJ they suspect PRC satellite reconnaissance and Russian locational intelligence are supporting Iranian targeting of US assets. Trump formally notified Congress under the War Powers Resolution on 10 Jul, putting a 60-day clock under the campaign. The pattern this file tracked through four rounds — hardline rhetoric giving way to renewed contact — broke in the fifth: Tehran's suspension landed instead. The 20–23 Jul state holds two paths open at once: Washington is exploring the four-party framework (Axios) while massing forces — Trump played the talks down on 22 Jul, then threatened Iran and the Houthis with “major military punishment” on 23 Jul and told Axios he is close to a decision on expanding strikes — the US “prepared to launch a massive attack”; “They haven't received enough pain yet.” The eleventh and twelfth strike nights reached Parchin, Bushehr Airport, Larak Island and western/north-western Iran; blockade enforcement continues. The two-path state resolved toward the talks on 24 Jul: a White House options meeting weighed expansion, then Trump reportedly ordered a strike hold hours after the Omani delegation reached Tehran — no wave has followed since. The blockade stays and turned lethal at the Lavine (24 Jul, two sailors reported killed per Iranian media; the Charminar boarded 25 Jul and released). Cheung frames the stance as diplomacy-preferred with military options live if Iran attacks allies or strait shipping; Trump says the US “is talking,” tells Axios “deep talks” are under way, and met Netanyahu in Washington (Bloomberg, 28 Jul), telling reporters there is a “good chance” talks with Iran make progress. The Jordan attack ended that posture: Trump promises to hit Iran hard (internal desk record), while the same day's joint strikes with Saudi Arabia on militia sites across Iraq were retaliation for militia attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure and US interests (ISW) — no resumed strikes on Iran itself, and no military response to the Jordan attack, through ISW's 29 Jul cutoff. The blockade stands. The Fed's 29 Jul hawkish hold with no forward guidance put the 30Y through its 2007 high, the war's oil leg cited in July's Treasury selloff. The hard-response posture then ran five days and inverted: a new attack ordered for the 1–2 Aug weekend (WSJ, 31 Jul) with energy infrastructure under consideration (CBS) — “We'll be hitting them very hard… at some point they'll say we just can't take it anymore” (Camp David cabinet meeting); Leavitt: Iran “will continue to pay until they come to the table in, what President Trump deems, a meaningful way” — then canceled on 1 Aug, Trump citing agreed deal parameters, with Axios reporting MBS raised concerns over the plans and the Washington Post a US general's warning that the Pentagon lacks sufficient forces to protect Israel. On 2 Aug he announced upcoming US-Iran talks on the strait and the nuclear file; on 3 Aug he framed the hold — “holding off on a big strike” because “everyone in the region” is “begging for talks.” The blockade stands with its first published tallies (45 redirected, two disabled, two boarded). Papic reads the reversal as domestic political constraint — higher energy costs weighing on midterm polling — rather than negotiating progress. Rubio narrows the immediate ask to the strait (4 Aug, FT), while White House spokesperson Kelly counters that the strait is “completely controlled” by the US Navy and the blockade, with Iran “extremely degraded.” The FT's Washington read has every route out politically fraught under three months from the midterms — Nasr: “Trump is stuck… periodically, he's lashing out.”
Strike ordered, then canceled ·
talks announced
Israel
Citrinowicz: intent intact, capacity to disrupt constrained. A “complete end to the war in Lebanon” is an explicit Iranian red line, so Israel’s Lebanon campaign is a direct obstacle to any settlement; Israel is not a party to the signed Clause 1 and remains in southern Lebanon. Israeli sources quoted by Nadav Eyal expect a prolonged “war between the wars” rather than full resumption, with Israel not wanting the MoU to collapse outright ahead of the 27 Oct elections. There is still no unilateral Israeli strike on Iran. Israel is nonetheless closer to the exchange than in any prior window: it intercepted an Iranian drone near the Syria border (19 Jul), its air defences near Eilat engaged debris from the Aqaba launch, and Defence Minister Katz warned Iran that Israel will re-engage if attacked. On the Lebanon front the Rome-brokered pilot-zones plan moved from structure to implementation — the Lebanese Armed Forces began deploying into the first zones on 16–17 Jul, with the next zone expected at Zawtar al Charqiyeh. Citrinowicz's current read (19 Jul): the greatest challenge is now escalation management — events slipping beyond anyone's control, mediators exhausted and losing leverage, key IRGC figures convinced by the funeral turnout that they have domestic backing to intensify. WSJ (22 Jul): Israel is deliberately sitting the campaign out — the trigger still unfired — while Axios reports the IDF preparing a possible full-scale joint campaign within days and Netanyahu warning that any Iranian attack draws massive strikes. Netanyahu met Trump in Washington as the pause held (Bloomberg, 28 Jul); ISW records no confirmed Israeli strike through its 27 Jul cutoff — Israel still out of the campaign. Friction returned to the Lebanon track — the LAF accuses the IDF of hindering the pilot zones (27 Jul, the second such accusation in a week) — and Mojtaba's “first condition” statement (26 Jul) prices Hezbollah's preservation into any settlement, keeping the Lebanon file the structural obstacle Citrinowicz named. The pilot zones produced their first result the same window: the LAF's first Hezbollah weapons-cache seizure (27 Jul, per Israeli public media, undocumented by ISW), with Rome talks to expand the zones set for 4–6 Aug. Barclays flags an Israeli strike on Iranian sites as a live if unlikely risk ahead of the 27 Oct election; through the window Israel stays out of the campaign and the trigger stays unfired. The ninth window does not displace the read: the ordered strike was canceled, Israel stayed out — Papic notes Iran has refrained from striking Israel, reading the restraint as forcing Israeli compliance with Trump's order to stay out — and Keane's on-record description of a plan that “exceeds everything that we did in Epic Fury” with Israeli participation is an escalation signal, unexecuted. The trigger has still not fired.
Good A/C →
regime change
Iran
Fractured — and the hardline camp is winning the fracture. Iran’s primary Hormuz objective is recognised sovereignty over the strait; it has used force to assert that control repeatedly, striking vessels on the Omani route and retaliating against the Gulf hosts, and on 16 Jul it named the strait an “inviolable red line.” On 18 Jul Tehran formally suspended the MoU — Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei declared Trump's signature “invalid,” Deputy FM Gharibabadi announced the suspension — and the red-line warning became execution: retaliation reached seven countries, adding Saudi Arabia (first strike on Saudi territory in about three months, with sirens at Yanbu), Syria (al Tanf) and southern Jordan (Aqaba), and Kuwaiti power, desalination and oil facilities were struck three days running. The killing of US troops crossed the one line every prior round had observed. The regime is split: Rezaei declares diplomacy over and threatens “full-scale destruction,” while Ghalibaf — branded a traitor by hardliners — defended the talks track on state TV on 16 Jul and a Nour News op-ed still argues for negotiation; Araghchi says some nuclear demands may remain “unresolvable.” Decision-making has its own new structure: Araghchi disclosed a six-person SNSC special committee (himself, Pezeshkian, Ghalibaf, Zolghadr, two unnamed — ISW assesses Vahidi very likely one) making on-the-spot decisions while Mojtaba, severely injured in the strikes that killed his father and unseen in public since, is reportedly hard to reach. Vali Nasr's structural read (FT): the MoU froze a balance of power both sides set out to change, Tehran has concluded restraint invites pressure, and it bets that closing Hormuz — potentially with Bab el-Mandeb and the Red Sea — forces Washington to blink first. In the 20–23 Jul window Iran confirmed receipt of the four-party framework while vowing to “crush the source of US aggression” (Baghaei), put first missiles on Dhahran's King Abdulaziz Air Base, targeted US early-warning radar in Kuwait, and opened a land-trade workaround with Pakistan ($3bn toward $10bn). From 24 Jul Iran wound its attacks down to a single Bahrain strike — and said so: a senior official told Reuters (26 Jul) the halt lasts as long as Washington's does, conveyed directly. The terms are unmoved: officials tell the NYT Iran accepts no temporary deal leaving Hormuz status unresolved, and the reported 23 Jul rejection via the Zaydi channel is carried as contested after his office's denial. The base-casualty campaign that ran to 24 Jul — sleeping quarters at Sheikh Isa, Muwaffaq Salti, al Udeid, Arifjan and Buehring, aimed at building US domestic pressure — stopped with the pause; Aliabadi's “capture and send to hell” threat (24 Jul) stands unexecuted. Mojtaba is reported out of contact “due to certain issues” (Haddad Adel, 25 Jul), extending the incapacitation question over who directs the file. ISW's 28 Jul three-faction map puts the IRGC-Vahidi group — negotiate, but keep total strait control — likely at the wheel, pressed by a Pezeshkian/Araghchi/Ghalibaf camp that differs over means and by the Paydari Front's outright rejection of talks — a small minority with reach through Saeed Jalili on the Supreme National Security Council. The economic floor is sagging under all three: the rial collapsed, US intelligence assessing the regime struggles to pay its forces, and the first mass protest since January — Malekshahr, Esfahan (28 Jul), over the execution of three winter protesters. The rhetoric stays armed through the pause: the Khatam ol Anbia headquarters called the US blockade an escalation the armed forces “will respond accordingly” to (27 Jul), and Gharibabadi says Iran “is not afraid” of acting to establish strait sovereignty, or of the war resuming (28 Jul). The threatened response followed on 28 Jul: the IRGC Aerospace Force fired ballistic missiles at Muwaffaq Salti — ISW assesses Vahidi almost certainly supported the decision, with the pro-negotiations camp possibly backing it too, sharing the strait objective — and on 29 Jul a senior official told Reuters the Omani design is “unrealistic.” The IRGC Navy claims three tanker strikes; regime media claims the “initiative” and tells the US to “accept defeat.” 13D's read that the nuclear issue is “no longer viewed as taboo in Tehran” logs at section 02. Iran seeks PRC air-defence assistance (ISW). The corridor split the regime on the record: negotiators around Araghchi reportedly back the US-Qatari design pending IRGC approval (WSJ, 3 Aug); Baghaei's formal response denies it opens the strait (2 Aug); Fars carries an “informed military source” saying the strait stays closed while US “hostile actions” continue; Rezaei rules out “a second corridor” “under any circumstances” (referent ambiguous per ISW); the Assembly of Experts brands “calls for surrender” an “unforgivable betrayal,” and Paydari parliamentarians prepare impeachment proceedings against Araghchi — while Pezeshkian says all SNSC members backed the MoU and defends staying in post, and Zarif argues the strait is a “bargaining chip” whose leverage decays, warning a prolonged closure could turn China against Iran. A Kharrazi claim that Mojtaba formally warned Pezeshkian against resigning is disputed by the Supreme Leader's own office the next day. Akraminia states Iran “fully exploited” the ceasefire to rearm. Iran's counter-demands on the corridor — monitoring and intervention rights, “service fees,” blockade and sanctions relief — restore the fee ambition the design dropped. Baghaei's second on-record statement (4 Aug, FT) describes provisional “protocols for the future management” of strait traffic covering inbound and outbound routes, framed as Iran-Oman business; the fee position is unmoved — Tehran insists it will eventually charge “service fees.”
Negotiators at the corridor ·
IRGC denies any deal
China
Publicly pushes Resolution (ceasefire, lanes reopened, Xi/Putin Beijing meeting), but the pivot is partly performative — PRC kept sending missile components and fuel precursors during the war. Per Pape, the war already shifted Beijing’s read of US resolve; munitions depletion (FT, Global21) reinforces it. Two new data points this window: US officials told the WSJ they suspect a Chinese reconnaissance satellite is supporting Iranian targeting of US assets — a step past performative neutrality if borne out — and China's state LNG buyers are contracting around the Gulf structurally (Qatari LNG to China down ~98% year on year Apr–Jun; Sinopec and PetroChina exploring 10+ year non-Gulf supply), the first permanent demand-side Gulf de-risking of the war. The intake's China read (Xie, Zakaria; circulated by David for the six-month scenario work): Beijing is absorbing the shock from its ~1.3–1.4bn-barrel reserve rather than cushioning prices for others, imports are down ~3.5–4mn bpd on stockpile draw, and some Hormuz transits reportedly settled in renminbi. Reuters (28 Jul, six sources): Beijing has asked the Houthis to pass its tankers through the Red Sea — one source describing Chinese officials clearing each ship individually — and at least four Saudi-oil cargoes bound for China have transited Bab el-Mandeb since the blockade began, repeating the 2024 arrangement Chinese and Russian diplomats reached with the Houthis in Oman. Self-arranged passage through the second chokepoint extends the absorb-the-shock read. The Atlantic (via David's channel) puts a number on the other half: China abruptly halved oil imports (~5mn bpd, about a quarter of the Hormuz loss) with no visible consumption decline and no explanation the experts can settle — “the most important factor in keeping prices down.” ISW adds that Iran is seeking PRC assistance to rebuild its air defences.
Pushes Resolution
Russia
Aligned with China publicly; has formally offered to take Iran’s HEU (acknowledged by Araghchi, “not currently under discussion”). Accepting HEU under the Security Guarantee architecture would be the technical pathway. Preserves Iran ties privately (drones via Caspian). WSJ (18 Jul): US officials suspect Russia is sharing locational intelligence on US warships and aircraft and advising on drone tactics. Zelenskyy (25 Jul): Russia is supplying satellite imagery of US Gulf bases, with imagery timing aligning to Iranian strikes (four bases surveilled 19–20 Jul); Reuters carries Western officials on “Russian-enhanced” Shaheds in the March CIA-outpost attack. Ukraine struck sanctioned Caspian vessels (25 Jul) that Russia reportedly uses to move military cargo toward Iran.
HEU custodian role available
Houthis / Yemen
The second front has an owner. The blockade of Saudi port calls — declared 20 Jul by spokesman Yahya Saree after two days of warnings to Saudi-owned ships, citing the Saudi siege of Sana'a — is the Houthis' first direct move against Riyadh in this war, and enforcement is calibrated: claimed missile and drone strikes on the Encelia and Layla (22 Jul), one hit confirmed by UK Maritime Trade Operations, a bow fire and no casualties per Saudi state media. Bab el-Mandeb transits fell from 64 to 30 before recovering to 40 by 23 Jul; at least seven vessels diverted and southern-Red-Sea war-risk cover doubled for some carriers.
