The Iranian hand is documented alongside the Houthis' own agenda: Reuters and ISW report a 13 Jul Mahan Air flight into Yemen carrying 10–21 IRGC personnel including senior commanders, missile- and drone-related equipment, training for “new missile systems” and gold to fund operations — diverted to Hudaydah when Saudi-backed forces struck Sanaa airport to block the landing. ISW: the Houthis “pursue their own agenda, but they remain a key Iranian partner,” and the Red Sea expansion serves Iran's campaign objective — degrading US willingness and ability to keep striking, and coercing acceptance of Iranian control over Hormuz. Trump fuses the two: the Houthis are a “Surrogate and/or Proxy of Iran,” and further attacks bring “major military punishment” on both. The stated off-ramp is bilateral — the blockade holds until Saudi Arabia lifts its blockade on Yemeni ports and airports. Enforcement ran through the US-Iran pause: the NCC Masa attacked (24 Jul), missiles at Yanbu intercepted by Greek-operated Saudi defences and munitions impacting Jizan, claimed strikes on the oil-transport corridor feeding the Red Sea hubs (27 Jul) — the Abqaiq fire unclaimed by any actor — while the Saudi coalition struck Hudaydah, Jawf and Marib and the Houthis downed a Saudi Akinci drone. Abdul Salam (24 Jul): the blockade applies to Saudi Arabia alone; ISW records the Houthis resisting Iran's full-closure ask for months, with NYT-cited officials saying that ask returns if Trump strikes Tehran or critical infrastructure. A third claimed attack on Saudi shipping followed: ballistic missiles on the NCC Ghazal (28 Jul, UKMTO-unconfirmed; the vessel left Yanbu on 23 Jul with AIS off). China's tankers pass by arrangement (Reuters, 28 Jul). The Houthis threaten to expand attacks on Saudi targets and, per regional sources (Reuters via ISW), may impose transit fees on commercial shipping in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb — a fee regime to mirror Iran's strait demand. Against them, Global21 carries the claimed ~50-nation Saudi coalition (single-source); the same piece has Houthi retaliation reaching Abha Airport in southern Saudi Arabia after the mid-July Sana'a strikes, and logs claimed East-West Pipeline drone hits. The second chokepoint took its first sinking: the Indian-flagged MSV Faize Noore Oliya likely sunk near Bab el-Mandeb by a one-way naval drone (4 Aug, per India's shipping minister); a drone hit Najran airport's main radar the same day (Saudi-unconfirmed); the IRGC reportedly helped reinforce launch sites overlooking the strait and Hudaydah (3 Aug). The Houthi operations centre formally denies imposing transit fees (1 Aug, answering the 29 Jul Reuters report) — with “authorized vessels” excluding the blockaded Saudi and Israeli ships. Saudi-Houthi indirect talks run via Omani mediation — the Houthis demanding salary payments and the Yemeni-port blockade lifted — with the US privately discouraging Saudi retaliation (Bloomberg, 4 Aug); Riyadh has not struck Yemen since 25 Jul. The Economist puts Saudi Red Sea exports at 3.5mn bpd against 120k pre-war; the export-halt claim from the Mearsheimer panel is contradicted and carried contested. Four ISW editions carry nothing on the claimed ~50-nation coalition.
First sinking at Bab el-Mandeb ·
fees denied, talks via Oman
GCC / Pakistan
Mediation delivered the ceasefire, and all GCC bar Oman reject permanent Iranian control of Hormuz; the bloc’s exposure has widened round by round as Iran coerces the hosts. In 17–19 Jul the bloc absorbed the heaviest and widest round yet: Kuwait's civilian critical infrastructure struck three days running, Saudi territory struck for the first time in months with sirens at Yanbu — the Red Sea terminal now carrying ~4mn bpd, ~60% of pre-war Saudi crude exports, as the Hormuz bypass — and Oman moved from rebuffed mediator to target, with US radar assets on Omani territory struck and Tehran accusing Muscat of yielding to US pressure. Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Qatar condemned the infrastructure strikes and Jordan summoned an Iranian diplomat. The Yemen dimension deepened: Houthi-Saudi cross-border attacks resumed for the first time since 2022, and Reuters reports Iran instructed the Houthis to prepare to close Bab el-Mandeb — which would trap the Yanbu bypass and put Abqaiq, the single upstream node behind it, at the centre of the board. Kuwait is reportedly negotiating an expanded defence pact with Pakistan (Reuters, early stage). A Bloomberg feature flags the ~$3tn Saudi-UAE rivalry for regional capital as a fault line between the two bypass-hosting states. The prepared closure executed this window: a declared blockade of Saudi Red Sea port calls from 20 Jul and claimed strikes on two Saudi tankers on 22 Jul (one UKMTO-confirmed), with transits down 64 to 30 before recovering to 40 and war-risk cover doubling — the full picture is in the Houthis / Yemen row above. Saudi territory took its first Dhahran strike, and the bloc's mediators answered at larger scale: the Qatar/Egypt/Pakistan/Oman framework is the bloc's own product. v14: the bloc's mediators are inside the Hormuz track — Qatar, Pakistan and Egypt involved alongside Oman and the US envoys — while the Saudi front stayed the one front still exchanging fire once the US-Iran pause took hold: Saudi-reported shoot-downs of drones from Iraq aimed at Riyadh and Eastern Province petroleum facilities, the oil-transport corridor claimed struck, coalition strikes into Yemen. Iraq's PM is working Hormuz-bypass pipeline diplomacy — Kirkuk-Tripoli with Beirut (27 Jul), Kirkuk-Ceyhan in Ankara (28 Jul), the decommissioned IPSA line to the Red Sea in Riyadh planned for 30 Jul, outcome unreported — a structural de-risking of the strait. On the drone claims Baghdad pushes back: the Islamic Resistance in Iraq calls them “accusations,” the Iraqi NSA sees “no evidence,” Zaydi orders an investigation, and Iraqi-Saudi high-level talks convened 28 Jul; Jordan intercepted further drones from Iraq on 27–28 Jul. v15: Riyadh crossed a line — joint strikes with the US on militia sites across Iraq (28 Jul), the first Saudi offensive strikes beyond Yemen we have on record, with at least four Quds Force officers reported killed; the Islamic Resistance in Iraq had already vowed to respond “harshly” to any “foolish” Saudi action (27 Jul, ISW), the PMF vows revenge for the strikes (Global21), and Baghdad's investigation into the drone claims now runs alongside open warfare on its territory. Global21's claimed coalition — African Red Sea states agreed, five European navies invited, a ~100k proxy ground force waiting — is carried single-source. v16: the warnings turn forward — Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Kuwait reportedly tell Baghdad they will strike militias inside Iraq on further attacks (31 Jul); Baghdad answers with a joint security committee, desert surveillance and “severe penalties” (1–4 Aug); the PMF reportedly evacuates its Ninewa headquarters; the US reportedly conditions ~$30bn of Saddam-era funds on militia disarmament. Kuwaiti air defences intercept drones on 1 Aug (unclaimed). David's 2 Aug note places the near-term risk at the Saudi-led 14-nation coalition and a Camp David weekend — beside the ~50-nation Global21 claim, still uncorroborated by ISW. The Saudi–Pakistan airspace cross-promise still binds Israeli unilateral action.
Blockaded at Bab el-Mandeb ·
mediation retried
Europe
Aligns with the diplomatic track; refused the US request to reopen the Strait, so it is constrained from leading any post-war architecture. A NATO contribution to the HEU Security Guarantee would be the test. Switzerland hosted the formal ceremony and the first implementation round; the post-war security architecture would sit with other parties. The UK moved first: Trump and PM Burnham agreed on 19 Jul that Britain will take an active role in demining and reopening Hormuz — the first operational European alignment with the reopening effort, alongside the defensive-mandate EU naval presence. The UK and France have offered to lead Hormuz demining once conditions allow, and Hegseth is pressing the UK to host a maritime-security summit on strait traffic (Bloomberg, 27 Jul). Global21's coalition claim has France, Germany, Italy, the UK and the Netherlands invited — warships already in the region, said to await a Washington go-ahead (single-source, unverified).
Diplomatic backer
Japan / Korea
Lean on the US for Resolution; ~60% of energy via Hormuz. The US warned Japan of up-to-two-year Tomahawk delays as the Pentagon prioritises Middle East restocking — US overstretch landing on an Indo-Pacific ally, reinforcing the hedge. Dormant nuclear conversations re-open if the scenario shifts to apex. Capital Economics names Japan, with Pakistan and the Philippines, among the economies most exposed to physical fuel shortage under a dual-chokepoint closure.
Hedging

The 8 Jun – 6 Aug: whipsaw, signing, breakdown, a war with US casualties, a second chokepoint, a mutual pause, the break, and the canceled strike

8–17 Jun
Ceasefire collapses then resolves onto de-escalation: Israeli and US strikes inside Iran (8–10 Jun); Trump declares the deal “complete” (15 Jun); the US and Iran sign the MoU two days early (17 Jun), with signed edits to Clause 1 (Lebanon) and Clause 5 (Hormuz). The blockade lifts and oil sanctions waive on signing.
19 Jun–12 Jul
Implementation, then four escalation rounds of rising scale: the first 60-day-track round at Bürgenstock (21–22 Jun); the Ever Lovely exchange and stand-down (25–30 Jun); the tanker attacks and oil-waiver revocation (6–8 Jul); the ~140-target wave reaching central Iran, five-Gulf-state retaliation, and Iran's rejection of Oman's two-corridor proposal (9–12 Jul). Talks resume at Iran's request (10 Jul) even as Trump maintains the ceasefire is over.
13–16 Jul
The blockade returns (14 Jul), targeted at Iranian-flagged shipping; the 20% fee floats and drops within a day; strikes reach roughly 200km inland (15 Jul); Iran strikes three vessels on the Omani route, retaliates against Kuwait, Bahrain and Jordan, and on 16 Jul declares the strait an “inviolable red line.” The Iran-Oman channel goes quiet; the mediation-breakdown trigger fires (v11).
17 Jul
An Iranian missile attack on Muwaffaq Salti Airbase, Jordan kills two US service members, with one missing — the first US deaths of the conflict. The sixth consecutive US strike night severs the bridges, rail and telecoms feeding Bandar Abbas; Iran strikes a Kuwaiti power-and-desalination plant and, for the first time, near al Tanf in Syria; a Thai-flagged vessel is struck on the Omani route; Kpler counts eight strait transits the prior day. General License X1 expires, revoking all Iranian-oil transaction authority; the MoU's 30-day full-lift deadline passes in breach. Murrin publishes WW3 116, declaring Chapter Two of the war.
18 Jul
Tehran formally suspends the MoU: Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei declares Trump's signature “invalid” and Deputy FM Gharibabadi announces suspension of commitments. The seventh US strike night; Iran fires a ballistic missile at a US base near al Kharj, Saudi Arabia — its first strike on Saudi territory in about three months, with sirens at Yanbu — and hits Kuwaiti power, desalination and oil facilities a second day. Brent settles ~$88, up 4.6%, the biggest weekly advance since April. A third US service member is fatally wounded in Iraqi Kurdistan disposing of ordnance from a downed Iranian drone.
19 Jul
CENTCOM announces the third US death. Iran's AEOI says a US strike hit the Darkhovin nuclear plant in Khuzestan (IAEA: very early construction, no nuclear material at the last inspection). Four ballistic missiles at Aqaba, southern Jordan — a first; Kuwaiti infrastructure hit a third day running. Araghchi disclosed a six-person SNSC committee deciding on the spot while the Supreme Leader is reportedly hard to reach, and says some nuclear demands may remain “unresolvable.” The eighth consecutive US strike night (18 Jul) included the IRGC unit behind the Jordan attack.
20 Jul
The IRGC Navy states its permission regime openly after halting four vessels: “not a single drop of oil, gas, or chemical fertilizer” passes without its coordination. The US moves more F-16s, F-35s and refuellers to the region; Israel's Katz warns Iran that Israel will re-engage if attacked. Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Qatar condemn the infrastructure strikes; Jordan summons an Iranian diplomat; China and Pakistan urge resumed dialogue. The Houthis declare a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia effective immediately (Yahya Saree), citing the Saudi siege of Sana'a; the Qatar/Egypt/Pakistan/Oman written framework circulates, and Iran's FM spokesperson confirms receipt.
21–22 Jul
The eleventh and twelfth consecutive US strike nights reach Bushehr Airport, Larak Island, Behbahan, western and north-western Iran, and the Parchin complex near Tehran. Iran puts first missiles on Dhahran's King Abdulaziz Air Base and strikes US early-warning radar in Kuwait. The Houthi blockade turns kinetic: missile and drone strikes claimed on the Saudi tankers Encelia and Layla (one hit later UKMTO-confirmed), Bab el-Mandeb transits down 64 to 30, an EU Naval Force warning out. Ukraine strikes the Caspian Pipeline Consortium, halting ~1mn bpd of Kazakh flow. Brent settles $88.52 on 21 Jul, the highest since 11 Jun.
23 Jul
Brent settles $100.69, up 7%, after touching $102 — the first settle above $100 since May — on the Red Sea tanker attacks. Trump threatens Iran and the Houthis with “major military punishment” if the attacks continue — the Houthis named a “Surrogate and/or Proxy of Iran” — and tells Axios he may expand strikes (“They haven't received enough pain yet”), squaring the desk digest's “major operation” line. US equities fall (S&P -1.2%, Nasdaq -2.2%, Tesla and Alphabet earnings-day falls compounding) and the 10Y moves through 4.65% to 4.69%. Rubio: Tehran's leadership is “not ready to make a deal” (BBC). Dozens of fighters and refuellers continue deploying; no talks are scheduled on the framework. UKMTO confirms a Saudi-tanker hit; transits recover to 40. Iranian-backed Iraqi militias likely drone Kuwait's Abdali border crossing (material damage, no casualties) with explosions on Bubiyan Island; the IRGC claims a southern-corridor tanker mined — unobserved by ISW. The 13th consecutive US strike night follows into 24 Jul, with missiles reported on Qeshm Island in the strait; the House votes to direct a halt to the campaign, and the Senate blocks a similar measure hours later. [The desk Bloomberg series later puts the day's peak at ~$94 — the print divergence with the AP settle is flagged at section 06.]
24 Jul
Strikes reach northern Iran for the first time (the IRGC Navy commando college in Gilan) as Iran's drone campaign against US base housing runs across Bahrain, Jordan, Qatar and Kuwait. US forces disable the LPG carrier Lavine in the Gulf of Oman — two sailors reported killed per Iranian media — the first deaths in this file's blockade-enforcement record. The NYT reports a 23 Jul Iranian rejection of the US framework carried by Iraqi PM Zaydi; Zaydi's office denies it the same day (24 Jul) — carried as contested. Trump convenes an options meeting, an Omani delegation arrives in Tehran, and a strike hold is reportedly ordered within hours: no overnight wave into 25 Jul, the first pause in 13 nights. Unclaimed airstrikes are reported on Hudaydah.
25–26 Jul
The pause holds on both sides — one Iranian attack (Bahrain) in the first window, then none; Iranian officials say the restraint lasts as long as the US hold does. Iranian and Omani delegations meet in Tehran (24–25 Jul) on a Hormuz agreement; Baghaei claims “progress” (26 Jul) while saying strait traffic is unchanged, and parliamentarians insist control is not returning to pre-war conditions. Pakistani officials say both Washington and Tehran “have responded” to the joint Pakistani-Qatari proposal. CENTCOM boards the Charminar (25 Jul). The Saudi-Houthi exchange runs on: coalition strikes on Hudaydah, Jawf and Marib; Houthi missiles at Yanbu intercepted by Greek-operated defences while munitions impact Jizan; the NCC Masa attacked; a Saudi Akinci drone downed over Jawf. Mojtaba Khamenei is reported out of contact “due to certain issues” (Haddad Adel). A senior Iranian official tells Reuters (26 Jul) Iran will halt attacks as long as the US halts, conveyed directly; Mojtaba's 26 Jul statement names Hezbollah's preservation the “first condition” for resolving the war. Ukraine strikes sanctioned Caspian cargo vessels; Zelenskyy says Russia supplies satellite imagery of US Gulf bases.
27 Jul
Saudi Arabia says it shot down drones from Iraq aimed at Eastern Province petroleum facilities and Riyadh — ISW assesses Iranian-backed Iraqi militias, preserving Tehran's deniability — and a fire burns at Abqaiq, unclaimed by any actor; Saree claims strikes on the oil-transport corridor to the Red Sea hubs. The LAF accuses the IDF of hindering the pilot zones. Bloomberg details the middle-passage proposal — UK/French demining offers, joint management with fees, Witkoff and Kushner involved; Trump tells Axios “deep talks” are under way. Iraq's PM works the bypass-pipeline circuit toward Ankara and Riyadh. A US official and mediators tell Western media the Omani track has tabled a formal 10-day truce — the strait reopened against the blockade lifted and asset-unfreezing considered, a regional consortium proposed for management — and Iran is refusing to concede control. The LAF makes its first pilot-zone weapons-cache seizure (unverified by ISW); the Islamic Resistance in Iraq denies the Saudi drone claims.
28 Jul
Trump meets Netanyahu in Washington and tells reporters there is a “good chance” talks with Iran make progress (Bloomberg). Brent settles $84.09, down 4.8% on the day and roughly 16% over three sessions — the worst run since April 2020 — with WTI at $79.26, CTA Brent length cut to 62% from 73%, and CIBC reading the move as positioning on “MOU 2.0” hopes; Hormuz traffic stays muted with transponders dark. Treasuries rally as oil retreats; swaps price roughly one-in-three odds of a hike at the FOMC, with Citadel Securities and PGIM calling for one and August fed-funds futures open interest at records. Macquarie warns a deal would leave Q4 oversupplied by ~2mn bpd; OPEC+ is expected to pause quota hikes after September. The Houthis claim ballistic missiles on the tanker NCC Ghazal — their third claimed attack on Saudi shipping since 22 Jul (UKMTO-unconfirmed). Reuters: China has asked the Houthis for safe passage for its tankers — one source describes each ship being cleared individually — and at least four Saudi-oil cargoes to China have transited Bab el-Mandeb since 20 Jul. The first mass protest since January in Malekshahr, Esfahan, over the execution of three winter protesters. Iraqi-Saudi talks convene on the drone claims; Rome pilot-zone expansion talks are set for 4–6 Aug.
28–29 Jul · the break
IRGC ballistic missiles target Muwaffaq Salti Airbase in Jordan — an “attempted surprise attack” per CENTCOM, five intercepted per the Jordanian Army — ending the four-day pause shortly after Iran rejects compromise on strait control (ISW). The IRGC Navy claims strikes on three tankers on the southern route. The US and Saudi Arabia jointly strike militia weapons and logistics sites across Iraq and the Iran-Iraq border — retaliation for militia attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure and US interests — with at least four IRGC Quds Force officers reported killed in Diyala. On 29 Jul a senior Iranian official rejects the Omani proposal to Reuters (“unrealistic”); Gharibabadi (28 Jul, per ISW) says Iran would go to war for strait sovereignty; an unattributed drone attack targets a US-owned tanker at Damietta, Egypt; the Houthis float Red Sea transit fees. The Fed holds 9–3 with no forward guidance — the 29 Jul US session sells off (S&P -1.5% to 7,316) with the 30Y through its 2007 high and oil surging; Trump promises to hit Iran hard (internal desk record).
30–31 Jul
The AI leg turns the 30 Jul US session — Microsoft +16%, a record ~$450bn one-day add — while Brent settles ~$88 (desk series; its 23 Jul peak ~$94, the AP divergence flagged at section 06) and the SPR ledger shows 307.6m barrels with ~25m contracted barrels left. Global21 carries the claimed Saudi coalition to force Bab el-Mandeb open (single-source). The Kospi closes a record 18% higher on 31 Jul as the AI trade returns. 13D's WILTW reports “the nuclear issue is no longer viewed as taboo in Tehran” and calls August the most dangerous month.
31 Jul–1 Aug · the canceled strike
WSJ reports Trump ordered a new attack on Iran “as soon as this weekend”; CBS reports energy infrastructure — refineries, power plants — under consideration; Trump at the Camp David cabinet meeting: “We'll be hitting them very hard.” WTI trades above $86 post-settlement. Iran's SNSC vows to strengthen strait control and close other waterways; the Strait Authority announces no transit permits until US operations end; CENTCOM says the strait remains open; UKMTO logs a projectile in the Gaslog Shanghai's engine room off Oman. On 1 Aug Trump says he canceled the strikes on being told deal parameters were agreed — Axios reports MBS raised concerns over the plans; the Washington Post reports a US general warning the Pentagon lacks sufficient forces to protect Israel; ISW records no US strike activity. The NYT carries two senior IRGC officers on Quds Force coordination with Hezbollah, the Houthis and Iraqi militias during the April ceasefire; the Houthi operations centre denies imposing Bab el-Mandeb transit fees. Japan's record ~¥8.45tn single-day yen intervention (30 Jul) is followed by the first joint US-Japan intervention in nearly 30 years (31 Jul, per the FT).
2–3 Aug
Trump announces US and Iranian officials will soon meet on reopening the strait and on nuclear issues (2 Aug). WSJ reports Qatari mediators presented a new reopening proposal with Iranian diplomats responding “positively”; Israeli media report Araghchi agreed to a US-Qatari split-route design — and the same day Baghaei says on the record the proposal “has nothing to do with” opening the strait (the Iran-formal-response trigger fires a third time) while IRGC-affiliated media deny any agreement. Artesh spokesperson Akraminia says Iran “fully exploited” the ceasefire to rearm, including new drones already used against US Gulf bases. On 3 Aug Trump frames the hold — “holding off on a big strike” because “everyone in the region” is “begging for talks”; WSJ reports negotiators support the corridor design but await IRGC approval; Rezaei rules out “a second corridor” (referent ambiguous per ISW); Zarif calls the strait a “bargaining chip” whose leverage decays; the Assembly of Experts brands “calls for surrender” an “unforgivable betrayal.” UKMTO logs further projectile incidents (2–3 Aug). The Mearsheimer panel transcript circulates on David's thread; the Monday session rallies (S&P +1.5% to 7,601) with crude falling.
4–6 Aug
The two-corridor design is detailed — inbound via Iranian waters, outbound via Omani waters, no tolls — and Iranian diplomats counter with monitoring and intervention rights, “service fees,” blockade relief and sanctions relief. CENTCOM publishes its first blockade tallies: 45 vessels redirected, two disabled, two boarded since 14 Jul. The Houthis likely sink the Indian-flagged MSV Faize Noore Oliya near Bab el-Mandeb — the first sinking at the second chokepoint — and hit Najran airport's main radar; Saudi-Houthi indirect talks run via Oman with the US privately discouraging retaliation. Rome talks on the Lebanon pilot zones resume (4–6 Aug). Japan's 10Y auction draws the weakest demand since May 2025; Bessent calls the yen's level a regional problem. The Tuesday session rallies further (S&P +1.8% to 7,737), the desk attributing crude's further fall to Iran confirming reopening talks — a desk attribution with no primary source behind it, flagged. Stavridis publishes the three-path piece (4 Aug); Gary forwards it and David designates it the scenario-stress starting position (5 Aug). Rubio narrows the immediate US ask to the strait — denuclearisation “the ultimate deal” (4 Aug); Baghaei describes provisional inbound/outbound management protocols on the Iran-Oman channel; Bessent predicts Iran may agree “today or tomorrow to open the strait” (CNBC, 4 Aug); the FT has oil easing below $80. The FT synthesis reaches the desk on 6 Aug via Gary, and the yen/JGB leg goes onto the firm's scenario-stress list (per David's 6 Aug note).
What it confirms: the strike order broke on the constraints the file carries — Saudi pushback, force availability, midterm energy costs — and the surviving channel produced the first no-toll design; Iran's counter restored the fee demand within two days. What it does not change: the bifurcated architecture, the apex held in the long-term allocation, the Murrin DD, the Brent bands. Watch-list: Iran-formal-response fires a third time — Baghaei's 2 Aug on-record statement is the Foreign Ministry's formal response to the corridor proposal, a denial that it opens the strait. The signed-deal item registers provisionally on the reported US-Saudi enrichment agreement (~22 Jul, single-source via the Mearsheimer panel; the signed execution of the greenlight WSJ reported at v13; corroboration outstanding). The Israeli-strike trigger stays unfired; nothing new on the Saudi-Pakistan airspace item. To watch: whether the corridor design survives the approval it awaits — the IRGC per ISW, “Tehran's senior leadership” per the FT; whether the announced US-Iran meeting convenes and whether the nuclear file sits on its agenda — Rubio already sequences it behind the strait (“the ultimate deal,” 4 Aug); the fee question inside Iran's counter-demands; the coalition claim, still uncorroborated by four ISW editions; Bab el-Mandeb after the first sinking; and the Lebanon pilot zones — Rome talks 4–6 Aug, judiciary search authorization outstanding. CE publishes a reopening checklist (“Key factors to watch if/when the Strait re-reopens,” 5 Aug, teaser-level on the desk) — to be read against the corridor design when the full report is filed.
The map — the suspension stands, the contest returns to the table

Stalemate stays modal because the US–Iran nuclear divide is wide and the hardliner faction blocks Good A. The ceasefire was a Stage-1 instrument that deferred every core; five escalation rounds of rising scale tested it, and in the fifth Tehran suspended its commitments outright while the exchange produced the first US deaths. The question v11 carried — whether hardline rhetoric again gives way to renewed contact — resolved toward breakdown: Ghalibaf's 16 Jul defence of the talks track was followed within two days by the suspension, and ISW records nothing on the negotiations file. What replaces it as the open question is narrower: whether a successor venue convenes (Qatar, Pakistan and Turkey circulate in intake reporting), and whether the split inside Tehran — a six-person committee deciding while the Supreme Leader is reportedly incapacitated, hardliners demanding revenge, Ghalibaf and Araghchi still holding the negotiation brief — resolves toward a reopened channel. The structural fault ISW identifies — Clause 5 read by Washington as restored passage and by Tehran as affirmed Iranian authority — is the same unresolved question the file has carried since v3, now stated by the primary source. v13 answers the venue half: the framework exists, in writing, with receipt confirmed; what has not happened is a table. The test the window sets is near-term — talks convene on the framework, or the escalation the President threatened on 23 Jul launches. v14 answers it: the talks convened — in Tehran rather than on the four-party text, Hormuz-first, with the US strike hold as the entry condition both sides observed. The narrower open question now is whether a middle-passage agreement can carry the weight assigned to it — the strait file is the same one that broke Clause 5, and Iran's stated term is unchanged: no temporary deal that leaves Hormuz status unresolved. ISW's 28 Jul edition sharpens it: the mediators' truce proposal met Iranian refusal on the strait, with ISW reading the refusal as showing Iran may calculate it can extract the blockade-lift without conceding control. v15: Iran rejected the proposal (a senior official to Reuters, 29 Jul) and ended the pause with the Jordan attack — testing whether it can extract the blockade-lift by force. Two questions are open: whether and where the US responds militarily to the Jordan attack, and whether any channel survives the break — the Pakistani-Qatari proposal is the one both sides still hold under review. v16 answers both: the US response came as an order canceled before it flew, and the surviving channel produced the US-Qatari corridor design with an announced meeting behind it. The open questions now sit inside Tehran — whether the IRGC approves a design its own outlets deny exists, and whether the counter-demands (monitoring rights, service fees, relief) are a negotiating position or the rejection in another form. ISW's read stands: even the inbound leg alone would preserve Iranian gatekeeping over entry to the Gulf.

06 · Market & thematic implications

Scenario views across equities, Brent, rates, and rotation.

Views only. Brent bands and the scenario architecture are unchanged from v12; the second chokepoint stays live at Bab el-Mandeb, and the prints round-tripped the band — $100.69 on 23 Jul to $84.09 on 28 Jul — the desk series puts the 23 Jul peak at ~$94 (divergence flagged below), with ~$88 settled on 30 Jul; v16: crude fell across the 3–4 Aug sessions on the cancellation and the talks — the FT has oil below $80 on 4 Aug, no desk-series settle yet.

ScenarioEquitiesBrentRatesSector & thematic rotation
Stalemate
Modal		 Mid-teens downside; EPS holds until ~2027 demand destruction. The 17 Jul session saw a broad US fall with SPX ending the week -1.5%, about 2% off its highs; Vanda (18 Jul) reads the right tail as “all but disappeared” with positioning still elevated and systematic flows biased down — the modal outcome flat, the skew down. The oil-to-equity transmission has compressed: roughly 1.5% S&P downside per 10% oil rise, versus ~4% in March. The 23 Jul session: Dow -1.0%, S&P -1.2%, Nasdaq -2.2% — oil pressure compounded by Tesla (-14.5%) and Alphabet (-7.1%) earnings-day falls — with European energy outperforming (Shell +1.6%, BP +3.1%) and American and Southwest down 8.4% and 6.2% on fuel bills despite earnings beats (AP). By 27–28 Jul the systematic pressure eased with oil: positioning back to neutral (+0.02 SD, the least crowded since early April), CTA risk ran live into the FOMC and big-tech earnings — ES1 below 7,440 restarts selling, above ~7,530 resumes buying — and Treasuries rallied as oil fell (Vanda). The sessions then split by leg: 29 Jul (FOMC day, the break) S&P -1.5% to 7,316 and Dow -2.2% with energy outperforming in Europe and the FTSE at an intraday all-time high on BP/Shell; the AI leg turned 30 Jul (Microsoft +16%, the biggest one-day dollar add in stock-market history) and the Kospi closed a record 18% higher on 31 Jul. Then three sessions up on the turn: S&P 7,490 (31 Jul), 7,601 (3 Aug), 7,737 (4 Aug), the desk attributing each leg to de-escalation pricing plus AI earnings (Amazon +15.3% on 31 Jul; Korea's July chip exports +178.8%). Tight, elevated, drawing inventory. The prints landed: Brent closed $82.96 on 16 Jul (desk series) and settled ~$88 on 17 Jul per Bloomberg — up 4.6%, the biggest weekly advance since April, on the troop deaths, the Saudi extension and the Axios refueller report — with the front month in backwardation (~-$1.3), the prompt-tightness signature of a strait that has not reopened. Kpler counted eight transits on 16 Jul. SPR 316.5m barrels (10 Jul, lowest since April 1983, ~34m contracted barrels left); total US crude stocks 730.8m, lowest since 1984; US gasoline ~$4.50–4.56. The gas complex has no bypass shield: Asia LNG +94% and TTF +79% versus pre-war. External calls bracket this file's bands — Barclays $65–80 below the floor (carried watch item), Murrin above $150 (his call, logged at section 01), CE +$15–20/bbl on a dual-chokepoint closure. The 21–23 Jul window: Brent settled $88.52 on 21 Jul, $89.75 intraday on 22 Jul, then $100.69 on 23 Jul — up 7%, $102 intraday, highest since May, YTD +62% (AP) — the first settled print inside the $90–110 band, on the Red Sea tanker attacks; three weeks earlier it was below $72. Gasoline prints diverge and are flagged: AAA $4.09 per AP (23 Jul) against the desk monitor's $4.65 AAA series (20 Jul), with the DOE weekly at $4.00; UK gas ~150p/therm from 98p at end-June (BBC). TTF took its first EUR60 handle since March and Asia LNG has doubled versus pre-war; the CPC strike subtracts ~1mn bpd of Kazakh supply outside the Gulf. The dual-chokepoint contingency is partially live: Saudi-flagged traffic is blocked at Bab el-Mandeb while Hormuz runs the IRGC permission regime. Then the round trip: Brent fell ~16% over three sessions to settle $84.09 on 28 Jul (WTI $79.26), the worst run since April 2020, on de-escalation positioning — CTA length 73% → 62% in a day, flow not normalised, dark transits continuing; December futures below $82.30. Macquarie projects a ~2mn bpd Q4 surplus on a deal; OPEC+ is expected to pause quota hikes after a final September increase. CE's Ukraine-drone note quantifies the third subtraction: ~4mn bpd of Russian refining capacity hit, CPC ~1mn bpd halted. v15: the desk Bloomberg series (Signaling Reserve v2.9) puts the 23 Jul peak at ~$94.26 against the AP-reported $100.69 settle — a print divergence: both prints are carried, and the desk series is used for the running ledger — and has ~$88 settled 30 Jul. SPR is 307.6m barrels at 24 Jul, a deepening 43-year low, with ~25m contracted barrels left (~5–6 weeks at the current pace, against an in-house operational-floor estimate near 200m); Hormuz transits run under 10/day. CE (30 Jul) calls the physical market “still dire” and flags a tipping point without a sustained flow recovery; the Atlantic's China piece attributes the price containment to a ~5mn bpd Chinese import halving no one can fully explain. Bands hold. v16: WTI above $86 post-settlement on 31 Jul on the CBS report, then two sessions down into 4 Aug on the cancellation and the talks — the FT has international oil easing below $80 on the 4 Aug session (no desk-series settle yet), with US petrol above $4/gallon, ~35% over pre-war. BCA's $70–100 behavioural range and Papic's $75–100 sit with Barclays' $65–80 below our floor — logged, not adopted; CE flags Bahrain's balance of payments at the brink under the closure, with Saudi or UAE support its base case. The re-closure scenario the market prices as a ~$150 shock remains the near-term, non-nuclear face of the escalation leg. Fiscal pressure lifts yields; energy tightening Jul–Sep adds to the curve. The 10Y sits near 4.60–4.65% (Vanda); CE traces the June rise in the 30-year mortgage rate (6.59%) partly to Iran-driven Treasury yields. The 10Y closed 4.628% on 21 Jul — 2.2bp from the shock monitor's Stage-4 threshold, the war's closest approach — then moved through it on 23 Jul — 4.69%, a one-year high (3.97% pre-war); the 30Y at 5.131%; MOVE back above its pre-war level; Fed-hike odds for the 28–29 Jul meeting jumped to 36% from 12% (CME via AP, 23 Jul), and the ECB held. Into the FOMC (Warsh's second), swaps priced roughly one-in-three for 25bp (28 Jul), Citadel Securities and PGIM called for a hike, August fed-funds futures open interest set records two days running, and a 25bp hike was fully priced by September. Vanda frames the war's rates move as a real-rate shock — the real 2Y near 2%, +112bp since the war's start — with CTAs near max-short the long end; Treasuries rallied 28 Jul as oil retreated, roughly half the prior week's selloff having been oil-driven. The FOMC held 3.50–3.75% (9–3; Logan, Hammack, Kashkari for a hike) with no forward guidance — the 30Y rose through its 2007 high, the 10Y to 4.66%, the 2Y down to 4.23%; September is ~60% priced and December fully priced, with the street split wide (BofA three hikes against Citi three cuts). July's Treasury selloff is attributed in part to the war's oil leg. Dudley (30 Jul): the hawkish-hold press conference lowered short-rate expectations while lifting term premia — the 2Y fell as the 10Y and 30Y rose — with roughly two-thirds odds of a September hike priced. Japan's record ~¥8.45tn single-day yen intervention (30 Jul) was followed by the first joint US-Japan intervention in nearly 30 years (31 Jul, per the FT), the yen closing 157.28; Bessent framed the level as a problem for the whole region (4 Aug), and Japan's 10Y auction drew its weakest demand since May 2025, BOJ-hike odds at 46% for September and above 90% for October. The yen/JGB leg is now tracked at firm level as a scenario-stress item (per David's 6 Aug note): war-driven oil feeds Japanese reflation, JGB yields press the BoJ toward its September meeting, and coordinated intervention holds the line — past rounds funded by selling Treasuries for dollars, this round with the US selling euros and offering lines instead (BCA) — with Japan the largest disclosed foreign holder of Treasuries, so the pressure runs to both bond markets if the loop is not cut. BCA's cyclical fair value for the yen sits near 130 against 157 traded. Iran-axis exposure screens unattractive on the retaliation vectors (UAE data centres, regional fintech, Gulf cable-dependent payments) — Jordan and Oman directly-struck hosts. The screen widens on two fronts: Gulf civilian utilities and energy infrastructure are now realised targets (Kuwait's desalination-dependent water system; the KPC oil facility), and the Red Sea / Bab el-Mandeb vector puts the Yanbu bypass (~4mn bpd, ~60% of pre-war Saudi crude exports) and Abqaiq — the single upstream node behind it — on the board. China's LNG contracting away from Qatar (down ~98% year on year) is the first structural demand-side shift. China sleeve re-rates up on the Beijing read of US weakness; munitions depletion (FT, Global21) is the observable marker. Energy-paradigm shift favours rare earths, security and infrastructure; defensive on regional refining. The undersea-cables / SWIFT non-oil vector carries. Two additions: the Red Sea leg is live risk (war-risk cover pulled on Saudi calls and southern-Red-Sea cover doubled for some carriers on 23 Jul — Reuters; the ~2.5mn bpd Asia-bound Yanbu leg rerouting via the Cape at 10–14 extra days), and a reported IRGC strike on an Amazon data centre in Bahrain (13D, single report) moves Gulf digital infrastructure from screened vector to claimed event. v14 adds: Saudi oil infrastructure inside the screen — the Abqaiq corridor claimed struck and drones on Eastern Province facilities — and, on the other side, Iraq's bypass-pipeline circuit (Kirkuk-Ceyhan, IPSA, Kirkuk-Tripoli) as the structural answer taking shape around the strait. v15 adds: the Mediterranean port vector (the Damietta drone) joins the screen; the claimed coalition puts Red Sea war-risk repricing on both sides of a possible forcing operation; and the Iraq front adds Gulf-adjacent infrastructure (border crossings, pilgrimage routes) to the exposure map. Energy outperformance held through the break (FTSE record on BP/Shell; Total, Eni). v16 adds: Citadel Securities forecasts $500bn+ of further AI-chip debt by 2028 on ~$570bn already absorbed — the financing leg of the AI trade carried as market context; CSIS interceptor inventories (via BCA) put Patriots at 759–827 from 2,330 pre-war and THAAD at 234–278 from 452, the hard series behind the munitions-depletion leg.
Resolution
US-Qatari corridor tabled		 Mid-single-digit upside. Declines toward $90–110 over months; market below the band for most of the deal's life — $82.96–~$88 settled 16–17 Jul, escalation-driven with no Resolution progress behind it, then into the band on the 23 Jul spike — pricing a clean reopening the substance does not support; trust rebuild takes quarters. v14: back below the floor at $84.09, this time on talks optimism, ahead of any agreement from the Tehran table. v15: ~$88 settled 30 Jul after the rejection, still below the floor. v16: crude fell across the 3–4 Aug sessions on the cancellation and the talks, ahead of any agreed term. Yields ease as the energy premium unwinds. Iran-axis exposure screens better selectively; the energy/renewables opportunity set persists on the structural energy-paradigm shift; the China sleeve recalibrates on a firmer Hormuz-access outcome.

Apex / tail: escalation toward $130–160+ Brent is held in the long-term allocation; first-use ($200+, SPX ~3,500) sits below the scenario-modelling threshold as structural tail protection. The deal's re-timing of this tail to the 60-day window is itself suspended as of 18 Jul, so the window is open-ended; the HEU stays in Iran, hardened, and unmentioned in this window's exchanges. The Darkhovin strike is the first kinetic touch on the nuclear file this cycle — an early-construction site with no nuclear material at the last IAEA inspection — and Murrin's $150+ call sits inside this leg as his conviction, ahead of the file's own. Two proliferation-adjacent data enter the log: WSJ reports Washington will greenlight a 30-year US-Saudi civil nuclear agreement potentially permitting Saudi enrichment, and the Pickaxe Mountain chatter extends to unattributed tactical-nuclear talk (13D) — both logged, neither carried. A third enters at v14: the NYT-reported US intelligence read on Mojtaba's weapon interest, against Albright's degraded-programme assessment — logged and not carried. v15 logs two more, neither carried: 13D's “the nuclear issue is no longer viewed as taboo in Tehran… the IRGC is spear-heading a new strategic doctrine” (WILTW, 30 Jul, full text on file — including a reported debate on NPT withdrawal), and Barclays' last-option framing of a strike on the Isfahan HEU stockpile or Pickaxe Mountain. v16 logs one more, not carried: the Mearsheimer-panel report of a US-Saudi enrichment agreement signed around 22 Jul without fullest IAEA inspection rights — the signed execution of the greenlight WSJ reported at v13, single-source here; the signed-deal watch item registers provisionally pending corroboration. The Taiwan-war and US-default extrapolations are held as backdrop only, outside the modelled set.

The $300bn in the signed terms is external Gulf investment funded by sanctions relief — not a US Treasury outlay — which reconciles the terms with Iran’s frozen-asset demand; the relief flows through GCC capital.

Resolution mechanics

The Resolution path follows the framework David specified: Mearsheimer’s “humble pie” off-ramp; a JPOA 2.0 nuclear architecture; the Ferguson Hormuz Council (Iran as Chair, a 45% / 30% / balance revenue split, transit fees at cost); HEU export under a Security Guarantee with Russia available as custodian; and a post-war Gulf Treaty Organisation with China and Russia as signatories. The realised Stage-1 MOU diverged from the Council mechanic on Hormuz — toll-free reopening under Iranian and Omani management rather than a chaired revenue split — and the deeper cores (HEU ~440kg, enrichment, sanctions sequencing) remained for the 60-day track. Bremmer's independent framing of the eventual off-ramp — institutionalised, divided Iranian management funded by a Gulf collective, on the Bosphorus or Malacca model — carries as a variant of the deferred mechanism. ISW's 18 Jul assessment put the primary source behind the fault line: the two sides interpreted Clause 5 in fundamentally different ways — Washington as a return to pre-war passage, Tehran as affirmation of Iranian authority with safe passage only through Iran's traffic-separation scheme — and that the divergence contributed to the collapse; the Gulf states rejected Iranian management and fees. Nasr's structural read runs the same direction from the Iranian side: the MoU froze a balance of power both parties set out to change, so the return to war is deliberate policy rather than a misreading of terms. With the track suspended from 18 Jul and Oman then compromised as a channel, the mechanics carried as the reference for whatever venue resumed them — Qatar, Pakistan and Turkey circulated in intake reporting as candidates, none convened through v13. The four-party framework is the first written variant of the deferred mechanism to reach the desk: dual-lane reopening with the fee question posed as Malacca-style Iranian service fees or an IMO-administered fund — the sovereignty-versus-fees question the file has carried since v3, now in proposal text. The Tehran table is working a second variant: reopening the likely-mined middle passage under a joint management system likely to include fees, with UK/French demining offered and the Witkoff/Kushner channel inside the room — the first negotiation since the collapse to put the strait itself first in sequence. Oman's regional-consortium proposal (ISW, 28 Jul) is a third variant — regional management echoing the defunct MoU's consultation clause, the nearest design yet to the Council mechanic — tabled inside a 10-day-truce frame Iran is so far refusing on the control question. Its voluntary-fee predecessor was itself refused: Iran rejected Oman's early-July donations design and maintained its demand to levy fees (WSJ via ISW, 2 Jul). The consortium variant is rejected too (a senior official to Reuters, 29 Jul, “unrealistic”) — every management design short of recognised Iranian control and levied fees has now been refused — answering the sovereignty question this file has carried open since v3. The mechanics stay as the reference for whatever channel survives; the Pakistani-Qatari proposal is the one both sides still hold under review. A fourth variant is on the table at v16: the US-Qatari two-corridor design — inbound through Iranian waters, outbound through Omani waters, no tolls — the first to drop the fee mechanism entirely rather than restructure it; Iran's counter (monitoring and intervention rights, “service fees,” blockade and sanctions relief) restores the fee demand and adds an enforcement role. Stavridis's dual-key prediction — Iran northbound, Oman southbound — is this design's shape, and his 60% renewed-negotiations path carries it; Mearsheimer's year-end expectation of a renegotiated MoU on terms worse for the US than 17 Jun is the same destination read from the withdrawal side. BCA's toll read — some vessels paying some form of toll to Iran as the most likely outcome — prices Iran's counter rather than the no-toll design. The mechanics stay as the reference for the announced meeting.

v17 · The corridor stalls in Tehran; reparations enter the terms · 11 Aug 2026
Architecture, verdict & Brent bands held · US, Iran, Houthi and GCC chips flipped · Resolution tier US-Qatari corridor tabled → Corridor stalled in Tehran · Iran-formal-response fires a fourth time · Rezaei to the SNSC · reparations demanded on both sides · Aramco's Jizan refinery struck · Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan defence pact · Brent ~$88

The architecture holds — Stalemate (modal) / Resolution (corridor stalled in Tehran) / apex in the long-term allocation. The corridor design v16 carried as tabled has not moved past Tehran's approval — Khamenei has not signed off (AP), and the IRGC is holding the draft to extract fees, traffic-control language and sanctions relief (WSJ). The week stacked preconditions in front of it: Zolghadr's six demands, his replacement at the SNSC by the hardliner Rezaei a day later, reparations demanded on both sides, and Araghchi's on-record refusal of direct talks — the fourth Iran-formal-response firing — leaving the meeting announced on 2 Aug unconvened. Brent priced the stall, ending near $88 on 10 Aug (Bloomberg), just under the $90–110 floor. Four chips move; the Resolution tier moves to Corridor stalled in Tehran; the verdict and the bands hold.

What moved from v16:

  • The corridor stalls on approval: two regional officials tell the AP (5 Aug) that Khamenei has not approved the draft Iran-Oman agreement, against Axios's 4 Aug report of leadership approval; regional mediators tell the WSJ (via ISW, 7 Aug) the IRGC is holding up the latest draft to extract more explicit Iranian traffic-management language, transit fees and blockade/sanctions-relief assurances, a mediator telling Axios the SNSC is reviewing the text. ISW's factional read: all three Iranian camps agree Iran must keep a level of strait control — the dispute is over tactics — and the negotiation rounds have run without the IRGC in the room, while low-level officials hold the domestic line that Iran negotiates only with Oman.
  • The fee mechanism is back: an IRGC-affiliated source (6 Aug, via ISW) describes inbound transit through Iranian waters and outbound through Omani waters for a “certain period,” then a central route with Iran managing entrances — carrying “insurance, fueling, and environmental fees” — and four industry sources tell Reuters the deal gives Iran “control” over inbound shipping; a Saudi “senior source” says the same day the agreement carries no transit fees or service charges. Fars publishes draft terms barring US, Israeli and “hostile” vessels outright — Israel-linked cargo banned, damage-causers barred until compensated, penalties up to 20% of cargo value (7 Aug, via Bloomberg). A 10 Aug Bloomberg headline — the Oman deal “covers fees for maritime services” — reached the desk headline-level.
  • Six demands, then a hardliner to the SNSC: Zolghadr conditions reopening on six US concessions (8 Aug), including lifting the naval blockade and sanctions, withdrawing forces from around Iran, paying war reparations, releasing frozen assets and ceasing attacks on Iran's regional allies. Khamenei replaces him the next day with Mohsen Rezaei, demoting Zolghadr to political adviser. ISW places Rezaei in the anti-concessions faction: willing to negotiate to lock in strait control and a US withdrawal, unwilling to trade what Iran's attacks have won — his own 3 Aug premise. Parliament Deputy Speaker Babai (9 Aug): Iran will attack “any country that wants to assist the United States” in restoring navigation.
  • The trigger fires a fourth time: Araghchi on the record (9 Aug, Reuters): Iran will not engage in talks with the US while it is in violation of the June MoU; the Iran-Oman track is in “final stages” but will not reopen the strait. The meeting Trump announced on 2 Aug has not convened; messages run through intermediaries.
  • Reparations enter the terms on both sides: Iranian officials tie reopening directly to compensation — Baghaei: “its reopening is contingent on the US ceasing its illegal actions, lifting the siege and compensating for damages” — with the signed Article 6 $300bn fund the textual hook. Trump answers with his own (10 Aug): compensation for roadside-bomb deaths and “hundreds of thousands of innocent protestors,” expanded shortly after to damages to Lebanon, Syria, Yemen and Gaza, put “firmly into any, and all, future negotiations,” while insisting compensation “was never mentioned in any of our negotiations or meetings.” Bloomberg's read: the hardening on both sides makes an immediate Hormuz pact unlikely.
  • The US posture turns economic: Trump signals restraint (Axios, 9 Aug) — “We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation… We are low-keying it” — and told reporters the next day that the strait is “open now” and US-controlled, leaving escalation rhetorical (“you'll find out,” 10 Aug). The pressure is visible in flow: the FT reports no crude loaded at Kharg Island for at least a week, tankers unable to return from Asia and storage constrained, with Pezeshkian conceding costlier import routes; the US Treasury adds shadow-banking sanctions (7 Aug). ISW's read: the costs have not yet moved the dominant faction off its maximalist position — and Citrinowicz (10 Aug, via Gary) argues they will not alone: Iran's record under pressure is absorption, and when cornered, escalation.
  • The Saudi front widens and arms: a Houthi drone strikes Saudi Aramco's Jizan refinery (8 Aug, fire confirmed by the Saudi Energy Ministry — at least the second blaze at the complex in a month); Iraqi militias reportedly planned “imminent” attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure coordinated with the IRGC and the Houthis, paused via Badr-leader Ameri's mediation under Iraqi deployments a security source calls “unprecedented” (ISW corroborates only a few); Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan sign a joint defence agreement (7 Aug) with a collective-defence provision, on top of the 2025 Saudi-Pakistan pact that already has 8,000 Pakistani troops in the kingdom. The Houthis also hit Najran province (11 civilians wounded) and Marib City (~20 ballistic missiles, at least two killed), and an Iranian missile strikes a UAE state-oil-company tanker in the strait (8 Aug, no casualties).
  • Chips flip: US “Strike ordered, then canceled · talks announced” → “Reparations demanded · 'low-keying it'.” Iran “Negotiators at the corridor · IRGC denies any deal” → “Rezaei to the SNSC · reopening tied to reparations.” Houthis “First sinking at Bab el-Mandeb · fees denied, talks via Oman” → “Jizan refinery struck · militia coordination reported.” GCC “Blockaded at Bab el-Mandeb · mediation retried” → “Defence pact with Turkey-Pakistan · militia attacks paused via Baghdad.” The Resolution tier moves US-Qatari corridor tabled → Corridor stalled in Tehran.
  • Prints: Brent rose about 5% on the 10 Aug session to end near $88 (Bloomberg), extending a rally of more than 5% over the prior three sessions — re-approaching the $90–110 floor from below; European diesel futures up more than 10% on the refinery attacks; no desk-series settle reached the desk. The S&P drifted off the 4 Aug high — 7,724 (5 Aug), 7,710 (6 Aug) — then closed 7,753 on 10 Aug, off 0.1% as yields and crude jumped on the reparations demands; the Topix advanced intraday on 11 Aug with crude firm, the desk report citing rekindled inflation worries.
  • A third chokepoint vector logs: a Straits Times synthesis (Eyal, Chairman-forwarded) reports drones — “almost certainly launched by pro-Iranian militias based in Iraq” — have struck shipping near the Suez Canal, alongside the Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb pattern, with up to 45% of seaborne trade affected across four contested waterways. Logged as a vector; the Suez leg has no primary corroboration on the desk.

The scenario architecture, the verdict on Murrin Article 2, the Brent bands and the apex placement are unchanged.

Bottom line · the corridor stalls in Tehran; reparations enter the terms

The scenario set stays bifurcated: Stalemate (modal) and Resolution (corridor stalled in Tehran), with the apex tail held in the long-term allocation below the scenario-modelling threshold. Tehran has not approved the US-Qatari corridor design — the IRGC is extracting fees, traffic-control language and sanctions relief — and both sides added reparations demands while the meeting announced on 2 Aug went unconvened: Khamenei put the hardliner Rezaei over the security council, and Araghchi refused direct talks on the record, the trigger's fourth firing. The blockade is biting — Kharg Island a week without loading crude (FT) — and Brent ended near $88 on 10 Aug, just under the $90–110 floor. Murrin’s Article 2 nuclear scenario remains the analytical foundation under structural tail protection. Full scenario stances, drivers, equity and Brent views are in section 03.

01 · Due Diligence on Murrin

Verdict unchanged — cannot rule it out. WW3 117's call for total war is his own advocacy; his checkable claims hold.

Capabilities corroborated (Tier 1); interpretive layers held as hypotheses (Tier 2); the policy conclusion treated as advocacy (Tier 3). The full claim-by-claim verifiability table sits in the v1 tab.

Murrin’s capabilities case is sound and OSINT-sourced. Timeline sits at the aggressive end of a 6–12 month band that overlaps Roaring Lion’s own assessment. The preemptive-nuclear-use conclusion is his advocacy. The Gallant “440 Kilograms” piece restates the ~440kg 60% HEU stockpile that anchors the capabilities case, and ISW, citing five US-intelligence sources via CNN, reports Iran is physically hardening that stockpile — collapsing tunnels and mining storage entrances to defeat any seizure — so the fissile core is intact, deferred, and being entrenched. Iran agreed to readmit IAEA inspectors, the first forward step on the nuclear file; it is not down-blending. That step has stalled: the inspection access is unresolved, with Grossi expecting entry while Iran ties it to a final deal and sanctions relief, and Tehran then suspended the MoU outright on 18 Jul — the US-Iran meeting announced on 2 Aug is the first prospective nuclear-file table since; that table has not convened — Araghchi ruled out direct talks on 9 Aug while the US remains “in violation” of the text. The ~440kg core stays inside Iran behind the entrenched tunnels. “Cannot rule out the nuclear scenario” holds as the analytical foundation; the apex is handled via the long-term allocation rather than modelled scenarios.

WW3 117 — the total-war call, graded

“WW3 117: Trump's Watershed Moment in Recognising a Common Autocratic Enemy” (28 Jul; reached the desk an hour after the v14 send) is Murrin's escalation call. The frame is a single integrated struggle — Ukraine, the Middle East and a coming Indo-Pacific theatre against one autocratic axis — hung on Senator Graham's funeral as the catalyst, and it concludes that Trump “has only one choice” — total war with Iran alongside Israel. It moves nothing in the architecture, the bands or the verdict.

ClaimTierChecked againstOur read
One integrated war. The regional wars are a single struggle against a shared autocratic axis; the fires merge. Interpretive BCA's Gertken (29 Jul, same intake) models the opposite as his base case: the wars stay separate on US political-will limits, Russia's two-front aversion and China's external constraints — with a Hormuz oil shock the tail that merges them. Pape frames the same linkages as read-through. The couplings themselves are documented on this desk: shared munitions strain, chokepoint tactics, Russian satellite targeting support. A live dispute between tracked sources. The file carries the wars as coupled through observable channels without adopting the single-war frame; the Graham-funeral catalyst is narrative. Gertken's own tail condition — an oil shock that kills demand — is the same transmission this file holds in the escalation legs.
“Iran's control of the strait remains unchallenged” after ~1,000 US strikes. Corroborated ISW's 26 Jul key assessment: the strikes have “likely failed to meaningfully affect” Iran's pursuit of strait control. Barclays (28 Jul): degradation achieved, “nothing that will meaningfully impact the IRGC's strategic calculus”; transits 3–6/day. Corroborated by both primary trackers — the third consecutive piece whose checkable core lands on ISW's own assessment. His ~1,000-strike figure matches ISW's count for the phase.
Axis logistics. The Caspian vessel strike, Russian satellite targeting for Iran, and Geran drones refitted with Chinese jet engines flowing back to Iran. Interpretive Ukraine's Caspian strikes on sanctioned vessels and Zelensky's satellite-imagery statements are already on this file (ISW, 25–26 Jul). The Chinese-engine transfer leg is his “believed to be,” unsourced; ISW separately reports Iran seeking PRC air-defence assistance. The component facts are carried from primary sources; the engine-transfer leg is uncorroborated; assembling them into one axis supply system is his frame. Held as a hypothesis, consistent with the WW3 116 treatment of the China-Russia claim.
Trump's “only one choice” — total war with Iran alongside Israel. Advocacy A prescription. The observable record at the cutoff is narrower: no US military response to the Jordan attack had followed, the day's joint US-Saudi strikes in Iraq retaliated for militia attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure and US interests, and Trump's promise to hit Iran hard is unexecuted against Iran itself; Israel remains out of the campaign. His conviction, kept in quotation — the same total-war advocacy graded at WW3 116 and Essential Lessons. The durable adjacent question is his interceptor-depletion cross-reference, already CSIS-corroborated in this file.

WW3 116, “The Battle for the Strait is On, so Prepare for Escalation” (17 Jul), is the tracked author's read of the current exchange. Murrin declares “Chapter Two” of the war — an existential contest for the strait and the Red Sea sea lanes that in his framing ends only with a victor and a vanquished. It is commentary rather than reporting: twenty-four distinct claims with no primary text of his own behind them, and the two that carry real weight are corroborated from outside the piece. Four of his headline claims have nothing on this desk that tests them either way.

ClaimTierChecked againstOur read
The MoU. An appeasement dwarfing Chamberlain's, and in full form it would have destroyed US maritime hegemony at a stroke. Interpretive The signed 14-point text is on file. ISW (18 Jul) attributes the collapse to divergent readings of Clause 5 — Iran reading it as affirming Iranian authority over the strait, Washington expecting pre-war traffic conditions. Corroborated at the level of mechanism: Clause 5 is where the deal failed, the leg he identified on signing day from the published clauses. The Chamberlain scaling and the hegemony conclusion are his register and carry no checkable content.
Breakout. The IRGC used the pause to repair and replenish while moving closer to a weapon day by day. Advocacy The IAEA puts the stockpile at 441kg of 60% HEU as of June 2025; ISW, citing US intelligence via CNN, reports it being physically hardened in tunnels. Nothing on the desk tests imminence. Retention and hardening are corroborated and stand independently of him. The imminence claim is his third dated one and carries no enrichment figure, no breakout estimate and no date, so it cannot be tested on its own terms. Timing stays at the aggressive end of the 6–12 month band.
Total war. An existential contest for the shipping lanes, resolved only with a victor and a vanquished; America should commit to defeating the IRGC with overwhelming firepower. Advocacy A prescription. No source is offered and nothing on the desk bears on it. Reported as his conviction and kept in quotation. The escalation direction is consistent with the 6–19 Jul record. The grand-strategy prescription carries no falsifiable content.
Trump's resolve. Hardened: the midterm gas-price motive is dead on poor ratings, and he reads Iran as having acted in bad faith. Interpretive The “scum” remark is on the record from the Ankara NATO summit and already carried here. Tehran suspended the MoU on 18 Jul. No polling has reached the desk. The hardening direction is consistent with the observable sequence. The popularity leg is asserted without a pollster and is not carried. His own oil call runs against it — a print above $150 would restore the gas-price motive he argues is dead.
Assassination plot. A reported IRGC plot against Trump, passed via Israeli intelligence, corroborated by the Secret Service switching him back to the older Air Force One, and possibly the decisive factor driving him to destroy the IRGC. Interpretive A single unnamed Israeli-intelligence channel, hedged by Murrin himself. The aircraft switch is asserted without source and is unverified here, including the donor state of the aircraft he names. Uncorroborated on this desk. That the switch evidences the plot is his inference rather than anyone's report. The escalation-driver conclusion rests on that unverified chain plus a psychological read of Trump.
China and Russia. Iran fights on with their approval, confirmed by supplies flowing into its replenishment; US strikes on supply-route bridges acknowledge it. Interpretive ISW (17–18 Jul) confirms strikes on bridges, roads, a tunnel and telecoms around Bandar Abbas, a senior US official (WSJ, 17 Jul) describing the aim as disrupting supply routes to the city — routes ISW describes as Iran's own interior-to-coast logistics. ISW separately assesses the PRC and Russia are likely supporting Iranian targeting, citing a PRC reconnaissance satellite, Russian geolocation of US warships and aircraft, and Russian drone tactics. Both component facts are corroborated; joining them is his. What ISW documents is targeting intelligence, and no source on the desk reports Chinese or Russian materiel entering Iran. Held as a hypothesis.
Interceptor stocks. Every month of war consumes US holdings of PAC-3, THAAD and SM-3. Corroborated CSIS (Cancian and Park, 30 May 2026): PAC-3 MSE runs at roughly 650 a year with half going to allies, against a US decade-average buy of 225; the 3,203 Patriots requested for FY2027 first deliver May 2029. THAAD runs at 96 a year against an 857-interceptor request first delivering mid-2029. Both sit in the slowest three-plus-year replacement tier. Corroborated for two of his three named systems, from a defence-budget source rather than a strategic commentator. SM-3 is excluded: CSIS records less use than ground-launched systems and attributes the lag to small past orders and 36–39 month lead times. The monthly-burn framing is not how CSIS measures it, and the piece predates three further escalation rounds.
Who gains. Depletion benefits Moscow, leaving Ukraine exposed as PAC-3 stocks fall, and benefits Beijing more still by raising first-strike confidence before US stocks recover. Interpretive CSIS documents the allocation friction — THAAD deliveries re-sequenced away from allies, Japan's Tomahawks possibly delayed, Ukraine Patriots pushed back in the queue — and states the depleted inventories created a window of vulnerability in the Western Pacific. It contests the conclusion: demonstrated US combat experience against a PLA with none may preserve deterrence until inventories are restored. It says nothing about Russia benefiting. The queue and the Western Pacific window are corroborated in the source's own words, stronger support than he offers himself. The further step — that Moscow and Beijing are prolonging the conflict for this reason — has no support on the desk.
Mobile launchers. The hard target, rather than the underground missile cities; the fix is compressing the kill chain with persistent armed ISR striking within minutes. Advocacy Self-labelled house conjecture. The only adjacent datum is one unelaborated Reuters line (three US officials, 16 Jul) describing recent strikes as “shaping operations.” Every missile-related strike ISW reports in the window is a fixed site — the Lar launch site, the Yazd Missile Base, Konarak airbase. No in-window evidence of the shift in either direction. One detail runs the other way: the 116 downed telecom towers and the strike on the Radio and Communications Regulatory Authority degrade Iran's control of its own Shahed drones, which is fixed-infrastructure suppression.
Order of battle. 135 MQ-9s, 18 RQ-4s, roughly 50 MQ-4C Tritons and an operational RQ-180 for that mission, with the binding constraint numerical — “not dozens but hundreds” of platforms. Interpretive No independent check on the desk. Every figure is asserted without source, and no coverage modelling sits behind the hundreds. Not carried, consistent with the numeric record in his work — 300kg and 460kg for the same HEU stock inside one article, “Fatyie Ii” for the Fattah-2, a moving SPR figure. The RQ-180 entry is the exception and is credited: he hedges it as classified and unconfirmed. The mass-over-sophistication constraint is sound in kind; the figure is illustrative.
The Ukraine model. The 250km strike-drone campaign that largely isolated Crimea by land transfers to Hormuz — drones from the Omani Peninsula interdicting Iran's coastal batteries. Advocacy The Crimea-isolation premise is stated flatly and unsourced. Nothing on the desk tests the 250km radius or the Omani basing proposition. Prescription. ISW's own Hormuz mechanic cuts against the payoff — a single successful attack, or the persistent threat of one, deters transits — so suppressing launchers need not restore traffic. Logged, not carried.
Bab el-Mandeb. Yemeni sources report the Houthis preparing to close it with al-Shabaab, holding closure in reserve as their own asset; the strait carries 10–12% of seaborne trade, and simultaneous disruption with Hormuz would exceed any modern maritime crisis. Interpretive A closure vector is independently reported (Reuters, 16 Jul), reaching this desk inside the Capital Economics note rather than read directly, and on a different causal account: Iran instructing the Houthis conditional on US strikes against Iranian power plants. ISW's 17 Jul edition carries no Yemen, Houthi, Bab el-Mandeb or al-Shabaab content at all. Bremmer and Barclays both attribute Houthi behaviour to a payments dispute with Riyadh. The trade share is asserted without source; Capital Economics instead quantifies the consequence at roughly 4mn bpd rerouted via Yanbu and +$15–20/bbl on a dual closure. The vector is live and the Sanaa-airport leg is already on this file. His account of agency — a Houthi-owned asset held in reserve, largely independent of Tehran — is not the account our sources give. The al-Shabaab coordination and drone-transfer legs are uncorroborated rather than contradicted, resting on unnamed sourcing alone. The consequence arithmetic is usable; the trade share is not carried. v13: the blockade landed 20 Jul on the Houthis' own Sana'a-siege grievance — a datum for his agency read — but Reuters and ISW report a 13 Jul flight carrying IRGC commanders, missile equipment and gold into Yemen, and ISW's read (“their own agenda… a key Iranian partner”) lands between his account and the instruction account; the scope, Saudi-flagged vessels and Saudi port calls, is narrower than the full closure he sketches. v14: Houthi negotiator Abdul Salam states the blockade applies to Saudi Arabia alone (24 Jul), and ISW records the Houthis resisting Iran's request to close the strait fully for several months — both closer to his reserve-asset read — while NYT-cited officials say Iran would seek full closure if Trump strikes Tehran or critical infrastructure.
Oil above $150. A surge in the weeks ahead as risk premia rise, with significant pressure on government bond markets. Advocacy $150 sits inside the $130–160+ escalation band this file already holds. Brent settled around $88 on 17 Jul. Barclays' $65–80 range is the genuine out-of-band divergence. The bond call names no market, tenor, level or horizon. The level is inside our own range. He carries $150 as a base expectation within weeks; this file holds it as a tail. No supply-outage volume or trigger level is given and the horizon has not elapsed, so the call is logged unscored. His section heading asserting oil is set to rocket higher overstates his own hedged text. v14: the fortnight since has run a round trip — $100.69 settled 23 Jul, then the worst three-day fall since April 2020 to $84.09 on 28 Jul. No $150 print; the call tracks against, with his “weeks ahead” horizon not fully elapsed. Still unscored. v15: two weeks on, the peak is $100.69 on the AP settle and ~$94 on the desk series (23 Jul; divergence flagged at section 06), with Brent at ~$88 — the call tracks against on either series. v16: crude fell across the 3–4 Aug sessions on the cancellation and the talks announcement, the FT putting oil below $80 on 4 Aug — three weeks on from the piece, no print has approached $150 on either series. v17: the 10 Aug session put Brent back near $88 (Bloomberg) as reopening hopes dimmed — the rally re-approaches the $90–110 floor from below and stays far from $150.

Track record — prior calls against the 20 May to 20 Jul record

The capability, structure and chokepoint calls have held, and three of them are now working assumptions in this file. Timing and agency are where he fails, consistently and across every piece. The rows below are not independent trials — the Israel-trigger thesis recurs in four pieces and is entered once, and several draw on the same escalation sequence — so this reads as a map of where he is reliable rather than a hit rate. Unfalsifiable framing and advocacy carrying no forecast content are excluded, as is a 2024 Lebanon ground-campaign piece re-stamped 29 May 2026 and circulated as current with its body text never revised.

His quantities do not travel into our text without independent confirmation. His timelines and his assignment of agency to Israel have failed repeatedly across the file.

Essential Lessons Part I — the retrospective, graded

“Essential Lessons from the Iran Conflict — Part I: Strategic Realities” (Murrinations, 21 Jul; reached the desk 26 Jul via Gary) is Murrin grading the war he has covered since WW3 112. It is doctrine — seven lessons and five predictions, one of them dated only as “inevitable.” The checkable lessons land close to sources this file already holds. It moves nothing in the architecture, the bands or the verdict. A Part II on operational lessons is flagged and will be read when it arrives.

02 · Scenario test

Live tail risk on a 6–12 month horizon — below the scenario-modelling threshold.

The conclusion is unchanged; the operational decision is to bear this tail in the long-term allocation rather than model it.

The apex first-use event is paradigm-break, so protection is structural rather than model-derived. As David noted, “in short, I probably don’t need to know what the damage would look like.” The deal did not lower the tail — it re-timed it, and with Tehran's 18 Jul suspension the 60-day track is no longer running, so the apex window is open-ended rather than deadline-bound; the placement is insensitive to that timing — the tail sits in the long-term allocation either way. Ten windows of armed exchange since late June have all stayed conventional, with the ~440kg HEU core unmentioned in any of them — intact, deferred, and being physically hardened inside Iran. The tenth window (5–10 Aug) holds the pattern: no US strikes on Iran through ISW's 9 Aug cutoff, the exchange running through the blockade, the strait and the Saudi front; the nuclear-file table announced on 2 Aug has not convened, and the week's new preconditions — six demands, then reparations on both sides — sit in front of the strait question that itself sits in front of the nuclear one. Rubio's sequencing stands: denuclearisation “the ultimate deal,” the strait the immediate one (4 Aug, FT). What stays in the long-term allocation is the nightmare convergence — nuclear Iran + reinvigorated Russia + hedging China + exhausted America + isolated Israel arriving together as oil buffers run dry; Murrin Article 3’s late-stage US-decline thesis sits on the “exhausted America” leg as backdrop conviction, with the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve at 307.6m barrels (24 Jul), the lowest since April 1983, monitored daily at the tip-of-iceberg layer. The window-by-window record is in the timeline and the prior tabs; the proliferation-adjacent log is at section 06.

Verdict

Murrin Article 2 cannot be ruled out and remains a live tail risk on a 6–12 month horizon. The apex probability sits below the threshold where another modelled scenario would change the prescription. Israeli unilateral action remains the most plausible trigger — unfired through ten windows, with Israel deliberately sitting the campaign out (WSJ) and the strait and the Lebanon front the live channels an escalation would run through; the armed exchanges under and since the MoU show the deal can turn kinetic through Hormuz directly, at rising stakes, without displacing that read. The ninth and tenth windows keep Israel out — the one Israeli strike in the window is a drone on a Lebanese Army bulldozer in Tyre District (7 Aug) — and the trigger stays unfired.
