External cross-check — Stavridis's three paths (4 Aug) · per David, the starting position for the scenario-stress work

Admiral Stavridis (Carlyle Compass, 4 Aug; via Gary, 5 Aug) weights three US paths: significant drawdown ~10%, major escalation ~30%, renewed negotiations backed by measured pressure ~60%. The 60% path lands where this file's Resolution track sits, and his predicted most-likely outcome — a dual-key reopening with Iran controlling northbound transit and Oman the southbound route — is structurally the US-Qatari corridor design tabled at v16 — stalled in Tehran as of v17 (section 03); the fee and international-law frictions he flags as the residue are where Iran's 4 Aug counter-demands landed. His 30% escalation path — strikes on economic targets at 300–500+ per 24-hour cycle, an initial ~30,000 ground troops to secure the strait, an all-out Iranian response against Gulf energy — maps onto the escalation leg this file holds in the $130–160+ band; the 10% drawdown path is unmodelled here and sits nearest Mearsheimer's withdrawal expectation. His inputs run close to the file's own: Iran at ~65% combat-power loss yet retaining the missile, drone, small-craft and mine capability that threatens shipping; US and Israeli interceptor and precision-munitions depletion against substantial residual combat power (~60,000 troops, two carrier strike groups); Tehran having banked regime survival, $25bn in unfrozen assets and the proposed $300bn fund from the initial ceasefire — his figures for the Article 11 and Article 6 terms. He dates Trump's posture from 3 Aug: “holding off on a big strike” because “everyone in the region” is “begging for talks.” One structural read runs beyond the window: strait control as a depreciating asset for Tehran, the energy system adapting away from the chokepoint over several years — the corridors thesis David's 2 Aug piece argues from the infrastructure side. Per David (5 Aug), the piece is the starting position for the firm's scenario-stress work, to be incorporated across the 14-point-MoU, oil-shock, SPR and Murrin streams.

04 · The signed MoU

What the text says — the milestone, Article by Article.

The 14-point text Bloomberg published on 16 June and the version a senior US official read aloud on signing (17 Jun); the Article text below is verbatim from those primary publications. Tehran announced on 18 Jul it is suspending its commitments under this text; the table is carried as the reference for whatever track resumes, with the implementation boxes tracking how each obligation has executed and reversed.

ArticleText (close paraphrase)Our reading
1 · Ceasefire Immediate and permanent end to the war on all fronts including Lebanon; no hostile actions; refrain from the threat or use of force; the final agreement confirms this. Signed edit: a Lebanese-sovereignty guarantee was added. Contested — Iran reads it as obliging an Israeli withdrawal; Israel is not a signatory and keeps striking. The one clause advancing: the Lebanese Armed Forces began deploying into the Rome-brokered pilot zones on 16–17 Jul.
2 · Sovereignty Both parties respect each other’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and refrain from interfering in internal affairs. Implicitly constrains US regime-change; the IRGC structure survives. Iran also leans on this to frame “managing” Hormuz as an internal affair.
3 · 60-day window Negotiate and reach a final agreement within a maximum of 60 days, extendable by mutual consent. The clock for every deferred core. Suspended by Tehran on 18 Jul at roughly the window's halfway mark: Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei declared the signature “invalid” and Deputy FM Gharibabadi announced Iran is suspending its commitments. Neither side has formally withdrawn from the text itself.
4 · US obligations Immediate: lift the naval blockade, prevent interference against Iran, restore traffic within 30 days to pre-war capacity proportional to Iran’s pre-war volume. US withdraws forces from surrounding areas within 30 days after the final agreement. Asymmetry: the blockade lifts at once, but force withdrawal waits on the final agreement. Signed term tested and reversed: the US reinstated the blockade on 14 Jul, targeted at Iranian-flagged vessels and Iranian cargo. Enforcement turned kinetic in July — by 16 Jul three vessels redirected, one disabled, the Curacao-flagged M/T Wen Yao boarded by the 11th MEU off Duqm — and CENTCOM's first published tallies (4 Aug) put the totals since 14 Jul at 45 vessels redirected, two disabled and two boarded. The 30-day full-traffic-restoration deadline passed in breach on 17 Jul. The FT reports (7 Aug, via ISW) no crude loaded at Kharg Island for at least a week and tankers unable to return after unloading in Asia; Pezeshkian concedes the blockade has forced costlier import routes.
5 · Iran obligations (Hormuz) Immediate: resume merchant shipping in the Gulf / Sea of Oman within 30 days to pre-war volume, removing technical obstacles and neutralising mines. Signed edit: a joint Iranian-Omani administration and a 60-day toll bar were added. Iran’s win — the text does not bar Iran from “managing” the strait. Tested and unresolved: Oman’s own two-corridor proposal was rejected by Iran on 12 Jul, and shipping avoids the Omani route despite US escorts. The IRGC Navy now states the regime openly — “not a single drop of oil, gas, or chemical fertilizer” passes without its coordination and permission — and a Thai-flagged vessel was struck on the southern route on 17 Jul. Iran's Environmental Protection Agency floated UNCLOS-based “environmental services” fees on 18 Jul, a new variant of the fee ambition.
6 · $300bn development US and regional partners build a rehabilitation and development plan financing at least $300bn; the implementation mechanism is set within 60 days. External Gulf money, not a US outlay (Trump: “no money changes hands”; Reuters: no US government funds). Gulf-funded, routing the financing into the Gulf-state track. The Article is now the reparations hook: Iranian officials tie reopening to compensation, Trump insists compensation “was never mentioned in any of our negotiations or meetings,” and the signed text's $300bn “rehabilitation and economic development” fund — its implementation mechanism due within 60 days of signing — is the clause both readings run through (Bloomberg, 11 Aug).
7 · Sanctions US commits to ending all sanctions — UNSC resolutions, IAEA Board resolutions, all unilateral US primary and secondary sanctions — on a schedule set in the final agreement. Exceeds the JCPOA’s scope in principle, but the schedule is deferred to the final agreement. Signed term tested in the other direction: the US Treasury added over 50 sanctions targets on 14–15 Jul (the Shamkhani network, IRGC procurement) — new sanctions rather than the wind-down the Article commits to.
8 · Nuclear Iran reiterates it will never produce nuclear weapons; the fate of enriched material and all nuclear-related issues, including Iran’s “nuclear needs,” is “adequately addressed” in the final agreement. A restatement of Iran’s standing position. The version read aloud on signing adds on-site down-blending under IAEA supervision as the baseline method — gated to the final agreement and cutting against Iran’s simultaneous hardening of its HEU tunnels. The ~440kg core stays in Iran through the window. The file was touched kinetically for the first time in the 17–19 Jul window: Iran's AEOI says a 19 Jul US strike hit the Darkhovin plant in Khuzestan (IAEA: very early construction, no nuclear material found at its last inspection). Araghchi said on 19 Jul that some nuclear demands may remain “unresolvable.”
9 · Status quo Pending the final agreement, Iran holds the status quo on its nuclear programme and the US imposes no new sanctions and does not strengthen its forces in the region. The strategic freeze: Iran’s programme stays intact while US leverage is capped. The most consequential clause for the deferral read. Both halves are now in breach — new US sanctions landed 14–15 Jul, and more F-16s, F-35s and refuellers are moving to the region.
10 · Oil waivers US Treasury issues waivers immediately after signing for Iranian crude, petrochemicals and derivatives, and related services (banking, insurance, transport). Signed edit tested: the waiver was revoked on 8 Jul — the first rollback of a core MoU economic term. The wind-down completed on 17 Jul: General License X1 expired, revoking all Iranian-oil transaction authority.
11 · Frozen assets Frozen and restricted Iranian funds released and made fully available in line with negotiation progress, directed by the Central Bank of Iran. Sequenced to negotiation progress — Iran’s leverage-extraction path. Vance conditions release on “verified steps” on the HEU; Vahidi insists the funds are not barred from military spending.
12 · Implementation A mechanism to oversee implementation and the commitment to the final agreement. Compliance architecture with no specified membership, voting or enforcement — to be designed in 60 days.
13 · Sequencing gate Nuclear negotiations begin only after Iran receives assurances on the implementation of Articles 4, 5, 10 and 11 (blockade, Hormuz, oil waivers, frozen assets); talks then address only the remaining articles. Iran’s verification gate — it can delay the nuclear talks by contesting any of those four implementations. The Article 10 revocation and the blockade's 14 Jul return each gave Iran grounds to invoke it. The 18 Jul suspension goes past the gate: rather than invoking Article 13 to pause the nuclear talks, Tehran suspended its commitments across the text.
14 · UNSC ratification The final agreement is approved through a binding UN Security Council resolution. China and Russia become structural guarantors — neither the US nor Israel can unilaterally exit the final deal without a UNSC crisis. Iran’s durability anchor.
Implementation — weeks 1–5 (carried)

The week-by-week implementation record through 16 Jul — the two-way first week, the kinetic second, the tanker attacks and waiver revocation of the third, the central-Iran strikes and Muscat rejection of the fourth, and the blockade's return in the fifth — is carried in the v7–v11 tabs. The through-line: each week tested a different Article, and by week five a core term (Article 4) had formally reversed.

Implementation — week 6 · v12

The window (Art 3): Tehran suspended its MoU commitments on 18 Jul — Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei declared Trump's signature “invalid,” Deputy FM Gharibabadi announced the suspension, and Rezaei said diplomacy and negotiations “are over,” while Ghalibaf (16 Jul, state TV) and a Nour News op-ed (18 Jul) still argued for the talks track. ISW's negotiations section for the window: “nothing significant to report.” Casualties: two US service members killed at Muwaffaq Salti Airbase, Jordan (17 Jul, ascribed to the IRGC); a third killed in Iraqi Kurdistan (18 Jul); US toll 17 since 28 Feb. Blockade (Art 4): enforcement kinetic — three vessels redirected, one disabled, the M/T Wen Yao boarded; General License X1 expired 17 Jul, completing the Article 10 reversal; the 30-day full-lift deadline passed in breach the same day. Hormuz (Art 5): the IRGC Navy's permission regime stated openly; a Thai-flagged vessel struck 17 Jul; Kpler counted eight transits on 16 Jul; UNCLOS-based “environmental services” fees floated. Strikes: sixth, seventh and eighth consecutive US nights (16–18 Jul) — Bandar Abbas bridges, rail and telecoms severed, Chabahar, Oghab 44, and the IRGC launch infrastructure behind the Gulf-state attacks; three US officials call them “shaping operations.” Retaliation: seven countries — Kuwait (power, desalination and oil facilities struck three days running), Bahrain, Qatar, Oman (US radar assets on the Salamah Archipelago and Ghanem Island), Saudi Arabia (al Kharj missile, sirens at Yanbu), Syria (al Tanf) and Jordan (Muwaffaq Salti, then four missiles at Aqaba on 19 Jul). Nuclear (Art 8): the AEOI says a US strike hit the Darkhovin plant (19 Jul); Araghchi calls some nuclear demands possibly “unresolvable.” Leadership: Araghchi disclosed a six-person SNSC special committee making on-the-spot decisions while Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei — severely injured in the strikes that killed his father — is reportedly hard to reach; ISW assesses Vahidi very likely a member. Yemen: Reuters (16 Jul, single root source) reports Iran instructed the Houthis to prepare to close Bab el-Mandeb if the US strikes Iranian power plants; Houthi-Saudi cross-border attacks resumed for the first time since 2022. Lebanon (Art 1): the LAF began deploying into the pilot zones 16–17 Jul — the one obligation moving forward.

Implementation — week 7 · v13

The window (20–23 Jul): the suspension holds — ISW's negotiations section still reads “nothing significant to report” — while a four-party written framework (Qatar, Egypt, Pakistan, Oman, ~20 Jul) revives the June interim agreement's shape: a 10-day ceasefire, both Hormuz lanes reopened (southern free of Iranian attack, northern free of US blockade), and the fee question posed as Malacca-style Iranian service fees or an IMO-administered fund. Iran confirmed receipt; no talks are scheduled. Second chokepoint: the Houthis blockaded Saudi Red Sea port calls from 20 Jul, citing the Saudi siege of Sana'a, and struck the Encelia and Layla on 22 Jul (one hit UKMTO-confirmed); Bab el-Mandeb transits fell 64 to 30, recovering to 40 by 23 Jul, with at least seven diversions and an EU Naval Force warning. Strikes: the eleventh and twelfth consecutive US nights reached Bushehr Airport, Larak Island, Behbahan (the IRGC 15th Special Forces Brigade base), western and north-western Iran, and the Parchin complex near Tehran; Iran struck Dhahran's King Abdulaziz Air Base (a first), US early-warning radar in Kuwait (an AN/FPS-117), Jordanian bases and Aqaba. Workarounds: Iran-Pakistan trade to expand from $3bn toward $10bn with five-fold truck traffic — the land answer to the naval blockade. Posture (23 Jul): Trump threatened Iran and the Houthis with “major military punishment” and told Axios he may expand strikes (“They haven't received enough pain yet”); equities fell and the 10Y hit a one-year high; dozens of fighters and refuellers continue moving to the region. Axis widening: Iranian-backed Iraqi militias likely droned Kuwait's Abdali border crossing on 23 Jul — the first Axis attack on a regional border crossing since 11 Jul — with explosions reported on Bubiyan Island; the IRGC claims a southern-corridor tanker struck a naval mine, a claim ISW cannot observe and reads as deterrence messaging against the Omani route.

Implementation — week 8 · v14

The window (24–28 Jul): the suspension stands on paper while both sides stop shooting — no US strikes in Iran after 24 Jul (the first pause in 13 nights), Iranian attacks ending with a single Bahrain strike in the first window, and a senior Iranian official telling Reuters (26 Jul) the halt lasts as long as Washington's does, conveyed directly. ISW's 27 Jul edition had “nothing significant to report” on negotiations; its 28 Jul edition leads with them — the pause itself remains behaviour, with no agreed term behind it. Blockade (Art 4): maintained and enforced through the pause — the LPG carrier Lavine disabled in the Gulf of Oman on 24 Jul after repeated run attempts, two sailors reported killed per Iranian media; the tanker Charminar boarded 25 Jul and released. Hormuz (Art 5): the Tehran table works the strait directly — Iran-Oman delegations met 24–25 Jul on restarting strait traffic — the lead proposal reopening the likely-mined middle passage — with the UK and France offering demining once safe and Iran seeking joint management likely to include fees (Bloomberg); Baghaei claims “progress” while saying strait traffic is unchanged, and ISW records no vessel attacks in the strait since 20 Jul with traffic fallen and deterrence running on the mine threat. The proposal's reported terms (27 Jul): a formal 10-day truce — the strait reopened; the blockade lifted, asset-unfreezing considered — with an Omani regional-consortium design echoing the defunct Clause 5 consultation requirement; Iran is refusing to concede control. Lebanon (Art 1): Mojtaba Khamenei reaffirms Hezbollah's preservation and full Israeli capitulation in Lebanon as the “first condition” for resolving the war under the 17 Jun MoU; the LAF accuses the IDF of hindering the pilot zones (27 Jul) while making its first pilot-zone weapons-cache seizure the same day (undocumented by ISW); Rome expansion talks are set for 4–6 Aug. Contested: the NYT reports Iran rejected the US framework carried by Iraqi PM Zaydi on 23 Jul — no temporary deal leaving Hormuz unresolved — and Zaydi's office denies it on 24 Jul; Pakistani officials say both Washington and Tehran “have responded” to the joint Pakistani-Qatari proposal, content uncharacterised.

Implementation — week 9 · v15

The window (28–31 Jul): the pause ends on Iran's initiative — IRGC ballistic missiles at Muwaffaq Salti Airbase (28 Jul, five intercepted per Jordan; CENTCOM: an “attempted surprise attack”), launched shortly after Iran rejected compromise on strait control (ISW). Hormuz (Art 5): the Omani proposal — reopen the strait against a lifted blockade with asset-unfreezing considered, a regional consortium and voluntary fees — is rejected (a senior official to Reuters, 29 Jul, “unrealistic”); Gharibabadi said on 28 Jul that Iran would go to war for strait sovereignty (per ISW); the IRGC Navy claims three tanker strikes on the southern route, the first strait vessel attacks since 20 Jul; transits run under 10/day (desk series). Blockade (Art 4): stands; Iran's Khatam ol Anbia headquarters had already called it an escalation the armed forces “will respond accordingly” to — the Jordan strike appears to be that response. The proxy front: joint US-Saudi strikes on militia weapons and logistics sites across Iraq and the Iran-Iraq border (28 Jul; retaliation for militia attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure and US interests per ISW; at least four Quds Force officers reported killed in Diyala); Trump promises to hit Iran hard; through ISW's 29 Jul cutoff no resumed US strikes on Iran itself, and no US answer to the Jordan attack. Lebanon (Art 1): carried — the first pilot-zone cache seizure stands (undocumented by ISW); Rome expansion talks 4–6 Aug. Second front: the Houthis threaten expanded attacks on Saudi targets and float Red Sea transit fees; Global21 carries a single-source claim of a ~50-nation Saudi coalition to force Bab el-Mandeb open, announcement expected “next week”; an unattributed drone attack targets a US-owned tanker at Damietta, Egypt (29 Jul) — a Mediterranean first, logged as a vector.

Implementation — week 10 · v16

The window (31 Jul–4 Aug): the suspension stands while both capitals work the corridor design. Strikes: a new attack ordered for the 1–2 Aug weekend (WSJ, 31 Jul) with energy infrastructure under consideration (CBS), then canceled on 1 Aug — Trump citing agreed deal parameters; ISW records no US strike activity in the window. Iran's SNSC vowed to strengthen strait control and close other waterways — “the price will be paid by US citizens and the global economy” — and IRGC-affiliated outlets published a six-country energy-facility target list. Blockade (Art 4): first published enforcement tallies — 45 vessels redirected, two disabled, two boarded since 14 Jul (CENTCOM, 4 Aug). Hormuz (Art 5): Iran's Strait Authority announces no transit permits until US operations end (31 Jul); CENTCOM states the strait remains open; at least four southern-route transits counted in the 31 Jul–1 Aug window; UKMTO projectile incidents 31 Jul (the Gaslog Shanghai), 2 Aug (a failed attack ISW ties to the IRGC Navy) and 3 Aug (a cargo ship in Omani waters). The US-Qatari two-corridor design — inbound Iranian waters, outbound Omani waters, no tolls — is floated 3–4 Aug; Iran counters with monitoring and intervention rights, “service fees,” blockade relief and sanctions relief. Talks (Art 3): Trump announces on 2 Aug that US and Iranian officials will soon meet on the strait and nuclear issues — the first prospective nuclear-file table since the suspension; Baghaei's formal response lands the same day, and the negotiator/IRGC split runs open. Reconstitution (Art 9): Artesh spokesperson Akraminia states on the record that Iran “fully exploited” the MoU and ceasefire to import, repair and produce new systems — including drones already used against US Gulf bases — the reconstitution ISW has assessed since July, now stated by the regime itself; separately, two senior IRGC officers tell the NYT that Quds Force commanders coordinated with Hezbollah, the Houthis and Iraqi militias during the April ceasefire to raise the war's cost, with Reuters carrying eight Iraqi sources on IRGC covert cells in Iraq. Lebanon (Art 1): Rome talks resumed 4–6 Aug on pilot-zone disarmament verification; the LAF seized a Grad-rocket shipment near Aarsal (4 Aug); judiciary authorization for private-property searches is outstanding, which ISW assesses will stall disarmament if unresolved. Second front: the Houthis likely sank the Indian-flagged MSV Faize Noore Oliya near Bab el-Mandeb (4 Aug, one-way naval drone, per India's shipping minister) and hit Najran airport's main radar (4 Aug, Saudi-unconfirmed); the Houthi operations centre denies imposing transit fees (1 Aug); Saudi-Houthi indirect talks run via Omani mediation with the US privately discouraging Saudi retaliation (Bloomberg, 4 Aug); Saudi Red Sea exports run at 3.5mn bpd per the Economist (30 Jul) — the panel-claimed halt is contradicted and carried contested. Iraq: Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Kuwait reportedly warn Baghdad they will strike militias inside Iraq on further attacks (31 Jul); Zaydi orders a joint security committee (1 Aug); the US reportedly withholds ~$30bn of Saddam-era funds pending militia disarmament (2 Aug); the PMF reportedly evacuates its Ninewa headquarters anticipating strikes (2 Aug); Iraqi sources put the 28 Jul strike toll at 20+ PMF members — a wider count than the ≥4 Quds Force officers carried at v15, different reference classes.

Implementation — week 11 · v17

The window (5–10 Aug): the suspension stands; the corridor design waits on Tehran. Talks (Art 3): the meeting announced on 2 Aug has not convened — Araghchi on the record (9 Aug): no talks with the US while it is “in violation” of the MoU, the Iran-Oman track in “final stages” but not reopening the strait; Zolghadr conditions reopening on six US concessions (8 Aug); Khamenei replaces him at the SNSC with Rezaei (9 Aug). Blockade (Art 4): enforced and visible in flow — the FT reports no crude loaded at Kharg Island for at least a week, tankers unable to return from Asia, storage constrained; Pezeshkian concedes costlier import routes; the US Treasury adds shadow-banking sanctions (7 Aug), central bank governor Hemmati calling them contradictory to Bessent's deal talk. Hormuz (Art 5): an Iranian missile strikes a UAE state-oil-company tanker (8 Aug, no casualties); UKMTO reports two explosions heard from a vessel in Omani waters (5 Aug); a Qatari-linked LNG carrier attacked in the strait reaches the desk as a delayed 10 Aug report, headline-level; Trump claims the strait is “open now” and US-controlled (10 Aug). Reparations (Art 6): Iran ties reopening to compensation; Trump counters with his own demands and denies compensation was ever discussed — the signed $300bn fund is the clause in contest. Second front: a Houthi drone strikes Aramco's Jizan refinery (8 Aug, fire confirmed; at least the second blaze in a month), an attack in Najran province wounds 11, and Marib City takes ~20 ballistic missiles (at least two killed); the Iraqi militias' planned IRGC- and Houthi-coordinated strikes on Saudi energy infrastructure pause via Ameri's mediation under Iraqi deployments described as “unprecedented” (ISW corroborates only a few); the Houthis reportedly run a coordination headquarters from a Kataib Hezbollah stronghold south of Baghdad. Alliances: Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan sign a joint defence agreement with a collective-defence provision (7 Aug). Lebanon (Art 1): the Rome round produces a tentative shortlist of countries to verify pilot-zone disarmament, the US to approve the final pick; direct negotiations resume 1 Sep; an Israeli drone strikes an LAF bulldozer in Tyre District (7 Aug, one soldier wounded). Workarounds: Lebanese ministers convene (10 Aug) on an Iraq-Syria-Lebanon overland oil route to Tripoli — per ISW no near-term alternative to Hormuz, and exposed to ISIS attack in Syria.

05 · Stakeholder map

Actor positions through the Stalemate / Resolution lens.

The Roaring Lion A/B/C framework is the analytical reference: Stalemate ≈ persistent Bad B; Resolution ≈ Good A via JPOA 2.0 + Hormuz Council + Security Guarantee. v17 moves the US, Iran, Houthi and GCC cells. Each cell carries the current position and its load-bearing points; the version-by-version record is in the prior tabs.

United States
The US terms — dismantle the nuclear programme, end Axis support — remain far harder than Iran's; the posture has run from ordered strike to cancellation to announced talks to economic pressure inside two weeks.
  • The posture is now economic: “We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation… We are low-keying it” (Axios, 9 Aug); no US strikes on Iran since 24 Jul; the blockade stands (45 vessels redirected, two disabled, two boarded per CENTCOM) with fresh shadow-banking sanctions (7 Aug), and Kharg Island a week without loading crude (FT). Trump told reporters the strait is “open now” and US-controlled, leaving escalation rhetorical (“you'll find out,” 10 Aug).
  • The reparations counter (10 Aug): compensation for roadside-bomb deaths and Iran's protest dead, expanded to Lebanon, Syria, Yemen and Gaza, put “firmly into any, and all, future negotiations” — Bloomberg reading the hardening on both sides as closing the window on a quick pact. Bessent's “today or tomorrow” prediction (4 Aug) did not land.
  • The canceled strike and the unconvened table: the attack ordered for the 1–2 Aug weekend (WSJ) was canceled on 1 Aug — Saudi pushback (Axios), a Pentagon force-availability warning (Washington Post) — and the US-Iran meeting announced on 2 Aug has not convened. Rubio narrows the immediate ask to the strait, denuclearisation “the ultimate deal” (4 Aug, FT).
  • The constraint reads: Papic — midterm energy costs, not negotiating progress, drove the reversal; Nasr — “Trump is stuck… periodically, he's lashing out”; the War Powers 60-day clock runs from 10 Jul. US officials suspect PRC satellite reconnaissance and Russian locational intelligence behind Iranian targeting (WSJ).
Reparations demanded ·
“low-keying it”
Israel
Citrinowicz's four dimensions hold: intent intact; capacity to disrupt constrained; the objective deeper than Good A; the trigger window opens as a deal closes.
  • The trigger has not fired: no unilateral Israeli strike through ten windows — Israel is deliberately sitting the campaign out (WSJ) while the IDF prepares options; Keane's on-record description of a plan that “exceeds everything that we did in Epic Fury” is an escalation signal, unexecuted; Barclays flags an Israeli strike as a live if unlikely risk ahead of the 27 Oct election. Papic reads Iran's own restraint — it has refrained from striking Israel — as forcing Israeli compliance with Trump's order to stay out. The tenth window's one Israeli strike is a drone on an LAF bulldozer in Tyre District (7 Aug, one soldier wounded).
  • The Lebanon file stays the structural obstacle: a “complete end to the war in Lebanon” is an explicit Iranian red line and Hezbollah's preservation is Mojtaba's stated “first condition”; the Rome track produced a tentative shortlist of countries to verify pilot-zone disarmament, with direct negotiations resuming 1 Sep.
  • Iran's conditions run through Israel: Netanyahu rejected the US-backed mediators' Gaza proposal (9 Aug, per Bloomberg) — one of the demands Iran attaches to reopening that Washington cannot deliver alone.
Good A/C →
regime change
Iran
Fractured — and the hardline camp is winning the fracture. The objective is recognised sovereignty over the strait, asserted by force through every window.
  • The corridor stalls from inside: Khamenei has not approved the draft (AP); the IRGC extracts — explicit traffic-control language, fees, blockade/sanctions relief (WSJ); the SNSC reviews the text (a mediator to Axios); IRGC-affiliated media describe a toll-bearing variant while negotiators around Araghchi reportedly back the design pending IRGC approval.
  • The SNSC changes hands: Rezaei — anti-concessions per ISW, on his own premise that Iran's attacks have pushed the US back and trading that away would be unwise — replaces Zolghadr the day after his six-demand list (blockade, sanctions, forces, frozen assets, war reparations, attacks on Iran's allies).
  • The formal line hardens: Araghchi on the record (9 Aug): no talks with the US while it is “in violation” of the June MoU — the trigger's fourth firing — with the Iran-Oman track “final stages”; Babai threatens any country assisting the US; reopening is tied to reparations, the siege lifted and “illegal actions” ceased (Baghaei). Force runs at the margins: a UAE state-oil-company tanker struck (8 Aug), explosions heard in Omani waters (5 Aug).
  • The factional map (ISW): the IRGC-Vahidi anti-concessions line likely guiding policy; the Pezeshkian/Araghchi/Ghalibaf camp differing over means; the Paydari Front against talks entirely — the Assembly of Experts branding “calls for surrender” an “unforgivable betrayal,” Paydari parliamentarians preparing impeachment proceedings against Araghchi. Zarif warns the strait's leverage decays and a prolonged closure could turn China against Iran.
  • The structure underneath: Nasr — the MoU froze a balance of power both sides set out to change, so the return to war is policy; the economic floor is sagging (the rial collapsed, US intelligence assesses the regime struggles to pay its forces, the first mass protest since January); Mojtaba's incapacitation question stands; Akraminia states Iran “fully exploited” the ceasefire to rearm.
Rezaei to the SNSC ·
reopening tied to reparations
China
Publicly pushes Resolution; the pivot is partly performative.
  • Absorbing the shock: imports abruptly halved (~5mn bpd) against the ~1.3–1.4bn-barrel reserve with no visible consumption decline — the Atlantic: “the most important factor in keeping prices down”; some Hormuz transits reportedly settled in renminbi; Beijing self-arranges Houthi passage for its own tankers (Reuters).
  • Structural de-risking: Qatari LNG to China down ~98% year on year; Sinopec and PetroChina exploring 10+ year non-Gulf supply — the first permanent demand-side Gulf shift of the war.
  • Beyond the public line: US officials suspect a PRC reconnaissance satellite supports Iranian targeting (WSJ); missile components and fuel precursors kept flowing through the war; Iran seeks PRC assistance rebuilding its air defences (ISW).
Pushes Resolution
Russia
Aligned with China publicly; preserves Iran ties privately.
  • The HEU custodian pathway: the formal offer to take Iran's HEU stands (Araghchi: “not currently under discussion”) — the technical route under the Security Guarantee architecture.
  • Operational support reported: locational intelligence on US warships and drone-tactics advice (WSJ); satellite imagery of US Gulf bases timed to Iranian strikes (Zelenskyy); Ukraine strikes the sanctioned Caspian vessels reportedly moving military cargo toward Iran.
HEU custodian role available
Houthis / Yemen
The second front has an owner: the blockade of Saudi port calls (declared 20 Jul, on the Houthis' own Sana'a-siege grievance) holds until Riyadh lifts its own on Yemeni ports, pays salaries and admits Iranian flights.
  • The blockade reaches Aramco: a drone strike on the Jizan refinery (8 Aug, fire confirmed by the Saudi Energy Ministry — at least the second blaze at the 400,000-bpd complex in a month); an attack wounding 11 in Najran province; ~20 ballistic missiles into Marib City (at least two killed); ROYG forces destroyed a naval drone near Mokha.
  • The chokepoint record: the first sinking at Bab el-Mandeb — the MSV Faize Noore Oliya (4 Aug); transit fees formally denied (1 Aug); Saudi Red Sea exports run at 3.5mn bpd per the Economist, so the export-halt claim is carried contested; the claimed ~50-nation coalition remains uncorroborated by ISW.
  • The Iranian hand beside their own agenda: ISW — “their own agenda… a key Iranian partner”; the 13 Jul flight carried IRGC commanders, missile equipment and gold; a coordination headquarters is reportedly run from a Kataib Hezbollah stronghold south of Baghdad, and a senior Saudi official reports planned “imminent” strikes on Saudi energy infrastructure coordinated with the IRGC and Iraqi militias.
  • The off-ramp channel: Saudi-Houthi indirect talks run via Omani mediation with the US privately discouraging Saudi retaliation (Bloomberg); Riyadh has not struck Yemen since 25 Jul.
Jizan refinery struck ·
militia coordination reported
GCC / Pakistan
Mediation delivered the ceasefire; all GCC bar Oman reject permanent Iranian control of Hormuz; the bloc's exposure has widened round by round.
  • The bloc arms: Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan sign a joint defence agreement (7 Aug, “mutual support only for defense”) on top of the 2025 Saudi-Pakistan pact — 8,000 Pakistani troops, a fighter squadron and air defence already in the kingdom — beside the proposed 14-country maritime coalition. Kuwait is separately reported negotiating an expanded defence pact with Pakistan (Reuters, early stage).
  • The militia threat pauses: the planned attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure pause via Badr-leader Ameri's mediation; a Shia Coordination Framework delegation goes to Tehran; the framework calls the 30 Sep disarmament deadline “flexible.” Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Kuwait had warned Baghdad they would strike militias inside Iraq on further attacks; the US reportedly conditions ~$30bn of Saddam-era funds on disarmament.
  • The bypass geography: Yanbu carries ~4mn bpd (~60% of pre-war Saudi crude exports) as the Hormuz bypass, with Abqaiq the single upstream node behind it — both inside the Houthi and militia target set; Iraq works the pipeline circuit (Kirkuk-Ceyhan, IPSA, Kirkuk-Tripoli) as the structural answer. A Bloomberg feature flags the ~$3tn Saudi-UAE rivalry for regional capital as a fault line between the two bypass-hosting states.
  • Standing constraint: the Saudi–Pakistan airspace cross-promise still binds Israeli unilateral action — the trilateral pact deepens it. David's 2 Aug note places the near-term risk at the Saudi-led 14-nation coalition, beside the ~50-nation Global21 claim ISW has not corroborated.
Defence pact with Turkey-Pakistan ·
militia attacks paused via Baghdad
Europe
Aligns with the diplomatic track; constrained from leading any post-war architecture after refusing the US reopening request. The UK and France have offered to lead Hormuz demining once conditions allow; Hegseth presses the UK to host a maritime-security summit on strait traffic; a NATO contribution to the HEU Security Guarantee would be the test.
Diplomatic backer
Japan / Korea
Lean on the US for Resolution; ~60% of energy via Hormuz. The Tomahawk-delay warning lands US overstretch on an Indo-Pacific ally, reinforcing the hedge; Capital Economics names Japan among the economies most exposed to physical fuel shortage under a dual-chokepoint closure; dormant nuclear conversations re-open if the scenario shifts to apex.
Hedging

The 8 Jun – 11 Aug: whipsaw, signing, breakdown, a war with US casualties, a second chokepoint, a mutual pause, the break, the canceled strike, and the corridor stall

8–17 Jun
Ceasefire collapses then resolves onto de-escalation: Israeli and US strikes inside Iran (8–10 Jun); Trump declares the deal “complete” (15 Jun); the US and Iran sign the MoU two days early (17 Jun), with signed edits to Clause 1 (Lebanon) and Clause 5 (Hormuz). The blockade lifts and oil sanctions waive on signing.
19 Jun–12 Jul
Implementation, then four escalation rounds of rising scale: the first 60-day-track round at Bürgenstock (21–22 Jun); the Ever Lovely exchange and stand-down (25–30 Jun); the tanker attacks and oil-waiver revocation (6–8 Jul); the ~140-target wave reaching central Iran, five-Gulf-state retaliation, and Iran's rejection of Oman's two-corridor proposal (9–12 Jul). Talks resume at Iran's request (10 Jul) even as Trump maintains the ceasefire is over.
13–16 Jul
The blockade returns (14 Jul), targeted at Iranian-flagged shipping; the 20% fee floats and drops within a day; strikes reach roughly 200km inland (15 Jul); Iran strikes three vessels on the Omani route, retaliates against Kuwait, Bahrain and Jordan, and on 16 Jul declares the strait an “inviolable red line.” The Iran-Oman channel goes quiet; the mediation-breakdown trigger fires (v11).
17 Jul
An Iranian missile attack on Muwaffaq Salti Airbase, Jordan kills two US service members, with one missing — the first US deaths of the conflict. The sixth consecutive US strike night severs the bridges, rail and telecoms feeding Bandar Abbas; Iran strikes a Kuwaiti power-and-desalination plant and, for the first time, near al Tanf in Syria; a Thai-flagged vessel is struck on the Omani route; Kpler counts eight strait transits the prior day. General License X1 expires, revoking all Iranian-oil transaction authority; the MoU's 30-day full-lift deadline passes in breach. Murrin publishes WW3 116, declaring Chapter Two of the war.
18 Jul
Tehran formally suspends the MoU: Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei declares Trump's signature “invalid” and Deputy FM Gharibabadi announces suspension of commitments. The seventh US strike night; Iran fires a ballistic missile at a US base near al Kharj, Saudi Arabia — its first strike on Saudi territory in about three months, with sirens at Yanbu — and hits Kuwaiti power, desalination and oil facilities a second day. Brent settles ~$88, up 4.6%, the biggest weekly advance since April. A third US service member is fatally wounded in Iraqi Kurdistan disposing of ordnance from a downed Iranian drone.
19 Jul
CENTCOM announces the third US death. Iran's AEOI says a US strike hit the Darkhovin nuclear plant in Khuzestan (IAEA: very early construction, no nuclear material at the last inspection). Four ballistic missiles at Aqaba, southern Jordan — a first; Kuwaiti infrastructure hit a third day running. Araghchi disclosed a six-person SNSC committee deciding on the spot while the Supreme Leader is reportedly hard to reach, and says some nuclear demands may remain “unresolvable.” The eighth consecutive US strike night (18 Jul) included the IRGC unit behind the Jordan attack.
20 Jul
The IRGC Navy states its permission regime openly after halting four vessels: “not a single drop of oil, gas, or chemical fertilizer” passes without its coordination. The US moves more F-16s, F-35s and refuellers to the region; Israel's Katz warns Iran that Israel will re-engage if attacked. Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Qatar condemn the infrastructure strikes; Jordan summons an Iranian diplomat; China and Pakistan urge resumed dialogue. The Houthis declare a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia effective immediately (Yahya Saree), citing the Saudi siege of Sana'a; the Qatar/Egypt/Pakistan/Oman written framework circulates, and Iran's FM spokesperson confirms receipt.
21–22 Jul
The eleventh and twelfth consecutive US strike nights reach Bushehr Airport, Larak Island, Behbahan, western and north-western Iran, and the Parchin complex near Tehran. Iran puts first missiles on Dhahran's King Abdulaziz Air Base and strikes US early-warning radar in Kuwait. The Houthi blockade turns kinetic: missile and drone strikes claimed on the Saudi tankers Encelia and Layla (one hit later UKMTO-confirmed), Bab el-Mandeb transits down 64 to 30, an EU Naval Force warning out. Ukraine strikes the Caspian Pipeline Consortium, halting ~1mn bpd of Kazakh flow. Brent settles $88.52 on 21 Jul, the highest since 11 Jun.
23 Jul
Brent settles $100.69, up 7%, after touching $102 — the first settle above $100 since May — on the Red Sea tanker attacks. Trump threatens Iran and the Houthis with “major military punishment” if the attacks continue — the Houthis named a “Surrogate and/or Proxy of Iran” — and tells Axios he may expand strikes (“They haven't received enough pain yet”), squaring the desk digest's “major operation” line. US equities fall (S&P -1.2%, Nasdaq -2.2%, Tesla and Alphabet earnings-day falls compounding) and the 10Y moves through 4.65% to 4.69%. Rubio: Tehran's leadership is “not ready to make a deal” (BBC). Dozens of fighters and refuellers continue deploying; no talks are scheduled on the framework. UKMTO confirms a Saudi-tanker hit; transits recover to 40. Iranian-backed Iraqi militias likely drone Kuwait's Abdali border crossing (material damage, no casualties) with explosions on Bubiyan Island; the IRGC claims a southern-corridor tanker mined — unobserved by ISW. The 13th consecutive US strike night follows into 24 Jul, with missiles reported on Qeshm Island in the strait; the House votes to direct a halt to the campaign, and the Senate blocks a similar measure hours later. [The desk Bloomberg series later puts the day's peak at ~$94 — the print divergence with the AP settle is flagged at section 06.]
24 Jul
Strikes reach northern Iran for the first time (the IRGC Navy commando college in Gilan) as Iran's drone campaign against US base housing runs across Bahrain, Jordan, Qatar and Kuwait. US forces disable the LPG carrier Lavine in the Gulf of Oman — two sailors reported killed per Iranian media — the first deaths in this file's blockade-enforcement record. The NYT reports a 23 Jul Iranian rejection of the US framework carried by Iraqi PM Zaydi; Zaydi's office denies it the same day (24 Jul) — carried as contested. Trump convenes an options meeting, an Omani delegation arrives in Tehran, and a strike hold is reportedly ordered within hours: no overnight wave into 25 Jul, the first pause in 13 nights. Unclaimed airstrikes are reported on Hudaydah.
25–26 Jul
The pause holds on both sides — one Iranian attack (Bahrain) in the first window, then none; Iranian officials say the restraint lasts as long as the US hold does. Iranian and Omani delegations meet in Tehran (24–25 Jul) on a Hormuz agreement; Baghaei claims “progress” (26 Jul) while saying strait traffic is unchanged, and parliamentarians insist control is not returning to pre-war conditions. Pakistani officials say both Washington and Tehran “have responded” to the joint Pakistani-Qatari proposal. CENTCOM boards the Charminar (25 Jul). The Saudi-Houthi exchange runs on: coalition strikes on Hudaydah, Jawf and Marib; Houthi missiles at Yanbu intercepted by Greek-operated defences while munitions impact Jizan; the NCC Masa attacked; a Saudi Akinci drone downed over Jawf. Mojtaba Khamenei is reported out of contact “due to certain issues” (Haddad Adel). A senior Iranian official tells Reuters (26 Jul) Iran will halt attacks as long as the US halts, conveyed directly; Mojtaba's 26 Jul statement names Hezbollah's preservation the “first condition” for resolving the war. Ukraine strikes sanctioned Caspian cargo vessels; Zelenskyy says Russia supplies satellite imagery of US Gulf bases.
27 Jul
Saudi Arabia says it shot down drones from Iraq aimed at Eastern Province petroleum facilities and Riyadh — ISW assesses Iranian-backed Iraqi militias, preserving Tehran's deniability — and a fire burns at Abqaiq, unclaimed by any actor; Saree claims strikes on the oil-transport corridor to the Red Sea hubs. The LAF accuses the IDF of hindering the pilot zones. Bloomberg details the middle-passage proposal — UK/French demining offers, joint management with fees, Witkoff and Kushner involved; Trump tells Axios “deep talks” are under way. Iraq's PM works the bypass-pipeline circuit toward Ankara and Riyadh. A US official and mediators tell Western media the Omani track has tabled a formal 10-day truce — the strait reopened against the blockade lifted and asset-unfreezing considered, a regional consortium proposed for management — and Iran is refusing to concede control. The LAF makes its first pilot-zone weapons-cache seizure (unverified by ISW); the Islamic Resistance in Iraq denies the Saudi drone claims.
28 Jul
Trump meets Netanyahu in Washington and tells reporters there is a “good chance” talks with Iran make progress (Bloomberg). Brent settles $84.09, down 4.8% on the day and roughly 16% over three sessions — the worst run since April 2020 — with WTI at $79.26, CTA Brent length cut to 62% from 73%, and CIBC reading the move as positioning on “MOU 2.0” hopes; Hormuz traffic stays muted with transponders dark. Treasuries rally as oil retreats; swaps price roughly one-in-three odds of a hike at the FOMC, with Citadel Securities and PGIM calling for one and August fed-funds futures open interest at records. Macquarie warns a deal would leave Q4 oversupplied by ~2mn bpd; OPEC+ is expected to pause quota hikes after September. The Houthis claim ballistic missiles on the tanker NCC Ghazal — their third claimed attack on Saudi shipping since 22 Jul (UKMTO-unconfirmed). Reuters: China has asked the Houthis for safe passage for its tankers — one source describes each ship being cleared individually — and at least four Saudi-oil cargoes to China have transited Bab el-Mandeb since 20 Jul. The first mass protest since January in Malekshahr, Esfahan, over the execution of three winter protesters. Iraqi-Saudi talks convene on the drone claims; Rome pilot-zone expansion talks are set for 4–6 Aug.
28–29 Jul · the break
IRGC ballistic missiles target Muwaffaq Salti Airbase in Jordan — an “attempted surprise attack” per CENTCOM, five intercepted per the Jordanian Army — ending the four-day pause shortly after Iran rejects compromise on strait control (ISW). The IRGC Navy claims strikes on three tankers on the southern route. The US and Saudi Arabia jointly strike militia weapons and logistics sites across Iraq and the Iran-Iraq border — retaliation for militia attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure and US interests — with at least four IRGC Quds Force officers reported killed in Diyala. On 29 Jul a senior Iranian official rejects the Omani proposal to Reuters (“unrealistic”); Gharibabadi (28 Jul, per ISW) says Iran would go to war for strait sovereignty; an unattributed drone attack targets a US-owned tanker at Damietta, Egypt; the Houthis float Red Sea transit fees. The Fed holds 9–3 with no forward guidance — the 29 Jul US session sells off (S&P -1.5% to 7,316) with the 30Y through its 2007 high and oil surging; Trump promises to hit Iran hard (internal desk record).
30–31 Jul
The AI leg turns the 30 Jul US session — Microsoft +16%, a record ~$450bn one-day add — while Brent settles ~$88 (desk series; its 23 Jul peak ~$94, the AP divergence flagged at section 06) and the SPR ledger shows 307.6m barrels with ~25m contracted barrels left. Global21 carries the claimed Saudi coalition to force Bab el-Mandeb open (single-source). The Kospi closes a record 18% higher on 31 Jul as the AI trade returns. 13D's WILTW reports “the nuclear issue is no longer viewed as taboo in Tehran” and calls August the most dangerous month.
31 Jul–1 Aug · the canceled strike
WSJ reports Trump ordered a new attack on Iran “as soon as this weekend”; CBS reports energy infrastructure — refineries, power plants — under consideration; Trump at the Camp David cabinet meeting: “We'll be hitting them very hard.” WTI trades above $86 post-settlement. Iran's SNSC vows to strengthen strait control and close other waterways; the Strait Authority announces no transit permits until US operations end; CENTCOM says the strait remains open; UKMTO logs a projectile in the Gaslog Shanghai's engine room off Oman. On 1 Aug Trump says he canceled the strikes on being told deal parameters were agreed — Axios reports MBS raised concerns over the plans; the Washington Post reports a US general warning the Pentagon lacks sufficient forces to protect Israel; ISW records no US strike activity. The NYT carries two senior IRGC officers on Quds Force coordination with Hezbollah, the Houthis and Iraqi militias during the April ceasefire; the Houthi operations centre denies imposing Bab el-Mandeb transit fees. Japan's record ~¥8.45tn single-day yen intervention (30 Jul) is followed by the first joint US-Japan intervention in nearly 30 years (31 Jul, per the FT).
2–3 Aug
Trump announces US and Iranian officials will soon meet on reopening the strait and on nuclear issues (2 Aug). WSJ reports Qatari mediators presented a new reopening proposal with Iranian diplomats responding “positively”; Israeli media report Araghchi agreed to a US-Qatari split-route design — and the same day Baghaei says on the record the proposal “has nothing to do with” opening the strait (the Iran-formal-response trigger fires a third time) while IRGC-affiliated media deny any agreement. Artesh spokesperson Akraminia says Iran “fully exploited” the ceasefire to rearm, including new drones already used against US Gulf bases. On 3 Aug Trump frames the hold — “holding off on a big strike” because “everyone in the region” is “begging for talks”; WSJ reports negotiators support the corridor design but await IRGC approval; Rezaei rules out “a second corridor” (referent ambiguous per ISW); Zarif calls the strait a “bargaining chip” whose leverage decays; the Assembly of Experts brands “calls for surrender” an “unforgivable betrayal.” UKMTO logs further projectile incidents (2–3 Aug). The Mearsheimer panel transcript circulates on David's thread; the Monday session rallies (S&P +1.5% to 7,601) with crude falling.
4–6 Aug
The two-corridor design is detailed — inbound via Iranian waters, outbound via Omani waters, no tolls — and Iranian diplomats counter with monitoring and intervention rights, “service fees,” blockade relief and sanctions relief. CENTCOM publishes its first blockade tallies: 45 vessels redirected, two disabled, two boarded since 14 Jul. The Houthis likely sink the Indian-flagged MSV Faize Noore Oliya near Bab el-Mandeb — the first sinking at the second chokepoint — and hit Najran airport's main radar; Saudi-Houthi indirect talks run via Oman with the US privately discouraging retaliation. Rome talks on the Lebanon pilot zones resume (4–6 Aug). Japan's 10Y auction draws the weakest demand since May 2025; Bessent calls the yen's level a regional problem. The Tuesday session rallies further (S&P +1.8% to 7,737), the desk attributing crude's further fall to Iran confirming reopening talks — a desk attribution with no primary source behind it, flagged. Stavridis publishes the three-path piece (4 Aug); Gary forwards it and David designates it the scenario-stress starting position (5 Aug). Rubio narrows the immediate US ask to the strait — denuclearisation “the ultimate deal” (4 Aug); Baghaei describes provisional inbound/outbound management protocols on the Iran-Oman channel; Bessent predicts Iran may agree “today or tomorrow to open the strait” (CNBC, 4 Aug); the FT has oil easing below $80. The FT synthesis reaches the desk on 6 Aug via Gary, and the yen/JGB leg goes onto the firm's scenario-stress list (per David's 6 Aug note).
5–7 Aug · the stall surfaces
Two regional officials tell the AP the supreme leader has not approved the draft Iran-Oman agreement, against Axios's 4 Aug approval report; ISW ties the delay to the factional split, the rounds run without the IRGC in the room. IRGC-affiliated media describe a toll-bearing variant — entrance management plus “insurance, fueling, and environmental fees” — while a Saudi source describes a fee-free one; Fars carries draft terms barring US and Israeli shipping with penalties to 20% of cargo value; Reuters' industry sources read the design as Iranian “control” over inbound traffic. Mediators tell the WSJ the IRGC is holding up the draft to extract fees, traffic-control language and relief. UKMTO: two explosions heard from a vessel in Omani waters (5 Aug). The US Treasury sanctions Iran's shadow-banking network (7 Aug). Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan sign a joint defence agreement; the Iraqi militias' planned attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure pause via Ameri's mediation.
8–9 Aug · six demands, a hardliner to the SNSC
Zolghadr conditions the strait's reopening on six US concessions, including the blockade, sanctions, force withdrawal, frozen assets and war reparations; Araghchi says Iran and Oman are close on a temporary route, reopening “subject to other conditions.” An Iranian missile strikes a UAE state-oil-company tanker; the FT reports Kharg Island at least a week without loading crude. A Houthi drone strikes Aramco's Jizan refinery (fire confirmed). On 9 Aug Khamenei appoints Mohsen Rezaei SNSC secretary, demoting Zolghadr; Babai threatens “any country that wants to assist the United States”; Araghchi rules out talks with the US while it violates the June MoU — the Iran-formal-response trigger fires a fourth time.
10–11 Aug · reparations enter the terms
After the weekend's positions — Araghchi's “very close” on an Oman pact beside his refusal of direct talks, Trump's “low-keying it” to Axios — Trump on Monday demands compensation for roadside-bomb deaths and Iran's protest dead, expanding it to Lebanon, Syria, Yemen and Gaza — “firmly into any, and all, future negotiations” — and claims the strait is “open now” and US-controlled; Baghaei ties reopening to the siege lifted and damages compensated. Brent rises about 5% to end near $88 (Bloomberg), extending a three-session rally above 5%; European diesel futures surge more than 10% on refinery attacks in Saudi Arabia, Libya and Russia; the S&P closes 7,753, off 0.1%, as yields jump. Citrinowicz's pressure-track read circulates via Gary.
What it confirms: the sovereignty read carried since v3 — every design with revenue attached stalls on the same question; the no-toll variant lasted days before the fee mechanism resurfaced in the IRGC's own media, and the faction that owns the strait file now also runs the SNSC. What it does not change: the bifurcated architecture, the apex held in the long-term allocation, the Murrin DD, the Brent bands. Watch-list:
  • Trigger status: Iran-formal-response fires a fourth time (Araghchi, 9 Aug); the Israeli-strike trigger stays unfired; the Saudi-Pakistan airspace item moves the other way — the trilateral pact deepens it; the signed-deal item stays provisional (the reported US-Saudi enrichment agreement, corroboration outstanding).
  • The corridor draft: whether it clears Khamenei and the IRGC — and in what fee form, the IRGC-media tolls variant against the Saudi-sourced fee-free account.
  • The announced meeting: whether it ever convenes against Araghchi's refusal.
  • The reparations exchange: a bargaining layer or a new wall — the signed Article 6 fund is the clause both sides now read differently.
  • The Saudi front: the militia-attack pause via Baghdad, held by mediation without an agreement behind it; Bab el-Mandeb after Jizan.
  • Lebanon and the checklist: the verifier shortlist, direct negotiations 1 Sep; CE's reopening checklist pending (teaser-level).
The map — the suspension stands, the corridor stalls in Tehran

Stalemate stays modal because the US–Iran nuclear divide is wide and the hardliner faction blocks Good A. The structural fault ISW identified — Clause 5 read by Washington as restored passage and by Tehran as affirmed Iranian authority — has run through every variant since, and the sovereignty question is answered in Iran's favour: every design short of recognised Iranian control with revenue attached has been refused. v16's open questions both moved toward the harder reading: approval has not come — Khamenei unsigned (AP), the IRGC extracting fees, control language and relief (WSJ) — and the demands grew, Zolghadr's six conditions and then reparations on both sides. The meeting announced on 2 Aug has not convened; Araghchi rules out direct talks while the US remains “in violation” of the June text. The corridor is stalled rather than dead — Araghchi calls the Iran-Oman track “very close” and “final stages” in the same breath as the refusals — but the SNSC now sits under Rezaei, and Citrinowicz's read of the pressure track argues the equilibrium is unlikely to hold: economic pain alone is unlikely to move Tehran off a core interest, and its record when cornered is escalation. The version-by-version map is in the prior tabs.

06 · Market & thematic implications

Scenario views across equities, Brent, rates, and rotation.

Views only. Brent bands unchanged from v12. The matrix carries the view per scenario; the detail blocks below carry the current state and the live flags, and the print-by-print history is in the timeline and the prior tabs. v17: Brent ended near $88 on 10 Aug (Bloomberg) as reopening hopes dimmed — just under the floor.

ScenarioEquitiesBrentRatesRotation
Stalemate
Modal		 Mid-teens downside; the modal outcome flat, the skew down. Tight, elevated, drawing inventory — near $88, just under the $90–110 floor. Yields up; the war's oil leg feeds the curve, the yen/JGB leg the stress item. Iran-axis exposure screens unattractive; rare earths, security and infrastructure favoured.

Corridor stalled in Tehran		 Mid-single-digit upside. Declines toward $90–110 over months on a realised reopening. Yields ease as the energy premium unwinds. Screens better selectively; the China sleeve recalibrates on a firmer Hormuz-access outcome.

Equities — the two legs

Mid-teens downside under Stalemate, with EPS holding until ~2027 demand destruction. The oil-to-equity transmission has compressed — roughly 1.5% S&P downside per 10% oil rise, against ~4% in March — and the war leg and the AI leg are pulling equities in opposite directions: FOMC-day selloffs against record AI sessions (Microsoft's ~$450bn day, the Kospi's record 31 Jul). Vanda's standing read: the US equity right tail has “all but disappeared” — the modal outcome flat, the skew down. The de-escalation rally stalled with the diplomacy: 7,724 (5 Aug), 7,710 (6 Aug), then 7,753 on 10 Aug — off 0.1% with yields and crude jumping on the reparations demands; the Topix advanced intraday on 11 Aug with crude firm, the desk report citing rekindled inflation worries.

Brent — the physical ledger

Near $88 on the 10 Aug session (Bloomberg), a rally of roughly 10% across four sessions as the stall priced — just under the $90–110 floor with the escalation premium rebuilding; European diesel futures up more than 10% on refinery attacks in Saudi Arabia, Libya and Russia; no desk-series settle reached the desk. The re-closure scenario the market prices as a ~$150 shock remains the near-term, non-nuclear face of the escalation leg. The live flags:

  • Print divergences: the desk series puts the 23 Jul peak at ~$94 against the AP $100.69 settle — desk series primary; the gasoline series stays split (AAA $4.09 per AP against the desk monitor's $4.65, the DOE weekly at $4.00 — unresolved), with US petrol ~35% over pre-war.
  • Inventory: SPR 307.6m barrels (24 Jul) with ~25m contracted left, against an in-house operational-floor estimate near 200m; total US crude stocks the lowest since 1984.
  • Flow: strait transits under 10/day; the gas complex unshielded (Asia LNG +94%, TTF +79% versus pre-war).
  • External calls: ranges below our floor (Barclays $65–80, BCA $70–100, Papic $75–100) flagged, not adopted; CE flags a tipping point without a sustained flow recovery and Bahrain's balance of payments at the brink under the closure; Murrin's $150+ logged at section 01.

Rates & FX — the curve and the yen leg

Fiscal pressure lifts yields and the war's oil leg feeds the curve. The FOMC hold (9–3, no guidance) left September roughly two-thirds priced — Dudley: short-rate expectations down, term premia up, the 30Y through its 2007 high — and Vanda frames the war's rates move as a real-rate shock (the real 2Y near 2%, +112bp since the war's start) with CTAs near max-short the long end. Yields jumped on the 10 Aug session as the reparations demands priced (desk report). The yen/JGB leg is tracked at firm level as a scenario-stress item (per David's 6 Aug note): war-driven oil feeds Japanese reflation, JGB yields press the BoJ toward its September meeting, and coordinated intervention holds the line — this round funded by US euro sales and swap lines rather than Treasury sales (BCA), with BCA's cyclical yen fair value near 130 against 157 traded. The follow-on reads sharpen the stress case: Eichengreen — both intervention legs signal Treasuries can no longer be freely mobilised, eroding the dollar's reserve standing; Felder — the 1998 parallel, intervention as a delay tactic. Gold caught a bid on the same logic.

Rotation — the thematic screen

  • Realised target set: Gulf civilian utilities and energy infrastructure (Kuwaiti power and desalination, the KPC facility, Aramco's Jizan refinery confirmed struck 8 Aug); Gulf digital infrastructure (the claimed Bahrain data-centre strike); Saudi oil infrastructure and the Red Sea leg (war-risk cover doubled; the Yanbu bypass and the Abqaiq node); the Mediterranean port vector (Damietta); UAE state shipping (the 8 Aug tanker strike).
  • A third chokepoint vector: Suez-adjacent drone strikes attributed to pro-Iranian Iraqi militias (Straits Times synthesis, primary corroboration outstanding). The refinery-attack set widens to Libya and Russia in one session's pricing, with European diesel the transmission.
  • Screened, unstruck vectors: UAE data centres, regional fintech, Gulf cable-dependent payments, the undersea-cables / SWIFT non-oil vector.
  • Thematic stances: the China sleeve re-rates on the Beijing read of US weakness; the energy-paradigm shift favours rare earths, security and infrastructure, defensive on regional refining. Structural answers: Iraq's bypass-pipeline circuit; China's LNG contracting away from Qatar (~98% down) as demand-side de-risking.
  • Context series: the AI-financing leg (Citadel Securities: $500bn+ further chip debt by 2028); CSIS interceptor inventories (Patriots 759–827 from 2,330 pre-war, THAAD 234–278 from 452) behind the munitions-depletion leg.

Apex / tail: escalation toward $130–160+ Brent is held in the long-term allocation; first-use ($200+, SPX ~3,500) sits below the scenario-modelling threshold as structural tail protection. The deal's re-timing of this tail to the 60-day window is itself suspended as of 18 Jul, so the window is open-ended; the HEU stays in Iran, hardened, and unmentioned in this window's exchanges. The Darkhovin strike is the first kinetic touch on the nuclear file this cycle — an early-construction site with no nuclear material at the last IAEA inspection — and Murrin's $150+ call sits inside this leg as his conviction, ahead of the file's own. Two proliferation-adjacent data enter the log: WSJ reports Washington will greenlight a 30-year US-Saudi civil nuclear agreement potentially permitting Saudi enrichment, and the Pickaxe Mountain chatter extends to unattributed tactical-nuclear talk (13D) — both logged, neither carried. A third enters at v14: the NYT-reported US intelligence read on Mojtaba's weapon interest, against Albright's degraded-programme assessment — logged and not carried. v15 logs two more, neither carried: 13D's “the nuclear issue is no longer viewed as taboo in Tehran… the IRGC is spear-heading a new strategic doctrine” (WILTW, 30 Jul, full text on file — including a reported debate on NPT withdrawal), and Barclays' last-option framing of a strike on the Isfahan HEU stockpile or Pickaxe Mountain. v16 logs one more, not carried: the Mearsheimer-panel report of a US-Saudi enrichment agreement signed around 22 Jul without fullest IAEA inspection rights — the signed execution of the greenlight WSJ reported at v13, single-source here; the signed-deal watch item registers provisionally pending corroboration. The Taiwan-war and US-default extrapolations are held as backdrop only, outside the modelled set.

The $300bn in the signed terms is external Gulf investment funded by sanctions relief — not a US Treasury outlay — which reconciles the terms with Iran’s frozen-asset demand; the relief flows through GCC capital.

Resolution mechanics

The Resolution path follows the framework David specified: Mearsheimer's “humble pie” off-ramp; a JPOA 2.0 nuclear architecture; the Ferguson Hormuz Council (Iran as Chair, a 45% / 30% / balance revenue split, transit fees at cost); HEU export under a Security Guarantee with Russia available as custodian; and a post-war Gulf Treaty Organisation with China and Russia as signatories. The realised Stage-1 MOU diverged from the Council mechanic on Hormuz — toll-free reopening under Iranian and Omani management rather than a chaired revenue split — and ISW's structural read of the collapse stands: the two sides read Clause 5 in fundamentally different ways, and the Gulf states rejected Iranian management and fees. The strait-management variants since:

  • Four-party framework (Qatar / Egypt / Pakistan / Oman, ~20 Jul) — dual-lane reopening, the fee question posed as Malacca-style Iranian service fees or an IMO-administered fund. Receipt confirmed; never convened as a table.
  • Tehran middle-passage table (24–25 Jul) — reopening the likely-mined middle passage under joint management likely to include fees, UK/French demining offered, the Witkoff/Kushner channel inside the room. Superseded by the Omani design.
  • Omani regional consortium (27–28 Jul) — a 10-day truce, the strait reopened against the blockade lifted, a regional consortium with voluntary fees. Rejected (“unrealistic,” a senior official to Reuters, 29 Jul) — the second Omani fee design refused.
  • US-Qatari two-corridor design (3–4 Aug) — inbound through Iranian waters, outbound through Omani waters, no tolls; the first to drop the fee mechanism entirely. Stalled in Tehran: approval absent (AP), the IRGC extracting fees, traffic-control language and relief (WSJ), the fee question back in the IRGC's own media — the toll outcome BCA priced, now described by the regime's own outlet — and the reparations exchange adding a term no prior variant carried. Whether the draft sent up to Tehran's leadership contains fees is itself unreported; US officials and mediators had said the design carried none.

Every design short of recognised Iranian control with revenue attached has been refused — the sovereignty question this file has carried since v3, answered in Iran's favour. Stavridis's dual-key prediction (Iran northbound, Oman southbound) is this design's shape, and his 60% renewed-negotiations path carries it; Mearsheimer's year-end expectation of a renegotiated MoU on terms worse for the US is the same destination read from the withdrawal side. The mechanics stay as the reference for a meeting that has not convened.

v18 · The deal lapses; the war reaches the UAE · 21 Aug 2026
Architecture, verdict & Brent bands held · US, Iran, Houthi, GCC, Russia and Japan/Korea cells moved · Resolution tier Corridor stalled in Tehran → MoU lapsed, channels ruptured · Iran-formal-response fires a fifth time · Mediation-breakdown fires a second · Brent settles inside the band at $90.08 · SPR 293.4m, lowest since 1982 · main body capped at eight pages, reference material in click-to-open appendices

The architecture holds — Stalemate (modal) / Resolution (MoU lapsed, channels ruptured) / apex in the long-term allocation. The signed text’s 60-day negotiation term expired on 17 Aug with the nuclear and sanctions files never opened. Trump warned of attacks on Oman that day, declared on 18 Aug that no talks exist or are scheduled, and pressed Oman against the corridor design; a senior Iranian official declared a “fully offensive” posture if diplomacy fails. Missiles the UAE attributes to Iran reached its territorial waters, and the UAE cut all economic ties — the first Gulf-state rupture of the war, severing the hub for ~80% of Iran’s imported foreign exchange. Brent settled inside the $90–110 band for the first time since 23 Jul.

What moved from v17 — the full change list
  • The deal’s clock ran out: the 60-day negotiation term in the signed text lapsed on 17 Aug — Baghaei called the deadline “entirely moot” — and Trump declared on 18 Aug that “there are no talks or conversations going on, or scheduled.” The Iran-formal-response trigger fires a fifth time. Mediation-breakdown fires a second: Trump threatened attacks on Oman, AP reports Washington told Oman it opposes joint Iranian-Omani management of the exit route, and the UAE channel is severed.
  • The war reached the UAE: two ballistic missiles the UAE says targeted maritime traffic, one landing inside its territorial waters (18 Aug; Iran denies) — on the Emirati account the first attack on UAE territory since May — answered by a halt to all trade and financial transactions: the first Gulf-state economic rupture of the war, severing the hub for roughly a third of Iran’s imports and ~80% of its imported foreign exchange (ISW). ISW expects Iran to answer with counter-pressure on the UAE.
  • Iran formalised the escalation preference: a senior official on the record (Reuters, 17 Aug) — Iran goes “fully offensive” and attacks to break the blockade if diplomacy fails; WSJ details IRGC wider-war plans laid during the MoU calm (Gulf internet cables, fomented unrest in Kuwait and Bahrain, potential ground operations in Kuwait, a coordinated Saudi confrontation). Rezaei’s first week added a region-wide ceasefire to the reopening conditions (11 Aug). The counter-datum: Axios reports Vahidi told a May US backchannel he fully supported the negotiating team and preferred a negotiated solution.
  • The second chokepoint turned fatal again: the Tihamah struck at Bab el-Mandeb (11 Aug; six killed) after Mocha Port (9 Aug, seven killed); Saudi Arabia is reportedly preparing a naval and possible land offensive against the Houthis (ISW, 10 Aug).
  • Brent entered the band: $90.08 settled 20 Aug — the first settle inside $90–110 since 23 Jul, after $89.79 the session before — with Murban at a four-month-high $97.75, both basins backwardated and the SPR at 293.4m barrels (week to 14 Aug), the lowest since 1982. The flow question is now the live dispute: 75–80% of traffic restored per the US Energy Secretary (via BCA; unconfirmed by shipping data) against the desk series’ 3, 2, 9 and 6 daily transits on 15–18 Aug and Citrinowicz’s few-dozen count.
  • The axis-supply leg is documented: NBC (18 Aug, citing a European government document) — Russian drone components, ammunition and TNT delivered to Iran via the Caspian as of July, over two dozen ships to Amirabad Port; the F-15E lost in April — disclosed 11 Aug — fell to a drone swarm using tactics ISW ties to direct Russian assistance in this war. The due-diligence tables at Appendix A1 record the move.
  • The rates leg went systemic: the 30-year closed at 5.31% (17 Aug) after auction records on 12–13 Aug, the debt crossed $40tn, and Treasury at least doubled long-end buybacks (19 Aug), pulling the 30-year to 5.18%. Per David’s note that evening, the doubling reads as a reach toward yield-curve control (“Bessent blinks”) — his conclusion, gold above $4,500; his 18–19 Aug strategy updates put markets at the neighbourhood of a bubble with the oil-inflation shock the amplifier.
  • Tehran consolidated command: the AFGS–KOACH merger ordered complete (10 Aug), Taeb to the Basij with a surveillance mandate, 23+ judiciary appointments (19 Aug); Baghdad asked Iran for “special status” strait exports (19 Aug), a channel that monetises strait control.
  • Cells move: US “Reparations demanded · ‘low-keying it’” → “Talks declared over · economic-pain track.” Iran “Rezaei to the SNSC · reopening tied to reparations” → “‘Fully offensive’ declared · missiles reach UAE waters (denied).” Houthis “Jizan refinery struck · militia coordination reported” → “Fatal strikes at Bab el-Mandeb · Saudi offensive reportedly prepared.” GCC “Defence pact with Turkey-Pakistan · militia attacks paused via Baghdad” → “UAE cuts all economic ties · the bloc arms wider.” Russia “HEU custodian role available” → “Caspian materiel resupply documented.” Japan/Korea “Hedging” → “Adapting around the strait · alliance strain.” The Resolution tier moves Corridor stalled in Tehran → MoU lapsed, channels ruptured.

Bottom line · the deal lapses; the war reaches the UAE

The scenario set stays bifurcated: Stalemate (modal) and Resolution (MoU lapsed, channels ruptured), with the apex tail held in the long-term allocation below the scenario-modelling threshold. The signed text’s 60-day term expired on 17 Aug with the nuclear and sanctions files never opened; Trump declared talks over while pressing Oman against the corridor design and threatening the mediator itself, and Iran declared a “fully offensive” posture if diplomacy fails. Missiles the UAE attributes to Iran — Tehran denies firing them — reached its territorial waters, and the UAE cut all economic ties with Iran, the first Gulf-state rupture of the war. Brent settled inside the $90–110 band on escalation pricing ($90.08, 20 Aug) with the strategic reserve at a fresh series low, and Treasury’s long-end buyback doubling — per David’s read, a reach toward yield-curve control — joined the war’s oil pressure to the fiscal strain. Murrin’s Article 2 nuclear scenario remains the analytical foundation under structural tail protection. Full scenario stances, drivers, equity and Brent views are in section 03.

01 · Due Diligence on Murrin

Verdict unchanged — cannot rule it out. WW3 117’s call for total war is his own advocacy; his checkable claims hold.

Murrin’s axis-supply claim moved to corroborated this window; his timeline and his policy conclusion have not. The claim-by-claim tables and the track-record scorecard are in Appendix A1; the full verifiability table sits in the v1 tab.

Murrin’s capabilities case is sound and OSINT-sourced. Timeline sits at the aggressive end of a 6–12 month band that overlaps Roaring Lion’s own assessment. The preemptive-nuclear-use conclusion is his advocacy. The ~440kg 60% HEU stockpile that anchors the capabilities case — the figure the Gallant “440 Kilograms” piece restates — stays inside Iran, physically hardened against seizure, and unmentioned through every window of armed exchange; inspector access stays unresolved, with Grossi expecting entry while Iran ties access to a final deal and sanctions relief, and Iran is not down-blending. The nuclear file itself has gone from deferred to unanchored: Tehran suspended the MoU on 18 Jul, the meeting announced on 2 Aug never convened, and the 60-day term in the signed text lapsed on 17 Aug with the file never opened — Trump declaring talks over the next day. On the claims themselves: Russian materiel entering Iran is now documented (NBC, 18 Aug) — the supply flow his WW3 116/117 pieces asserted — and the Ankara MANPADS disclosure hardens two legs of his assassination-plot row. The materiel component is corroborated; joining the legs into one war stays his frame. “Cannot rule out the nuclear scenario” holds as the analytical foundation; the apex is handled via the long-term allocation rather than modelled scenarios.

02 · Scenario test

Live tail risk on a 6–12 month horizon — below the scenario-modelling threshold.

The conclusion is unchanged; the operational decision is to bear this tail in the long-term allocation rather than model it.

The apex first-use event is paradigm-break, so protection is structural rather than model-derived. As David noted, “in short, I probably don’t need to know what the damage would look like.” Eleven windows of armed exchange since late June have stayed conventional, the ~440kg HEU core unmentioned in any of them. The eleventh window (11–20 Aug) ran through the blockade, the UAE incident and the Saudi front, with no US strikes on Iran through ISW’s 19 Aug edition; the 60-day text lapsed mid-window, so the deal’s re-timing anchor is gone and the apex window stays open-ended rather than deadline-bound — the placement is insensitive to that timing either way. The buffers thinned again: SPR 293.4m barrels (week to 14 Aug), the lowest since 1982, with the IEA counting global inventories down 410m barrels since the war began. What stays in the long-term allocation is the nightmare convergence — nuclear Iran + reinvigorated Russia + hedging China + exhausted America + isolated Israel arriving together as oil buffers run dry. Murrin Article 3’s late-stage US-decline thesis sits on the “exhausted America” leg as backdrop conviction. The window-by-window record is in Appendix A4 and the prior tabs.

Verdict

Murrin Article 2 cannot be ruled out and remains a live tail risk on a 6–12 month horizon. The apex probability sits below the threshold where another modelled scenario would change the prescription. Israeli unilateral action remains the most plausible trigger — unfired through eleven windows, with Israel deliberately sitting the campaign out (WSJ) and the strait and the Lebanon front the live channels an escalation would run through. The eleventh window’s editions on the desk record no Israeli strike. Citrinowicz keyed the trigger window to a closing deal; with the deal lapsed, the read rests on intent and the open-ended escalation phase — Barclays’ flag of a strike risk ahead of Israel’s 27 Oct election stands as the one dated catalyst. The Lebanon file moved toward process: a third-country monitoring mechanism agreed (Reuters, 12 Aug), Rome direct talks resuming in September, the LAF accusing the IDF of obstructing its deployments.

External cross-check — Stavridis’s three paths (4 Aug)
External cross-check — Stavridis’s three paths (4 Aug) · per David, the starting position for the scenario-stress work

Admiral Stavridis (Carlyle Compass, 4 Aug; via Gary, 5 Aug) weights three US paths: significant drawdown ~10%, major escalation ~30%, renewed negotiations backed by measured pressure ~60%. The 60% path lands where this file’s Resolution track sits, and his predicted most-likely outcome — a dual-key reopening with Iran controlling northbound transit and Oman the southbound route — is structurally the US-Qatari corridor design, now the only drafted text and orphaned by the lapse: unapproved in Tehran, part-opposed in Washington. The 17–18 Aug record leans the map toward his 30% escalation path — strikes on economic targets at 300–500+ per 24-hour cycle, an initial ~30,000 ground troops to secure the strait, an all-out Iranian response against Gulf energy — which maps onto the escalation leg this file holds in the $130–160+ band; the 10% drawdown path sits nearest Mearsheimer’s withdrawal expectation. His inputs run close to the file’s own: Iran at ~65% combat-power loss yet retaining the missile, drone, small-craft and mine capability that threatens shipping; Tehran having banked regime survival, $25bn in unfrozen assets and the proposed $300bn fund — his figures for the Articles 11 and 6 terms. One structural read runs beyond the window: strait control as a depreciating asset, the energy system adapting away from the chokepoint — measurable this window in Japan’s rebuilt import mix (US share ~3% to ~25%, ~200 days of reserve cover; ANRE, 14 Aug).
