The map — the lapse hardens the stalemate

Stalemate stays modal because the US–Iran nuclear divide is wide and the hardliner faction blocks Good A. The structural fault ISW identified — Clause 5 read by Washington as restored passage and by Tehran as affirmed Iranian authority — has run through every variant since, and the sovereignty question is answered in Iran’s favour: every design short of recognised Iranian control with revenue attached has been refused. The stall has resolved toward rupture: the term lapsed with the files never opened, Washington now opposes part of the only drafted design, the mediator has been threatened, and the UAE channel is severed. Washington’s chosen instrument is economic — “unprecedented economic pain,” the blockade, the UAE rupture beside it. Tehran’s is positional — “fully offensive,” the conditions stack, missiles into UAE waters on the Emirati account. Three counter-reads now point the same way — BCA’s peak-leverage question, Papic’s peak-geopolitical-risk call, the 75–80% flow-restoration claim — and they turn on the flow question the desk series answers differently: 3, 2, 9 and 6 daily transits on 15–18 Aug against a ~100–140 pre-war baseline. The desk holds Citrinowicz’s side of it — economic pain alone is unlikely to move Tehran off a core interest, and its record when cornered is escalation. The version-by-version map is in the prior tabs.

What it confirms: the sovereignty read carried since v3 — the deal died on the question of who controls the strait, and its term has now lapsed on the same question. What it does not change: the bifurcated architecture, the apex held in the long-term allocation, the Murrin due diligence, the Brent bands. Watch-list:
  • Trigger status: Iran-formal-response fires a fifth time (the “entirely moot” deadline and the “fully offensive” declaration, 17 Aug); Mediation-breakdown fires a second (talks disavowed, the mediator threatened, the UAE channel severed); the Israeli-strike trigger stays unfired; the Saudi-Pakistan airspace item stays on the list, deepened by the trilateral pact; the signed-deal item stays provisional (the reported US-Saudi enrichment agreement, corroboration outstanding).
  • Bessent’s Iran plan, Monday 24 Aug — flagged in David’s 21 Aug note alongside the fiscal plan “soon”; the nearest catalyst on the calendar.
  • The UAE-Iran cycle: ISW expects Iranian military or economic pressure on the UAE; the next escalation, if it comes, has a named target.
  • The Saudi offensive: the reported naval and possible land preparation against the Houthis.
  • The flow question: 75–80% restored (the US Energy Secretary, via BCA) against the desk series’ 3, 2, 9 and 6 daily transits (15–18 Aug) and Citrinowicz’s few-dozen count — whichever reading holds decides whether Iran’s leverage is eroding, the question the BCA and Papic counter-theses turn on.
  • The Iraq channel: the “special status” export ask and the central-bank payment mechanism — strait control turning into income while the militia-disarmament file runs against a 30 Sep deadline.
  • Lebanon: the third-country monitoring mechanism (12 Aug) and the September Rome round — the window’s one de-escalatory line.

Equities — the two-sided tape

Mid-teens downside under Stalemate, with EPS holding until ~2027 demand destruction. The oil-to-equity transmission has compressed — roughly 1.5% S&P downside per 10% oil rise — and the war and the AI cycle are pulling equities in opposite directions. The war side won this window: 7,745 (17 Aug, −0.5% on the lapse and the Oman warning), 7,692 (18 Aug, chipmakers down as the 30-year touched 2007-era levels), then 7,708 (19 Aug) on the July-minutes release and the buyback ramp. The bubble question moved to the centre of the firm’s own reading: David’s 18–19 Aug strategy updates place markets at the neighbourhood of a bubble — made bigger or nearer its end if the oil-inflation shock lands — with Yardeni’s vigilantes stirring at a 5–6% 30-year range, NDR uneasy at 25x against 5.5%, and Dudley (20 Aug) putting the burst before end-2027 on CAPE 41 and a 240% Buffett Indicator. The AI financing is the flagged fault line: WSJ counts ~$3tn of off-balance-sheet commitments across nine companies against ~$600bn of trailing capex.

Brent — the physical ledger

Inside the band: $90.08 settled 20 Aug — a fourth consecutive higher session per the desk monitor, after $89.79 (19 Aug) — on the lapse, the UAE rupture and the talks-ended record, with Murban at a four-month-high $97.75 and both basins backwardated. The round trip now reads ~$71.80 (2 Jul) → $100.69 (23 Jul, AP settle; desk series ~$94 — divergence flagged below) → $80.46 (6 Aug) → $90.08 (20 Aug). The re-closure scenario the market prices as a ~$150 shock remains the near-term, non-nuclear face of the escalation leg. The live flags:

  • Inventory: SPR 293.4m barrels (week to 14 Aug) — a fresh series low, ~11.5m contracted barrels left, no tender since June, 93.4m of cushion above the desk monitor’s ~200m operational-floor estimate (18–21 weeks at the current draw). The floor debate is public: Hochstein — “I don’t know anyone who believes we can go below 300” — against DOE’s cavern rebuttal, with the reserve already below it. Commercial crude rebuilt to its five-year average (428.8m), so the strain concentrates in the strategic layer; IEA counts global inventories down 410m barrels since the war began.
  • Flow, contested: 75–80% of normal traffic restored per US Energy Secretary Wright (weekend reporting relayed by BCA, unconfirmed by shipping data; convoys and dark transits echo the Tanker War) — against the desk series’ 3, 2, 9 and 6 daily transits on 15–18 Aug (ten-day average 11; pre-war ~100–140) and Citrinowicz’s few-dozen count from his ~12 Aug briefing. Kharg’s western terminal reactivated 12 Aug after a 25-day halt (two VLCCs; the eastern terminal idle, 16–17 tankers waiting); Aramco resumed VLCC loadings inside the strait; ADNOC cut spot offers to Asia ~5%. The gas complex stays the unshielded leg.
  • Print divergences: the desk series remains primary (the 23 Jul peak ~$94 against the AP $100.69 settle); the gasoline series stays split — the desk monitor has $4.79 (18 Aug), grinding higher — and distillates are the sharper strain: stocks ~13% below the five-year average with diesel margins at records; the monitor flags a diesel-crisis risk as the likelier near-term break.
  • External calls: Barclays $65–80 sits below our floor; BCA $70–100 and Papic’s new $85–100 (12 Aug) straddle it — and Papic pairs his range with “oil prices are unlikely to decline much.” All flagged, not adopted; EIA raised its 2026 Brent forecast to $87 (11 Aug); Murrin’s $150+ logged in Appendix A1.

Rates & FX — the curve, the buyback turn and the yen

Fiscal pressure lifts yields and the war’s oil pressure feeds the curve. This window it went systemic: the 10-year auction at 4.683% (12 Aug) and the 30-year at 5.216% (13 Aug) — the highest since 2007 and 2001 — then a 5.31% 30-year close (17 Aug) with the debt through $40tn and July’s $432bn deficit the largest monthly shortfall since early 2021. Treasury answered on 19 Aug by at least doubling long-end liquidity-support buybacks — the 30-year fell to 5.18%, the dollar to a three-month low — and Bessent followed: possibly more than $4bn per issue, “part of it is signaling,” a fiscal-consolidation announcement due within days. Per David’s 19 Aug note, the doubling reads as a reach toward yield-curve control (“Bessent blinks”), funded at the short end; his conclusion is gold above $4,500, on the confidence channel. Saravelos: “soft-form financial repression.” The structural bid thins underneath — June TIC has the weakest foreign long-term buying since February (China’s YTD sales $40.3bn; JPM’s 2026 foreign-demand forecast cut to $450bn) just as hyperscaler issuance competes for the long end (~$2tn expected in 2026). The yen/JGB leg is tracked at firm level as a scenario-stress item (per David’s 6 Aug note) and tightened this window: 30-year JGBs above 4% for the first time, Japan’s PPI at 8% against CPI and wages near 3%, Eurizon calling the joint intervention “a watershed” with an eventual 125 target against BCA’s ~130 fair value. Gold holds the other side of the same logic — above $4,250 for the first time since June (UBS, 7 Aug; central banks bought 289 tonnes in Q2), UBS targeting $5,000 by H1 2027, and David’s own studies framing gold as a question about global debt rather than a price call.

Rotation — the thematic screen
  • Realised target set: Gulf civilian utilities and energy infrastructure (Kuwaiti power and desalination, the KPC facility, Aramco’s Jizan refinery); Saudi oil infrastructure and the Red Sea leg; the Mediterranean port vector (Damietta); UAE state shipping — and now UAE waters on the Emirati account (18 Aug), with the rupture putting UAE-Iran trade exposure (a third of Iran’s imports) into the screen.
  • A third chokepoint vector: Suez-adjacent drone strikes attributed to pro-Iranian Iraqi militias (Straits Times synthesis, primary corroboration outstanding). The second chokepoint’s record turned fatal at the Tihamah (11 Aug).
  • Screened, unstruck vectors: UAE data centres, regional fintech, Gulf cable-dependent payments, the undersea-cables / SWIFT non-oil vector — the cables vector moved from screened toward planned: WSJ’s 17 Aug reporting has preemptive strikes on Gulf internet cables inside the IRGC’s drawn-up options.
  • Thematic stances: the China sleeve re-rates on the Beijing read of US weakness; the energy-paradigm shift favours rare earths, security and infrastructure, defensive on regional refining; Japan’s rebuilt import mix (US share ~25%) is the adaptation trade in practice.
  • Context series: the AI-financing series (WSJ’s ~$3tn off-balance-sheet count; Nvidia backing up to $105bn of financing for a data-centre campus leased by OpenAI; SK Hynix’s $29bn buyback); CSIS interceptor inventories behind the munitions-depletion read.

Apex / tail: escalation toward $130–160+ Brent is held in the long-term allocation; first-use ($200+, SPX ~3,500) sits below the scenario-modelling threshold as structural tail protection. The deal’s re-timing of this tail ended with the text itself: the 60-day term lapsed on 17 Aug, so the window is open-ended; the HEU stays in Iran, hardened, and unmentioned in this window’s exchanges. The proliferation-adjacent log is carried in the prior tabs; the reported US-Saudi enrichment agreement stays single-sourced, the signed-deal watch item provisional. The Taiwan-war and US-default extrapolations are held as backdrop only, outside the modelled set.

The $300bn in the signed terms is external Gulf investment funded by sanctions relief — not a US Treasury outlay — which reconciles the terms with Iran’s frozen-asset demand; the relief flows through GCC capital.

WW3 117 — the total-war call, graded

“WW3 117: Trump's Watershed Moment in Recognising a Common Autocratic Enemy” (28 Jul; reached the desk an hour after the v14 send) is Murrin's escalation call. The frame is a single integrated struggle — Ukraine, the Middle East and a coming Indo-Pacific theatre against one autocratic axis — hung on Senator Graham's funeral as the catalyst, and it concludes that Trump “has only one choice” — total war with Iran alongside Israel. It moves nothing in the architecture, the bands or the verdict.

ClaimTierChecked againstOur read
One integrated war. The regional wars are a single struggle against a shared autocratic axis; the fires merge. Interpretive BCA's Gertken (29 Jul, same intake) models the opposite as his base case: the wars stay separate on US political-will limits, Russia's two-front aversion and China's external constraints — with a Hormuz oil shock the tail that merges them. Pape frames the same linkages as read-through. The couplings themselves are documented on this desk: shared munitions strain, chokepoint tactics, Russian satellite targeting support. A live dispute between tracked sources. The file carries the wars as coupled through observable channels without adopting the single-war frame; the Graham-funeral catalyst is narrative. Gertken's own tail condition — an oil shock that kills demand — is the same transmission this file holds in the escalation legs.
“Iran's control of the strait remains unchallenged” after ~1,000 US strikes. Corroborated ISW's 26 Jul key assessment: the strikes have “likely failed to meaningfully affect” Iran's pursuit of strait control. Barclays (28 Jul): degradation achieved, “nothing that will meaningfully impact the IRGC's strategic calculus”; transits 3–6/day. Corroborated by both primary trackers — the third consecutive piece whose checkable core lands on ISW's own assessment. His ~1,000-strike figure matches ISW's count for the phase.
Axis logistics. The Caspian vessel strike, Russian satellite targeting for Iran, and Geran drones refitted with Chinese jet engines flowing back to Iran. Interpretive Ukraine's Caspian strikes on sanctioned vessels and Zelensky's satellite-imagery statements are already on this file (ISW, 25–26 Jul). The Chinese-engine transfer leg is his “believed to be,” unsourced; ISW separately reports Iran seeking PRC air-defence assistance. The component facts are carried from primary sources; the engine-transfer leg is uncorroborated; assembling them into one axis supply system is his frame. Held as a hypothesis, consistent with the WW3 116 treatment of the China-Russia claim. v18: the resupply flow is documented — NBC (18 Aug, citing a European government document) reports drone components, ammunition and TNT delivered to Iran across the Caspian as of July, over two dozen Russian ships to Amirabad Port. The engine-transfer leg specifically remains uncorroborated; the materiel component no longer is.
Trump's “only one choice” — total war with Iran alongside Israel. Advocacy A prescription. The observable record at the cutoff is narrower: no US military response to the Jordan attack had followed, the day's joint US-Saudi strikes in Iraq retaliated for militia attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure and US interests, and Trump's promise to hit Iran hard is unexecuted against Iran itself; Israel remains out of the campaign. His conviction, kept in quotation — the same total-war advocacy graded at WW3 116 and Essential Lessons. The durable adjacent question is his interceptor-depletion cross-reference, already CSIS-corroborated in this file.

WW3 116, “The Battle for the Strait is On, so Prepare for Escalation” (17 Jul), is the tracked author's read of the current exchange. Murrin declares “Chapter Two” of the war — an existential contest for the strait and the Red Sea sea lanes that in his framing ends only with a victor and a vanquished. It is commentary rather than reporting: twenty-four distinct claims with no primary text of his own behind them, and the two that carry real weight are corroborated from outside the piece. Four of his headline claims have nothing on this desk that tests them either way.

ClaimTierChecked againstOur read

ISW (18 Jul) attributes the collapse to divergent readings of Clause 5 — Iran reading it as affirming Iranian authority over the strait, Washington expecting pre-war traffic conditions. A reported IRGC plot against Trump, passed via Israeli intelligence, corroborated by the Secret Service switching him back to the older Air Force One, and possibly the decisive factor driving him to destroy the IRGC. The escalation-driver conclusion rests on that unverified chain plus a psychological read of Trump. v18: two legs hardened — US intelligence identified a MANPADS-armed individual near the Ankara NATO summit on 8 Jul before Trump switched to a more secure aircraft, and NYT sources describe a credible threat from Iranian proxy forces prompting the change (disclosed 11 Aug, via ISW). The donor-state detail and the decisive-driver conclusion remain his alone.

ISW separately assesses the PRC and Russia are likely supporting Iranian targeting, citing a PRC reconnaissance satellite, Russian geolocation of US warships and aircraft, and Russian drone tactics. Both component facts are corroborated; joining them is his. What ISW documents is targeting intelligence, and no source on the desk reported Chinese or Russian materiel entering Iran when this row was graded. v18: that changed — NBC documents Russian drone components, ammunition and TNT entering Iran via the Caspian as of July (18 Aug), and the April F-15E downing (disclosed 11 Aug) ran on drone-swarm tactics ISW ties to direct Russian assistance in this war. The supply component is corroborated; joining the legs into one axis system stays his.
Interceptor stocks. Every month of war consumes US holdings of PAC-3, THAAD and SM-3. Corroborated CSIS (Cancian and Park, 30 May 2026): PAC-3 MSE runs at roughly 650 a year with half going to allies, against a US decade-average buy of 225; the 3,203 Patriots requested for FY2027 first deliver May 2029. THAAD runs at 96 a year against an 857-interceptor request first delivering mid-2029. Both sit in the slowest three-plus-year replacement tier. Corroborated for two of his three named systems, from a defence-budget source rather than a strategic commentator. SM-3 is excluded: CSIS records less use than ground-launched systems and attributes the lag to small past orders and 36–39 month lead times. The monthly-burn framing is not how CSIS measures it, and the piece predates three further escalation rounds.
Who gains. Depletion benefits Moscow, leaving Ukraine exposed as PAC-3 stocks fall, and benefits Beijing more still by raising first-strike confidence before US stocks recover. Interpretive CSIS documents the allocation friction — THAAD deliveries re-sequenced away from allies, Japan's Tomahawks possibly delayed, Ukraine Patriots pushed back in the queue — and states the depleted inventories created a window of vulnerability in the Western Pacific. It contests the conclusion: demonstrated US combat experience against a PLA with none may preserve deterrence until inventories are restored. It says nothing about Russia benefiting. The queue and the Western Pacific window are corroborated in the source's own words, stronger support than he offers himself. The further step — that Moscow and Beijing are prolonging the conflict for this reason — has no support on the desk.
Mobile launchers. The hard target, rather than the underground missile cities; the fix is compressing the kill chain with persistent armed ISR striking within minutes. Advocacy Self-labelled house conjecture. The only adjacent datum is one unelaborated Reuters line (three US officials, 16 Jul) describing recent strikes as “shaping operations.” Every missile-related strike ISW reports in the window is a fixed site — the Lar launch site, the Yazd Missile Base, Konarak airbase. No in-window evidence of the shift in either direction. One detail runs the other way: the 116 downed telecom towers and the strike on the Radio and Communications Regulatory Authority degrade Iran's control of its own Shahed drones, which is fixed-infrastructure suppression.
Order of battle. 135 MQ-9s, 18 RQ-4s, roughly 50 MQ-4C Tritons and an operational RQ-180 for that mission, with the binding constraint numerical — “not dozens but hundreds” of platforms. Interpretive No independent check on the desk. Every figure is asserted without source, and no coverage modelling sits behind the hundreds. Not carried, consistent with the numeric record in his work — 300kg and 460kg for the same HEU stock inside one article, “Fatyie Ii” for the Fattah-2, a moving SPR figure. The RQ-180 entry is the exception and is credited: he hedges it as classified and unconfirmed. The mass-over-sophistication constraint is sound in kind; the figure is illustrative.
The Ukraine model. The 250km strike-drone campaign that largely isolated Crimea by land transfers to Hormuz — drones from the Omani Peninsula interdicting Iran's coastal batteries. Advocacy The Crimea-isolation premise is stated flatly and unsourced. Nothing on the desk tests the 250km radius or the Omani basing proposition. Prescription. ISW's own Hormuz mechanic cuts against the payoff — a single successful attack, or the persistent threat of one, deters transits — so suppressing launchers need not restore traffic. Logged, not carried.
Bab el-Mandeb. Yemeni sources report the Houthis preparing to close it with al-Shabaab, holding closure in reserve as their own asset; the strait carries 10–12% of seaborne trade, and simultaneous disruption with Hormuz would exceed any modern maritime crisis. Interpretive A closure vector is independently reported (Reuters, 16 Jul), reaching this desk inside the Capital Economics note rather than read directly, and on a different causal account: Iran instructing the Houthis conditional on US strikes against Iranian power plants. ISW's 17 Jul edition carries no Yemen, Houthi, Bab el-Mandeb or al-Shabaab content at all. Bremmer and Barclays both attribute Houthi behaviour to a payments dispute with Riyadh. The trade share is asserted without source; Capital Economics instead quantifies the consequence at roughly 4mn bpd rerouted via Yanbu and +$15–20/bbl on a dual closure. The vector is live and the Sanaa-airport leg is already on this file. His account of agency — a Houthi-owned asset held in reserve, largely independent of Tehran — is not the account our sources give. The al-Shabaab coordination and drone-transfer legs are uncorroborated rather than contradicted, resting on unnamed sourcing alone. The consequence arithmetic is usable; the trade share is not carried. v13: the blockade landed 20 Jul on the Houthis' own Sana'a-siege grievance — a datum for his agency read — but Reuters and ISW report a 13 Jul flight carrying IRGC commanders, missile equipment and gold into Yemen, and ISW's read (“their own agenda… a key Iranian partner”) lands between his account and the instruction account; the scope, Saudi-flagged vessels and Saudi port calls, is narrower than the full closure he sketches. v18: the vector turned fatal — the first sinking (4 Aug) and the Tihamah strike (11 Aug, six killed) — and WSJ reporting has the IRGC supervising Red Sea deployments and passing target lists, a datum against his largely-independent-agency read. v14: Houthi negotiator Abdul Salam states the blockade applies to Saudi Arabia alone (24 Jul), and ISW records the Houthis resisting Iran's request to close the strait fully for several months — both closer to his reserve-asset read — while NYT-cited officials say Iran would seek full closure if Trump strikes Tehran or critical infrastructure.
Oil above $150. A surge in the weeks ahead as risk premia rise, with significant pressure on government bond markets. Advocacy $150 sits inside the $130–160+ escalation band this file already holds. Brent settled around $88 on 17 Jul. Barclays' $65–80 range is the genuine out-of-band divergence. The bond call names no market, tenor, level or horizon. The level is inside our own range. He carries $150 as a base expectation within weeks; this file holds it as a tail. No supply-outage volume or trigger level is given and the horizon has not elapsed, so the call is logged unscored. His section heading asserting oil is set to rocket higher overstates his own hedged text. v14: the fortnight since has run a round trip — $100.69 settled 23 Jul, then the worst three-day fall since April 2020 to $84.09 on 28 Jul. No $150 print; the call tracks against, with his “weeks ahead” horizon not fully elapsed. Still unscored. v15: two weeks on, the peak is $100.69 on the AP settle and ~$94 on the desk series (23 Jul; divergence flagged at section 05), with Brent at ~$88 — the call tracks against on either series. v16: crude fell across the 3–4 Aug sessions on the cancellation and the talks announcement, the FT putting oil below $80 on 4 Aug — three weeks on from the piece, no print has approached $150 on either series. v17: the 10 Aug session put Brent back near $88 (Bloomberg) as reopening hopes dimmed — the rally re-approaches the $90–110 floor from below and stays far from $150. v18: the band is entered — $90.08 settled 20 Aug, on escalation pricing — still far from $150; the call keeps tracking against, unscored.

Track record — prior calls against the 20 May to 20 Jul record

The capability, structure and chokepoint calls have held, and three of them are now working assumptions in this file. Timing and agency are where he fails, consistently and across every piece. The rows below are not independent trials — the Israel-trigger thesis recurs in four pieces and is entered once, and several draw on the same escalation sequence — so this reads as a map of where he is reliable rather than a hit rate. Unfalsifiable framing and advocacy carrying no forecast content are excluded, as is a 2024 Lebanon ground-campaign piece re-stamped 29 May 2026 and circulated as current with its body text never revised.

Across four pieces		 Israel is the uncontainable spoiler, and the IDF is the actor that moves on Iran's nuclear file. Not borne out Entered once though it recurs in four pieces. The prior read: No Pacific escalation event has reached the desk in eight weeks, while the confrontation consuming US strike assets, munitions and diplomatic bandwidth was Hormuz. Khamenei was killed and Mojtaba succeeded him, but ISW assesses the strait attacks as chain-of-command decisions by senior IRGC officers, so the institution is functioning.

WW3 116 moves nothing in the scenario architecture, the Brent bands or the verdict. The two claims in it that carry weight are corroborated from outside the piece: CSIS puts PAC-3 and THAAD replenishment on a three-plus-year queue with FY2027 deliveries starting in 2029, supplying the numbers behind an interceptor mechanism he asserts without any, and ISW's Clause 5 finding vindicates the MoU read he made on signing day. The four claims nothing here tests are the assassination plot and the aircraft switch offered as its corroboration, the al-Shabaab coordination and drone transfer, the persistent-armed-ISR doctrine shift, and the Bear Island and Japan-Okinawa passages. The Bab el-Mandeb vector is the one genuinely new watch item, and the account of agency behind it is not his: Reuters has Iran instructing the Houthis conditional on US strikes against Iranian power plants, while Bremmer and Barclays both attribute Houthi behaviour to a payments dispute with Riyadh. The capability, structure and chokepoint reads are the durable part of his work, and three of them are now working assumptions in this file. His quantities do not travel into our text without independent confirmation. His timelines and his assignment of agency to Israel have failed repeatedly across the file.

Essential Lessons Part I — the retrospective, graded

“Essential Lessons from the Iran Conflict — Part I: Strategic Realities” (Murrinations, 21 Jul; reached the desk 26 Jul via Gary) is Murrin grading the war he has covered since WW3 112. It is doctrine — seven lessons and five predictions, one of them dated only as “inevitable.” The checkable lessons land close to sources this file already holds. It moves nothing in the architecture, the bands or the verdict. A Part II on operational lessons is flagged and will be read when it arrives.

ClaimTierChecked againstOur read
Air power cannot win alone. The campaign failed to force submission; Iran's hardened, dispersed depth defeated it. Corroborated ISW's own key assessment (26 Jul): the current level and type of US strikes have “likely failed to meaningfully affect” Iran's pursuit of strait control — ~1,000 targets since 12 Jul against ~13,000 in the war's first phase, with Iranian control consolidating via the mine threat. Corroborated by the primary source this file weights most, in the same week he published. The Vietnam and Kosovo parallels and the JCS air-power-bias counterfactual are his framing; the operative claim stands on ISW alone.
Time as a weapon. Iran survives the assault, uses pauses to repair and replenish, and emerges stronger. Corroborated ISW (27 Jul) assesses Iran is using the current pause to reconstitute, quoting a regime-linked analyst on rebuilding combat capacity, with the 8 Apr ceasefire as precedent. Corroborated in the v14 window — the pause v14 wrote into the file is the mechanism he describes. It cuts both ways for the diplomatic track: the pause that enables the table also lets Iran reconstitute (ISW, 27 Jul).
“Could hardly have been worse.” A mortal blow to US credibility; allies will question the security umbrella. Interpretive Pape (Foreign Affairs, same intake) argues the same direction: the 1991-dated unipolar era is over, with the Iran war as the demonstration. Mead (WSJ, 28 Jul) argues a tactical pause inside a longer campaign by a president “unlikely to give up.” Desk observables cut both ways — Japan's Tomahawk delays and Kuwait's reported Pakistan pact exploration against a blockade still enforced. A live dispute between tracked sources. The file's “exhausted America” leg already carries the credibility question as backdrop; the piece sharpens it without settling it. The “mortal blow” grading is his register.
Chokepoints are the US blind spot. The Houthi A2/AD episode is a test bed for Iranian and Chinese strategy. Interpretive ISW's standing assessment has the Red Sea expansion serving Iran's Hormuz objective; Pape extends the same logic to Taiwan (drone-armed denial of Chinese ports). Nothing on the desk addresses US Navy institutional posture. The chokepoint mechanism is a working assumption of this file. The institutional blind-spot claim and the sea-power-chairman counterfactual are untestable here; the Taiwan read-through is logged as backdrop alongside Pape's.
The next war. A future US-Iran confrontation is “inevitable” — economic pressure, cyber, proxies, drones — on Iran's timetable, from strength. Advocacy No horizon and no falsifiable content. ISW's reconstitution read is consistent in kind; nothing tests inevitability. His conviction, kept in quotation. The file's architecture already carries the substance — Stalemate modal, the apex re-timed and open-ended — without the inevitability claim.
A2 · The signed MoU, Article by Article — signed 17 Jun · suspended 18 Jul · term lapsed 17 Aug
A2 · The signed MoU

What the text says — the milestone, Article by Article.

The 14-point text Bloomberg published on 16 June and the version a senior US official read aloud on signing (17 Jun); the Article text below is verbatim from those primary publications. Tehran announced on 18 Jul it is suspending its commitments under this text; the table is carried as the reference for whatever track resumes, with the implementation boxes tracking how each obligation has executed and reversed. The text’s own 60-day negotiation term lapsed on 17 Aug 2026 with the nuclear and sanctions files never opened.

ArticleText (close paraphrase)Our reading
1 · Ceasefire Immediate and permanent end to the war on all fronts including Lebanon; no hostile actions; refrain from the threat or use of force; the final agreement confirms this. Signed edit: a Lebanese-sovereignty guarantee was added. Contested — Iran reads it as obliging an Israeli withdrawal; Israel is not a signatory and keeps striking. The one clause advancing: the Lebanese Armed Forces began deploying into the Rome-brokered pilot zones on 16–17 Jul.
2 · Sovereignty Both parties respect each other’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and refrain from interfering in internal affairs. Implicitly constrains US regime-change; the IRGC structure survives. Iran also leans on this to frame “managing” Hormuz as an internal affair.
3 · 60-day window Negotiate and reach a final agreement within a maximum of 60 days, extendable by mutual consent. The clock for every deferred core. Suspended by Tehran on 18 Jul at roughly the window's halfway mark: Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei declared the signature “invalid” and Deputy FM Gharibabadi announced Iran is suspending its commitments. Neither side has formally withdrawn from the text itself. The window lapsed on 17 Aug with the deferred files never opened — Baghaei called the deadline “entirely moot,” and Trump declared the next day that no talks exist or are scheduled.
4 · US obligations Immediate: lift the naval blockade, prevent interference against Iran, restore traffic within 30 days to pre-war capacity proportional to Iran’s pre-war volume. US withdraws forces from surrounding areas within 30 days after the final agreement. Asymmetry: the blockade lifts at once, but force withdrawal waits on the final agreement. Signed term tested and reversed: the US reinstated the blockade on 14 Jul, targeted at Iranian-flagged vessels and Iranian cargo. Enforcement turned kinetic in July — by 16 Jul three vessels redirected, one disabled, the Curacao-flagged M/T Wen Yao boarded by the 11th MEU off Duqm — and CENTCOM's first published tallies (4 Aug) put the totals since 14 Jul at 45 vessels redirected, two disabled and two boarded. The 30-day full-traffic-restoration deadline passed in breach on 17 Jul. The FT reports (7 Aug, via ISW) no crude loaded at Kharg Island for at least a week and tankers unable to return after unloading in Asia; Pezeshkian concedes the blockade has forced costlier import routes.
5 · Iran obligations (Hormuz) Immediate: resume merchant shipping in the Gulf / Sea of Oman within 30 days to pre-war volume, removing technical obstacles and neutralising mines. Signed edit: a joint Iranian-Omani administration and a 60-day toll bar were added. Iran’s win — the text does not bar Iran from “managing” the strait. Tested and unresolved: Oman’s own two-corridor proposal was rejected by Iran on 12 Jul, and shipping avoids the Omani route despite US escorts. The IRGC Navy now states the regime openly — “not a single drop of oil, gas, or chemical fertilizer” passes without its coordination and permission — and a Thai-flagged vessel was struck on the southern route on 17 Jul. Iran's Environmental Protection Agency floated UNCLOS-based “environmental services” fees on 18 Jul, a new variant of the fee ambition.
6 · $300bn development US and regional partners build a rehabilitation and development plan financing at least $300bn; the implementation mechanism is set within 60 days. External Gulf money, not a US outlay (Trump: “no money changes hands”; Reuters: no US government funds). Gulf-funded, routing the financing into the Gulf-state track. The Article is now the reparations hook: Iranian officials tie reopening to compensation, Trump insists compensation “was never mentioned in any of our negotiations or meetings,” and the signed text's $300bn “rehabilitation and economic development” fund — its implementation mechanism due within 60 days of signing (lapsed undelivered, 17 Aug) — is the clause both readings run through (Bloomberg, 11 Aug).
7 · Sanctions US commits to ending all sanctions — UNSC resolutions, IAEA Board resolutions, all unilateral US primary and secondary sanctions — on a schedule set in the final agreement. Exceeds the JCPOA’s scope in principle, but the schedule is deferred to the final agreement. Signed term tested in the other direction: the US Treasury added over 50 sanctions targets on 14–15 Jul (the Shamkhani network, IRGC procurement) — new sanctions rather than the wind-down the Article commits to.
8 · Nuclear Iran reiterates it will never produce nuclear weapons; the fate of enriched material and all nuclear-related issues, including Iran’s “nuclear needs,” is “adequately addressed” in the final agreement. A restatement of Iran’s standing position. The version read aloud on signing adds on-site down-blending under IAEA supervision as the baseline method — gated to the final agreement and cutting against Iran’s simultaneous hardening of its HEU tunnels. The ~440kg core stays in Iran through the window. The file was touched kinetically for the first time in the 17–19 Jul window: Iran's AEOI says a 19 Jul US strike hit the Darkhovin plant in Khuzestan (IAEA: very early construction, no nuclear material found at its last inspection). Araghchi said on 19 Jul that some nuclear demands may remain “unresolvable.”
9 · Status quo Pending the final agreement, Iran holds the status quo on its nuclear programme and the US imposes no new sanctions and does not strengthen its forces in the region. The strategic freeze: Iran’s programme stays intact while US leverage is capped. The most consequential clause for the deferral read. Both halves are now in breach — new US sanctions landed 14–15 Jul, and more F-16s, F-35s and refuellers are moving to the region.
10 · Oil waivers US Treasury issues waivers immediately after signing for Iranian crude, petrochemicals and derivatives, and related services (banking, insurance, transport). Signed edit tested: the waiver was revoked on 8 Jul — the first rollback of a core MoU economic term. The wind-down completed on 17 Jul: General License X1 expired, revoking all Iranian-oil transaction authority.
11 · Frozen assets Frozen and restricted Iranian funds released and made fully available in line with negotiation progress, directed by the Central Bank of Iran. Sequenced to negotiation progress — Iran’s leverage-extraction path. Vance conditions release on “verified steps” on the HEU; Vahidi insists the funds are not barred from military spending.
12 · Implementation A mechanism to oversee implementation and the commitment to the final agreement. Compliance architecture with no specified membership, voting or enforcement — to be designed in 60 days.
13 · Sequencing gate Nuclear negotiations begin only after Iran receives assurances on the implementation of Articles 4, 5, 10 and 11 (blockade, Hormuz, oil waivers, frozen assets); talks then address only the remaining articles. Iran’s verification gate — it can delay the nuclear talks by contesting any of those four implementations. The Article 10 revocation and the blockade's 14 Jul return each gave Iran grounds to invoke it. The 18 Jul suspension goes past the gate: rather than invoking Article 13 to pause the nuclear talks, Tehran suspended its commitments across the text.
14 · UNSC ratification The final agreement is approved through a binding UN Security Council resolution. China and Russia become structural guarantors — neither the US nor Israel can unilaterally exit the final deal without a UNSC crisis. Iran’s durability anchor.
Implementation — weeks 1–5 (carried)

The week-by-week implementation record through 16 Jul — the two-way first week, the kinetic second, the tanker attacks and waiver revocation of the third, the central-Iran strikes and Muscat rejection of the fourth, and the blockade's return in the fifth — is carried in the v7–v11 tabs. The through-line: each week tested a different Article, and by week five a core term (Article 4) had formally reversed.

Implementation — week 6 · v12

The window (Art 3): Tehran suspended its MoU commitments on 18 Jul — Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei declared Trump's signature “invalid,” Deputy FM Gharibabadi announced the suspension, and Rezaei said diplomacy and negotiations “are over,” while Ghalibaf (16 Jul, state TV) and a Nour News op-ed (18 Jul) still argued for the talks track. ISW's negotiations section for the window: “nothing significant to report.” Casualties: two US service members killed at Muwaffaq Salti Airbase, Jordan (17 Jul, ascribed to the IRGC); a third killed in Iraqi Kurdistan (18 Jul); US toll 17 since 28 Feb. Blockade (Art 4): enforcement kinetic — three vessels redirected, one disabled, the M/T Wen Yao boarded; General License X1 expired 17 Jul, completing the Article 10 reversal; the 30-day full-lift deadline passed in breach the same day. Hormuz (Art 5): the IRGC Navy's permission regime stated openly; a Thai-flagged vessel struck 17 Jul; Kpler counted eight transits on 16 Jul; UNCLOS-based “environmental services” fees floated. Strikes: sixth, seventh and eighth consecutive US nights (16–18 Jul) — Bandar Abbas bridges, rail and telecoms severed, Chabahar, Oghab 44, and the IRGC launch infrastructure behind the Gulf-state attacks; three US officials call them “shaping operations.” Retaliation: seven countries — Kuwait (power, desalination and oil facilities struck three days running), Bahrain, Qatar, Oman (US radar assets on the Salamah Archipelago and Ghanem Island), Saudi Arabia (al Kharj missile, sirens at Yanbu), Syria (al Tanf) and Jordan (Muwaffaq Salti, then four missiles at Aqaba on 19 Jul). Nuclear (Art 8): the AEOI says a US strike hit the Darkhovin plant (19 Jul); Araghchi calls some nuclear demands possibly “unresolvable.” Leadership: Araghchi disclosed a six-person SNSC special committee making on-the-spot decisions while Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei — severely injured in the strikes that killed his father — is reportedly hard to reach; ISW assesses Vahidi very likely a member. Yemen: Reuters (16 Jul, single root source) reports Iran instructed the Houthis to prepare to close Bab el-Mandeb if the US strikes Iranian power plants; Houthi-Saudi cross-border attacks resumed for the first time since 2022. Lebanon (Art 1): the LAF began deploying into the pilot zones 16–17 Jul — the one obligation moving forward.

Implementation — week 7 · v13

The window (20–23 Jul): the suspension holds — ISW's negotiations section still reads “nothing significant to report” — while a four-party written framework (Qatar, Egypt, Pakistan, Oman, ~20 Jul) revives the June interim agreement's shape: a 10-day ceasefire, both Hormuz lanes reopened (southern free of Iranian attack, northern free of US blockade), and the fee question posed as Malacca-style Iranian service fees or an IMO-administered fund. Iran confirmed receipt; no talks are scheduled. Second chokepoint: the Houthis blockaded Saudi Red Sea port calls from 20 Jul, citing the Saudi siege of Sana'a, and struck the Encelia and Layla on 22 Jul (one hit UKMTO-confirmed); Bab el-Mandeb transits fell 64 to 30, recovering to 40 by 23 Jul, with at least seven diversions and an EU Naval Force warning. Strikes: the eleventh and twelfth consecutive US nights reached Bushehr Airport, Larak Island, Behbahan (the IRGC 15th Special Forces Brigade base), western and north-western Iran, and the Parchin complex near Tehran; Iran struck Dhahran's King Abdulaziz Air Base (a first), US early-warning radar in Kuwait (an AN/FPS-117), Jordanian bases and Aqaba. Workarounds: Iran-Pakistan trade to expand from $3bn toward $10bn with five-fold truck traffic — the land answer to the naval blockade. Posture (23 Jul): Trump threatened Iran and the Houthis with “major military punishment” and told Axios he may expand strikes (“They haven't received enough pain yet”); equities fell and the 10Y hit a one-year high; dozens of fighters and refuellers continue moving to the region. Axis widening: Iranian-backed Iraqi militias likely droned Kuwait's Abdali border crossing on 23 Jul — the first Axis attack on a regional border crossing since 11 Jul — with explosions reported on Bubiyan Island; the IRGC claims a southern-corridor tanker struck a naval mine, a claim ISW cannot observe and reads as deterrence messaging against the Omani route.

Implementation — week 8 · v14

The window (24–28 Jul): the suspension stands on paper while both sides stop shooting — no US strikes in Iran after 24 Jul (the first pause in 13 nights), Iranian attacks ending with a single Bahrain strike in the first window, and a senior Iranian official telling Reuters (26 Jul) the halt lasts as long as Washington's does, conveyed directly. ISW's 27 Jul edition had “nothing significant to report” on negotiations; its 28 Jul edition leads with them — the pause itself remains behaviour, with no agreed term behind it. Blockade (Art 4): maintained and enforced through the pause — the LPG carrier Lavine disabled in the Gulf of Oman on 24 Jul after repeated run attempts, two sailors reported killed per Iranian media; the tanker Charminar boarded 25 Jul and released. Hormuz (Art 5): the Tehran table works the strait directly — Iran-Oman delegations met 24–25 Jul on restarting strait traffic — the lead proposal reopening the likely-mined middle passage — with the UK and France offering demining once safe and Iran seeking joint management likely to include fees (Bloomberg); Baghaei claims “progress” while saying strait traffic is unchanged, and ISW records no vessel attacks in the strait since 20 Jul with traffic fallen and deterrence running on the mine threat. The proposal's reported terms (27 Jul): a formal 10-day truce — the strait reopened; the blockade lifted, asset-unfreezing considered — with an Omani regional-consortium design echoing the defunct Clause 5 consultation requirement; Iran is refusing to concede control. Lebanon (Art 1): Mojtaba Khamenei reaffirms Hezbollah's preservation and full Israeli capitulation in Lebanon as the “first condition” for resolving the war under the 17 Jun MoU; the LAF accuses the IDF of hindering the pilot zones (27 Jul) while making its first pilot-zone weapons-cache seizure the same day (undocumented by ISW); Rome expansion talks are set for 4–6 Aug. Contested: the NYT reports Iran rejected the US framework carried by Iraqi PM Zaydi on 23 Jul — no temporary deal leaving Hormuz unresolved — and Zaydi's office denies it on 24 Jul; Pakistani officials say both Washington and Tehran “have responded” to the joint Pakistani-Qatari proposal, content uncharacterised.

Implementation — week 9 · v15

The window (28–31 Jul): the pause ends on Iran's initiative — IRGC ballistic missiles at Muwaffaq Salti Airbase (28 Jul, five intercepted per Jordan; CENTCOM: an “attempted surprise attack”), launched shortly after Iran rejected compromise on strait control (ISW). Hormuz (Art 5): the Omani proposal — reopen the strait against a lifted blockade with asset-unfreezing considered, a regional consortium and voluntary fees — is rejected (a senior official to Reuters, 29 Jul, “unrealistic”); Gharibabadi said on 28 Jul that Iran would go to war for strait sovereignty (per ISW); the IRGC Navy claims three tanker strikes on the southern route, the first strait vessel attacks since 20 Jul; transits run under 10/day (desk series). Blockade (Art 4): stands; Iran's Khatam ol Anbia headquarters had already called it an escalation the armed forces “will respond accordingly” to — the Jordan strike appears to be that response. The proxy front: joint US-Saudi strikes on militia weapons and logistics sites across Iraq and the Iran-Iraq border (28 Jul; retaliation for militia attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure and US interests per ISW; at least four Quds Force officers reported killed in Diyala); Trump promises to hit Iran hard; through ISW's 29 Jul cutoff no resumed US strikes on Iran itself, and no US answer to the Jordan attack. Lebanon (Art 1): carried — the first pilot-zone cache seizure stands (undocumented by ISW); Rome expansion talks 4–6 Aug. Second front: the Houthis threaten expanded attacks on Saudi targets and float Red Sea transit fees; Global21 carries a single-source claim of a ~50-nation Saudi coalition to force Bab el-Mandeb open, announcement expected “next week”; an unattributed drone attack targets a US-owned tanker at Damietta, Egypt (29 Jul) — a Mediterranean first, logged as a vector.

Implementation — week 10 · v16

The window (31 Jul–4 Aug): the suspension stands while both capitals work the corridor design. Strikes: a new attack ordered for the 1–2 Aug weekend (WSJ, 31 Jul) with energy infrastructure under consideration (CBS), then canceled on 1 Aug — Trump citing agreed deal parameters; ISW records no US strike activity in the window. Iran's SNSC vowed to strengthen strait control and close other waterways — “the price will be paid by US citizens and the global economy” — and IRGC-affiliated outlets published a six-country energy-facility target list. Blockade (Art 4): first published enforcement tallies — 45 vessels redirected, two disabled, two boarded since 14 Jul (CENTCOM, 4 Aug). Hormuz (Art 5): Iran's Strait Authority announces no transit permits until US operations end (31 Jul); CENTCOM states the strait remains open; at least four southern-route transits counted in the 31 Jul–1 Aug window; UKMTO projectile incidents 31 Jul (the Gaslog Shanghai), 2 Aug (a failed attack ISW ties to the IRGC Navy) and 3 Aug (a cargo ship in Omani waters). The US-Qatari two-corridor design — inbound Iranian waters, outbound Omani waters, no tolls — is floated 3–4 Aug; Iran counters with monitoring and intervention rights, “service fees,” blockade relief and sanctions relief. Talks (Art 3): Trump announces on 2 Aug that US and Iranian officials will soon meet on the strait and nuclear issues — the first prospective nuclear-file table since the suspension; Baghaei's formal response lands the same day, and the negotiator/IRGC split runs open. Reconstitution (Art 9): Artesh spokesperson Akraminia states on the record that Iran “fully exploited” the MoU and ceasefire to import, repair and produce new systems — including drones already used against US Gulf bases — the reconstitution ISW has assessed since July, now stated by the regime itself; separately, two senior IRGC officers tell the NYT that Quds Force commanders coordinated with Hezbollah, the Houthis and Iraqi militias during the April ceasefire to raise the war's cost, with Reuters carrying eight Iraqi sources on IRGC covert cells in Iraq. Lebanon (Art 1): Rome talks resumed 4–6 Aug on pilot-zone disarmament verification; the LAF seized a Grad-rocket shipment near Aarsal (4 Aug); judiciary authorization for private-property searches is outstanding, which ISW assesses will stall disarmament if unresolved. Second front: the Houthis likely sank the Indian-flagged MSV Faize Noore Oliya near Bab el-Mandeb (4 Aug, one-way naval drone, per India's shipping minister) and hit Najran airport's main radar (4 Aug, Saudi-unconfirmed); the Houthi operations centre denies imposing transit fees (1 Aug); Saudi-Houthi indirect talks run via Omani mediation with the US privately discouraging Saudi retaliation (Bloomberg, 4 Aug); Saudi Red Sea exports run at 3.5mn bpd per the Economist (30 Jul) — the panel-claimed halt is contradicted and carried contested. Iraq: Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Kuwait reportedly warn Baghdad they will strike militias inside Iraq on further attacks (31 Jul); Zaydi orders a joint security committee (1 Aug); the US reportedly withholds ~$30bn of Saddam-era funds pending militia disarmament (2 Aug); the PMF reportedly evacuates its Ninewa headquarters anticipating strikes (2 Aug); Iraqi sources put the 28 Jul strike toll at 20+ PMF members — a wider count than the ≥4 Quds Force officers carried at v15, different reference classes.

Implementation — week 11 · v17

The window (5–10 Aug): the suspension stands; the corridor design waits on Tehran. Talks (Art 3): the meeting announced on 2 Aug has not convened — Araghchi on the record (9 Aug): no talks with the US while it is “in violation” of the MoU, the Iran-Oman track in “final stages” but not reopening the strait; Zolghadr conditions reopening on six US concessions (8 Aug); Khamenei replaces him at the SNSC with Rezaei (9 Aug). Blockade (Art 4): enforced and visible in flow — the FT reports no crude loaded at Kharg Island for at least a week, tankers unable to return from Asia, storage constrained; Pezeshkian concedes costlier import routes; the US Treasury adds shadow-banking sanctions (7 Aug), central bank governor Hemmati calling them contradictory to Bessent's deal talk. Hormuz (Art 5): an Iranian missile strikes a UAE state-oil-company tanker (8 Aug, no casualties); UKMTO reports two explosions heard from a vessel in Omani waters (5 Aug); a Qatari-linked LNG carrier attacked in the strait reaches the desk as a delayed 10 Aug report, headline-level; Trump claims the strait is “open now” and US-controlled (10 Aug). Reparations (Art 6): Iran ties reopening to compensation; Trump counters with his own demands and denies compensation was ever discussed — the signed $300bn fund is the clause in contest. Second front: a Houthi drone strikes Aramco's Jizan refinery (8 Aug, fire confirmed; at least the second blaze in a month), an attack in Najran province wounds 11, and Marib City takes ~20 ballistic missiles (at least two killed); the Iraqi militias' planned IRGC- and Houthi-coordinated strikes on Saudi energy infrastructure pause via Ameri's mediation under Iraqi deployments described as “unprecedented” (ISW corroborates only a few); the Houthis reportedly run a coordination headquarters from a Kataib Hezbollah stronghold south of Baghdad. Alliances: Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan sign a joint defence agreement with a collective-defence provision (7 Aug). Lebanon (Art 1): the Rome round produces a tentative shortlist of countries to verify pilot-zone disarmament, the US to approve the final pick; direct negotiations resume 1 Sep; an Israeli drone strikes an LAF bulldozer in Tyre District (7 Aug, one soldier wounded). Workarounds: Lebanese ministers convene (10 Aug) on an Iraq-Syria-Lebanon overland oil route to Tripoli — per ISW no near-term alternative to Hormuz, and exposed to ISIS attack in Syria.

The series closes at week 11. The 60-day term lapsed on 17 Aug with the two 60-day deliverables — the Article 6 implementation mechanism and the Article 12 security-architecture design — undelivered; the running record continues in Appendix A4.

A3 · Resolution mechanics and the strait-management variants

Resolution mechanics

The Resolution path follows the framework David specified: Mearsheimer's “humble pie” off-ramp; a JPOA 2.0 nuclear architecture; the Ferguson Hormuz Council (Iran as Chair, a 45% / 30% / balance revenue split, transit fees at cost); HEU export under a Security Guarantee with Russia available as custodian; and a post-war Gulf Treaty Organisation with China and Russia as signatories. The realised Stage-1 MOU diverged from the Council mechanic on Hormuz — toll-free reopening under Iranian and Omani management rather than a chaired revenue split — and ISW's structural read of the collapse stands: the two sides read Clause 5 in fundamentally different ways, and the Gulf states rejected Iranian management and fees. The strait-management variants since:

  • Four-party framework (Qatar / Egypt / Pakistan / Oman, ~20 Jul) — dual-lane reopening, the fee question posed as Malacca-style Iranian service fees or an IMO-administered fund. Receipt confirmed; never convened as a table.
  • Tehran middle-passage table (24–25 Jul) — reopening the likely-mined middle passage under joint management likely to include fees, UK/French demining offered, the Witkoff/Kushner channel inside the room. Superseded by the Omani design.
  • Omani regional consortium (27–28 Jul) — a 10-day truce, the strait reopened against the blockade lifted, a regional consortium with voluntary fees. Rejected (“unrealistic,” a senior official to Reuters, 29 Jul) — the second Omani fee design refused.
  • US-Qatari two-corridor design (3–4 Aug) — inbound through Iranian waters, outbound through Omani waters, no tolls; the first to drop the fee mechanism entirely. Stalled in Tehran: approval absent (AP), the IRGC extracting fees, traffic-control language and relief (WSJ), the fee question back in the IRGC's own media — the toll outcome BCA priced, now described by the regime's own outlet — and the reparations exchange adding a term no prior variant carried. Whether the draft sent up to Tehran's leadership contains fees is itself unreported; US officials and mediators had said the design carried none. Orphaned by the lapse: the term expired 17 Aug, Washington told Oman it opposes the joint-management leg (AP, 18 Aug), and no talks are scheduled.

Every design short of recognised Iranian control with revenue attached has been refused — the sovereignty question this file has carried since v3, answered in Iran's favour. Stavridis's dual-key prediction (Iran northbound, Oman southbound) is this design's shape, and his 60% renewed-negotiations path carries it — though the 17–18 Aug record leans toward his 30% escalation path (section 03); Mearsheimer's year-end expectation of a renegotiated MoU on terms worse for the US is the same destination read from the withdrawal side. With the term lapsed, talks disavowed and every producing channel — Doha, Muscat, the Tehran table, the UAE — severed or stalled, the mechanics stay as the reference for whatever table forms next.

A4 · Escalation timeline — 8 Jun to 20 Aug

The 8 Jun – 20 Aug record

8–17 Jun
Ceasefire collapses then resolves onto de-escalation: Israeli and US strikes inside Iran (8–10 Jun); Trump declares the deal “complete” (15 Jun); the US and Iran sign the MoU two days early (17 Jun), with signed edits to Clause 1 (Lebanon) and Clause 5 (Hormuz). The blockade lifts and oil sanctions waive on signing.
19 Jun–12 Jul
Implementation, then four escalation rounds of rising scale: the first 60-day-track round at Bürgenstock (21–22 Jun); the Ever Lovely exchange and stand-down (25–30 Jun); the tanker attacks and oil-waiver revocation (6–8 Jul); the ~140-target wave reaching central Iran, five-Gulf-state retaliation, and Iran's rejection of Oman's two-corridor proposal (9–12 Jul). Talks resume at Iran's request (10 Jul) even as Trump maintains the ceasefire is over.
13–16 Jul
The blockade returns (14 Jul), targeted at Iranian-flagged shipping; the 20% fee floats and drops within a day; strikes reach roughly 200km inland (15 Jul); Iran strikes three vessels on the Omani route, retaliates against Kuwait, Bahrain and Jordan, and on 16 Jul declares the strait an “inviolable red line.” The Iran-Oman channel goes quiet; the mediation-breakdown trigger fires (v11).
17 Jul
An Iranian missile attack on Muwaffaq Salti Airbase, Jordan kills two US service members, with one missing — the first US deaths of the conflict. The sixth consecutive US strike night severs the bridges, rail and telecoms feeding Bandar Abbas; Iran strikes a Kuwaiti power-and-desalination plant and, for the first time, near al Tanf in Syria; a Thai-flagged vessel is struck on the Omani route; Kpler counts eight strait transits the prior day. General License X1 expires, revoking all Iranian-oil transaction authority; the MoU's 30-day full-lift deadline passes in breach. Murrin publishes WW3 116, declaring Chapter Two of the war.
18 Jul
Tehran formally suspends the MoU: Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei declares Trump's signature “invalid” and Deputy FM Gharibabadi announces suspension of commitments. The seventh US strike night; Iran fires a ballistic missile at a US base near al Kharj, Saudi Arabia — its first strike on Saudi territory in about three months, with sirens at Yanbu — and hits Kuwaiti power, desalination and oil facilities a second day. Brent settles ~$88, up 4.6%, the biggest weekly advance since April. A third US service member is fatally wounded in Iraqi Kurdistan disposing of ordnance from a downed Iranian drone.
19 Jul
CENTCOM announces the third US death. Iran's AEOI says a US strike hit the Darkhovin nuclear plant in Khuzestan (IAEA: very early construction, no nuclear material at the last inspection). Four ballistic missiles at Aqaba, southern Jordan — a first; Kuwaiti infrastructure hit a third day running. Araghchi disclosed a six-person SNSC committee deciding on the spot while the Supreme Leader is reportedly hard to reach, and says some nuclear demands may remain “unresolvable.” The eighth consecutive US strike night (18 Jul) included the IRGC unit behind the Jordan attack.
20 Jul
The IRGC Navy states its permission regime openly after halting four vessels: “not a single drop of oil, gas, or chemical fertilizer” passes without its coordination. The US moves more F-16s, F-35s and refuellers to the region; Israel's Katz warns Iran that Israel will re-engage if attacked. Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Qatar condemn the infrastructure strikes; Jordan summons an Iranian diplomat; China and Pakistan urge resumed dialogue. The Houthis declare a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia effective immediately (Yahya Saree), citing the Saudi siege of Sana'a; the Qatar/Egypt/Pakistan/Oman written framework circulates, and Iran's FM spokesperson confirms receipt.
21–22 Jul
The eleventh and twelfth consecutive US strike nights reach Bushehr Airport, Larak Island, Behbahan, western and north-western Iran, and the Parchin complex near Tehran. Iran puts first missiles on Dhahran's King Abdulaziz Air Base and strikes US early-warning radar in Kuwait. The Houthi blockade turns kinetic: missile and drone strikes claimed on the Saudi tankers Encelia and Layla (one hit later UKMTO-confirmed), Bab el-Mandeb transits down 64 to 30, an EU Naval Force warning out. Ukraine strikes the Caspian Pipeline Consortium, halting ~1mn bpd of Kazakh flow. Brent settles $88.52 on 21 Jul, the highest since 11 Jun.
23 Jul
Brent settles $100.69, up 7%, after touching $102 — the first settle above $100 since May — on the Red Sea tanker attacks. Trump threatens Iran and the Houthis with “major military punishment” if the attacks continue — the Houthis named a “Surrogate and/or Proxy of Iran” — and tells Axios he may expand strikes (“They haven't received enough pain yet”), squaring the desk digest's “major operation” line. US equities fall (S&P -1.2%, Nasdaq -2.2%, Tesla and Alphabet earnings-day falls compounding) and the 10Y moves through 4.65% to 4.69%. Rubio: Tehran's leadership is “not ready to make a deal” (BBC). Dozens of fighters and refuellers continue deploying; no talks are scheduled on the framework. UKMTO confirms a Saudi-tanker hit; transits recover to 40. Iranian-backed Iraqi militias likely drone Kuwait's Abdali border crossing (material damage, no casualties) with explosions on Bubiyan Island; the IRGC claims a southern-corridor tanker mined — unobserved by ISW. The 13th consecutive US strike night follows into 24 Jul, with missiles reported on Qeshm Island in the strait; the House votes to direct a halt to the campaign, and the Senate blocks a similar measure hours later. [The desk Bloomberg series later puts the day's peak at ~$94 — the print divergence with the AP settle is flagged at section 05.]
24 Jul
Strikes reach northern Iran for the first time (the IRGC Navy commando college in Gilan) as Iran's drone campaign against US base housing runs across Bahrain, Jordan, Qatar and Kuwait. US forces disable the LPG carrier Lavine in the Gulf of Oman — two sailors reported killed per Iranian media — the first deaths in this file's blockade-enforcement record. The NYT reports a 23 Jul Iranian rejection of the US framework carried by Iraqi PM Zaydi; Zaydi's office denies it the same day (24 Jul) — carried as contested. Trump convenes an options meeting, an Omani delegation arrives in Tehran, and a strike hold is reportedly ordered within hours: no overnight wave into 25 Jul, the first pause in 13 nights. Unclaimed airstrikes are reported on Hudaydah.
25–26 Jul
The pause holds on both sides — one Iranian attack (Bahrain) in the first window, then none; Iranian officials say the restraint lasts as long as the US hold does. Iranian and Omani delegations meet in Tehran (24–25 Jul) on a Hormuz agreement; Baghaei claims “progress” (26 Jul) while saying strait traffic is unchanged, and parliamentarians insist control is not returning to pre-war conditions. Pakistani officials say both Washington and Tehran “have responded” to the joint Pakistani-Qatari proposal. CENTCOM boards the Charminar (25 Jul). The Saudi-Houthi exchange runs on: coalition strikes on Hudaydah, Jawf and Marib; Houthi missiles at Yanbu intercepted by Greek-operated defences while munitions impact Jizan; the NCC Masa attacked; a Saudi Akinci drone downed over Jawf. Mojtaba Khamenei is reported out of contact “due to certain issues” (Haddad Adel). A senior Iranian official tells Reuters (26 Jul) Iran will halt attacks as long as the US halts, conveyed directly; Mojtaba's 26 Jul statement names Hezbollah's preservation the “first condition” for resolving the war. Ukraine strikes sanctioned Caspian cargo vessels; Zelenskyy says Russia supplies satellite imagery of US Gulf bases.
27 Jul
Saudi Arabia says it shot down drones from Iraq aimed at Eastern Province petroleum facilities and Riyadh — ISW assesses Iranian-backed Iraqi militias, preserving Tehran's deniability — and a fire burns at Abqaiq, unclaimed by any actor; Saree claims strikes on the oil-transport corridor to the Red Sea hubs. The LAF accuses the IDF of hindering the pilot zones. Bloomberg details the middle-passage proposal — UK/French demining offers, joint management with fees, Witkoff and Kushner involved; Trump tells Axios “deep talks” are under way. Iraq's PM works the bypass-pipeline circuit toward Ankara and Riyadh. A US official and mediators tell Western media the Omani track has tabled a formal 10-day truce — the strait reopened against the blockade lifted and asset-unfreezing considered, a regional consortium proposed for management — and Iran is refusing to concede control. The LAF makes its first pilot-zone weapons-cache seizure (unverified by ISW); the Islamic Resistance in Iraq denies the Saudi drone claims.
28 Jul
Trump meets Netanyahu in Washington and tells reporters there is a “good chance” talks with Iran make progress (Bloomberg). Brent settles $84.09, down 4.8% on the day and roughly 16% over three sessions — the worst run since April 2020 — with WTI at $79.26, CTA Brent length cut to 62% from 73%, and CIBC reading the move as positioning on “MOU 2.0” hopes; Hormuz traffic stays muted with transponders dark. Treasuries rally as oil retreats; swaps price roughly one-in-three odds of a hike at the FOMC, with Citadel Securities and PGIM calling for one and August fed-funds futures open interest at records. Macquarie warns a deal would leave Q4 oversupplied by ~2mn bpd; OPEC+ is expected to pause quota hikes after September. The Houthis claim ballistic missiles on the tanker NCC Ghazal — their third claimed attack on Saudi shipping since 22 Jul (UKMTO-unconfirmed). Reuters: China has asked the Houthis for safe passage for its tankers — one source describes each ship being cleared individually — and at least four Saudi-oil cargoes to China have transited Bab el-Mandeb since 20 Jul. The first mass protest since January in Malekshahr, Esfahan, over the execution of three winter protesters. Iraqi-Saudi talks convene on the drone claims; Rome pilot-zone expansion talks are set for 4–6 Aug.
28–29 Jul · the break
IRGC ballistic missiles target Muwaffaq Salti Airbase in Jordan — an “attempted surprise attack” per CENTCOM, five intercepted per the Jordanian Army — ending the four-day pause shortly after Iran rejects compromise on strait control (ISW). The IRGC Navy claims strikes on three tankers on the southern route. The US and Saudi Arabia jointly strike militia weapons and logistics sites across Iraq and the Iran-Iraq border — retaliation for militia attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure and US interests — with at least four IRGC Quds Force officers reported killed in Diyala. On 29 Jul a senior Iranian official rejects the Omani proposal to Reuters (“unrealistic”); Gharibabadi (28 Jul, per ISW) says Iran would go to war for strait sovereignty; an unattributed drone attack targets a US-owned tanker at Damietta, Egypt; the Houthis float Red Sea transit fees. The Fed holds 9–3 with no forward guidance — the 29 Jul US session sells off (S&P -1.5% to 7,316) with the 30Y through its 2007 high and oil surging; Trump promises to hit Iran hard (internal desk record).
30–31 Jul
The AI leg turns the 30 Jul US session — Microsoft +16%, a record ~$450bn one-day add — while Brent settles ~$88 (desk series; its 23 Jul peak ~$94, the AP divergence flagged at section 05) and the SPR ledger shows 307.6m barrels with ~25m contracted barrels left. Global21 carries the claimed Saudi coalition to force Bab el-Mandeb open (single-source). The Kospi closes a record 18% higher on 31 Jul as the AI trade returns. 13D's WILTW reports “the nuclear issue is no longer viewed as taboo in Tehran” and calls August the most dangerous month.
31 Jul–1 Aug · the canceled strike
WSJ reports Trump ordered a new attack on Iran “as soon as this weekend”; CBS reports energy infrastructure — refineries, power plants — under consideration; Trump at the Camp David cabinet meeting: “We'll be hitting them very hard.” WTI trades above $86 post-settlement. Iran's SNSC vows to strengthen strait control and close other waterways; the Strait Authority announces no transit permits until US operations end; CENTCOM says the strait remains open; UKMTO logs a projectile in the Gaslog Shanghai's engine room off Oman. On 1 Aug Trump says he canceled the strikes on being told deal parameters were agreed — Axios reports MBS raised concerns over the plans; the Washington Post reports a US general warning the Pentagon lacks sufficient forces to protect Israel; ISW records no US strike activity. The NYT carries two senior IRGC officers on Quds Force coordination with Hezbollah, the Houthis and Iraqi militias during the April ceasefire; the Houthi operations centre denies imposing Bab el-Mandeb transit fees. Japan's record ~¥8.45tn single-day yen intervention (30 Jul) is followed by the first joint US-Japan intervention in nearly 30 years (31 Jul, per the FT).
2–3 Aug
Trump announces US and Iranian officials will soon meet on reopening the strait and on nuclear issues (2 Aug). WSJ reports Qatari mediators presented a new reopening proposal with Iranian diplomats responding “positively”; Israeli media report Araghchi agreed to a US-Qatari split-route design — and the same day Baghaei says on the record the proposal “has nothing to do with” opening the strait (the Iran-formal-response trigger fires a third time) while IRGC-affiliated media deny any agreement. Artesh spokesperson Akraminia says Iran “fully exploited” the ceasefire to rearm, including new drones already used against US Gulf bases. On 3 Aug Trump frames the hold — “holding off on a big strike” because “everyone in the region” is “begging for talks”; WSJ reports negotiators support the corridor design but await IRGC approval; Rezaei rules out “a second corridor” (referent ambiguous per ISW); Zarif calls the strait a “bargaining chip” whose leverage decays; the Assembly of Experts brands “calls for surrender” an “unforgivable betrayal.” UKMTO logs further projectile incidents (2–3 Aug). The Mearsheimer panel transcript circulates on David's thread; the Monday session rallies (S&P +1.5% to 7,601) with crude falling.
4–6 Aug
The two-corridor design is detailed — inbound via Iranian waters, outbound via Omani waters, no tolls — and Iranian diplomats counter with monitoring and intervention rights, “service fees,” blockade relief and sanctions relief. CENTCOM publishes its first blockade tallies: 45 vessels redirected, two disabled, two boarded since 14 Jul. The Houthis likely sink the Indian-flagged MSV Faize Noore Oliya near Bab el-Mandeb — the first sinking at the second chokepoint — and hit Najran airport's main radar; Saudi-Houthi indirect talks run via Oman with the US privately discouraging retaliation. Rome talks on the Lebanon pilot zones resume (4–6 Aug). Japan's 10Y auction draws the weakest demand since May 2025; Bessent calls the yen's level a regional problem. The Tuesday session rallies further (S&P +1.8% to 7,737), the desk attributing crude's further fall to Iran confirming reopening talks — a desk attribution with no primary source behind it, flagged. Stavridis publishes the three-path piece (4 Aug); Gary forwards it and David designates it the scenario-stress starting position (5 Aug). Rubio narrows the immediate US ask to the strait — denuclearisation “the ultimate deal” (4 Aug); Baghaei describes provisional inbound/outbound management protocols on the Iran-Oman channel; Bessent predicts Iran may agree “today or tomorrow to open the strait” (CNBC, 4 Aug); the FT has oil easing below $80. The FT synthesis reaches the desk on 6 Aug via Gary, and the yen/JGB leg goes onto the firm's scenario-stress list (per David's 6 Aug note).
5–7 Aug · the stall surfaces
Two regional officials tell the AP the supreme leader has not approved the draft Iran-Oman agreement, against Axios's 4 Aug approval report; ISW ties the delay to the factional split, the rounds run without the IRGC in the room. IRGC-affiliated media describe a toll-bearing variant — entrance management plus “insurance, fueling, and environmental fees” — while a Saudi source describes a fee-free one; Fars carries draft terms barring US and Israeli shipping with penalties to 20% of cargo value; Reuters' industry sources read the design as Iranian “control” over inbound traffic. Mediators tell the WSJ the IRGC is holding up the draft to extract fees, traffic-control language and relief. UKMTO: two explosions heard from a vessel in Omani waters (5 Aug). The US Treasury sanctions Iran's shadow-banking network (7 Aug). Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan sign a joint defence agreement; the Iraqi militias' planned attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure pause via Ameri's mediation.
8–9 Aug · six demands, a hardliner to the SNSC
Zolghadr conditions the strait's reopening on six US concessions, including the blockade, sanctions, force withdrawal, frozen assets and war reparations; Araghchi says Iran and Oman are close on a temporary route, reopening “subject to other conditions.” An Iranian missile strikes a UAE state-oil-company tanker; the FT reports Kharg Island at least a week without loading crude. A Houthi drone strikes Aramco's Jizan refinery (fire confirmed). On 9 Aug Khamenei appoints Mohsen Rezaei SNSC secretary, demoting Zolghadr; Babai threatens “any country that wants to assist the United States”; Araghchi rules out talks with the US while it violates the June MoU — the Iran-formal-response trigger fires a fourth time.
10–11 Aug · reparations enter the terms
After the weekend's positions — Araghchi's “very close” on an Oman pact beside his refusal of direct talks, Trump's “low-keying it” to Axios — Trump on Monday demands compensation for roadside-bomb deaths and Iran's protest dead, expanding it to Lebanon, Syria, Yemen and Gaza — “firmly into any, and all, future negotiations” — and claims the strait is “open now” and US-controlled; Baghaei ties reopening to the siege lifted and damages compensated. Brent rises about 5% to end near $88 (Bloomberg), extending a three-session rally above 5%; European diesel futures surge more than 10% on refinery attacks in Saudi Arabia, Libya and Russia; the S&P closes 7,753, off 0.1%, as yields jump. Citrinowicz's pressure-track read circulates via Gary.
11–16 Aug
A strike on the Egyptian cargo ship Tihamah at Bab el-Mandeb kills four crew and two Yemeni coastguard responders (11 Aug) — the second fatal incident at the second chokepoint after Mocha Port (9 Aug, seven killed). Rezaei’s first week adds a region-wide ceasefire (Lebanon and Gaza) to Iran’s reopening conditions (11 Aug). Kharg Island’s western terminal reactivates on 12 Aug after a 25-day halt — two VLCCs load through 16 Aug while the eastern terminal sits idle and 16–17 tankers wait offshore — and Saudi Aramco resumes VLCC loadings from inside the strait after a three-week gap. Trump curtails the premier annual US–South Korea exercise over Seoul’s refusal to help open the strait (16 Aug, per Bloomberg). Brent settles $86.82 (12 Aug) then $85.94 (13 Aug); the 10-year auction draws 4.683% (12 Aug) and the 30-year 5.216% (13 Aug), the highest since 2007 and 2001.
17 Aug · the term lapses
The signed text’s 60-day negotiation window expires with the nuclear and sanctions files never opened — Baghaei calls the deadline “entirely moot.” Trump warns of attacks against Oman, the mediator, the same day; a senior Iranian official tells Reuters Iran goes “fully offensive” and attacks to break the blockade if diplomacy fails; WSJ details IRGC plans laid during the MoU calm — preemptive strikes on Gulf internet cables, fomented unrest in Kuwait and Bahrain, potential ground operations in Kuwait, a Saudi confrontation coordinated with Iraqi militias and the Houthis. The 30-year Treasury closes at 5.31%, the highest since 2007; the S&P falls 0.5% to 7,745 on the expiry and the Oman warning. Kim Jong Un answers Trump’s overtures.
18–19 Aug · the war reaches the UAE
Two ballistic missiles fly toward the UAE (18 Aug) — one into its territorial waters, targeting maritime traffic on the Emirati account, the first attack on UAE territory since May; Iran denies firing them. The UAE halts all trade and financial transactions with Iran “until further notice” — the first Gulf-state economic rupture of the war: roughly a third of Iran’s imports, ~37% of its essential goods and ~80% of its imported foreign exchange transit the UAE (ISW). Trump: “There are no talks or conversations going on, or scheduled, with the Islamic Republic of Iran” (18 Aug); AP reports Washington told Oman it opposes joint Iranian-Omani management of the strait’s exit route. NBC documents Russian materiel entering Iran via the Caspian — drone components, ammunition, TNT — as of July. Rubio calls Sheikh Tahnoon on Hormuz security; Brent settles $89.79 on 19 Aug, trading above $91 intraday; Baghdad asks Iran for “special status” strait exports, and an Iraqi militia hands 20 Iranian-made drones to the government in front of US officials.
19–20 Aug · the buyback turn
The US Treasury announces it is at least doubling 10–30 year liquidity-support buybacks; the 30-year falls up to 10bp to 5.18% and the dollar hits a three-month low — Deutsche Bank’s Saravelos: “Operation twist is here… soft-form financial repression.” Per David’s 19 Aug note, the move is a reach toward yield-curve control — his conclusion, gold above $4,500. Bessent follows (20 Aug): buybacks may exceed $4bn per issue, a fiscal-consolidation announcement due within days; the national debt crosses $40tn the same week, and David’s 21 Aug note flags Bessent’s Iran plan for Monday 24 Aug. Brent settles $90.08 on 20 Aug — a fourth consecutive higher session per the desk monitor, and the first settle inside the $90–110 band since 23 Jul — with Murban at a four-month-high $97.75 and the SPR at 293.4m barrels (week to 14 Aug), the lowest since 1982.
