v19 · The Treasury takes the war; the strait under escort · 7 Sep 2026
Architecture, verdict & Brent bands held · US, Iran, Israel, China, Russia, Houthi and GCC cells moved · Resolution tier MoU lapsed, channels ruptured → Economic-pressure phase; corridor dead · Iran-formal-response fires a sixth time · Mediation-breakdown a third · Israeli-strike fires for the first time · Brent round-trips the floor: $92.67 → $86.30 → $92.09, ~$97 intraday · record backwardation · SPR 286.6m · Murrin WW3 119 into the due diligence · a dated update covering 21 Aug – 7 Sep

The architecture holds — Stalemate (modal) / Resolution (economic-pressure phase; corridor dead) / apex in the long-term allocation. The Iran plan v18 carried as a watch item landed on 24 Aug as Operation Economic Outcast, and the campaign’s centre of gravity moved from the blockade to the Treasury. Iran’s economy broke visibly; the Iran-Oman corridor was tabled, claimed signed by the IRGC, and died without opening; US strikes inside Iran resumed 30 Aug while escort and mine clearance moved strait flow back toward pre-war levels; the IDF cleared the Ali al Taher IRGC complex in Lebanon on 3 Sep. Brent round-tripped the band floor and re-entered on escalation pricing.

What moved from v18 — the full change list
  • The Bessent plan landed (24 Aug): Operation Economic Outcast — 60-plus designations across Iran’s five “lifelines” (digital assets, technology, gold, aviation, shipping), Section 311 on Banque Misr’s Emirati branches (28 Aug), every country given a “defined timeline to shut down” Iran-linked activity, Bessent addressing Iranian soldiers directly and naming “regime collapse” as the aim. Major Chinese banks were spared ahead of the 24 Sep Trump-Xi summit; Beijing vowed “all necessary measures.” Ghalibaf answered on the record — “no one buys their bombast” — and the Iran-formal-response trigger fires a sixth time.
  • Iran’s economy broke into the acute phase: the rial at a record 2.02m/USD (24 Aug), depreciation running 110% annualised since the 14 Jul blockade reimposition (Brooks), inflation printed 66% (ISW) to ~80% (CE), a $500m central-bank FX injection (25 Aug). The split went on the record: Pezeshkian — “it would be better to end [the war] now”; Ghalibaf — Iran cannot endure the war hungry; Khamenei’s office instructing officials to stop highlighting the economy; 30 alleged protest-organiser arrests and a 313,000-personnel internal-security exercise. ISW reads the anti-concession camp as strengthened by Tehran’s own conclusion that the US subverted the MoU.
  • The corridor died without opening: Iran and Oman announced an “interim framework” (25 Aug); the IRGC claimed a fee-sharing agreement a day later — single-source, confirmed by neither ministry, so the Signed-deal trigger does not fire; Oman never announced it and it never opened (Signaling Reserve V3.2). ISW’s read of the Pakistani channel — mediators “only ferrying unchanged viewpoints” — and Barclays’ “no signs of any negotiations” put the Mediation-breakdown trigger through a third time. The residual channel: Araghchi — diplomacy “isn’t impossible” after “creative discussions” via Qatar (28 Aug).
  • Fighting resumed inside Iran: CENTCOM struck IRGC rocket launchers on Larak Island as they prepared to fire sea mines (30 Aug) — the first US strikes inside Iran in a month (ISW dates the prior strike 29 Jul) — then ~100 IRGC targets on 1 Sep and a second wave overnight 2–3 Sep against radar and mine-laying capability, with a new tanker-for-tanker policy (Axios) and a claimed strike on a Sirik wedding (4+ dead) that CENTCOM denies targeting. Iran struck US bases across five countries — Jordan, Kuwait, Bahrain, Iraq and, for the first time, the UAE (al Minhad, 3 Sep) — with the Artesh stating a preemptive-strike doctrine.
  • The strait came under escort and the flow dispute resolved: CENTCOM declared the traffic separation scheme mine-cleared (27–28 Aug; allies privately doubt full clearance), 500+ escorted ships in 30 days with ~2% hit by Iranian fire, 20–30 tankers a night on the southern route, 17m barrels through on 31 Aug against a ~21.6m bpd pre-war average, ~40 vessels on 1 Sep. v18’s contested flow picture moves toward restoration (counter-data: Axios’s ~50%-of-pre-war summary, Barclays’ ~60%, and Iran’s verification channel authorising ~40% of transits); ISW reads hardline dissatisfaction as flowing from exactly this lost force leverage, the strikes now timed toward the US midterms — the frame BCA and Barclays carry independently.
  • The Israeli front reopened: the IDF cleared the Ali al Taher IRGC/Hezbollah underground complex in Nabatieh after a months-long siege (3 Sep) — 12+ IRGC Qods dead including two senior officers — against a reported mid-Aug Iranian warning that seizing it triggers a “large-scale attack” on Israel (unconfirmed, via Reuters). The Israeli-strike trigger fires for the first time (the caveat is at section 04).
  • Oil round-tripped the floor with record backwardation: Brent settled $92.67 (21 Aug) → $86.30 (27 Aug, on the sanctions-pivot de-escalation read) → $92.09 (2 Sep, +5.9% on the week) and traded to ~$97 intraday 2–3 Sep; Brent and Dubai prompt premiums printed their widest ever (−$3.54 / −$10.08); the SPR drew to 286.6m (28 Aug) with ~4.7m contracted barrels left; CE raised its end-2026 Brent forecast to $100; NDR moved crude bearish → neutral. The $90–110 floor held both ways.
  • The rates leg kept moving: Warsh’s first Jackson Hole speech (28 Aug) drew the largest 2s30s flattening at any Jackson Hole since 1989 and put a September hike near 55–60%; the doubled buybacks run 9 Sep – 4 Nov (Druckenmiller’s WSJ objection on the record); NBIM proposed cutting government bonds from ~70% to 50% of its bond portfolio (~$75bn less in Treasuries); August payrolls beat at +162k; Bessent’s yen campaign has a BOJ hike ~98–99% priced for 18 Sep. CPI 11 Sep and the FOMC 15–16 Sep are the next catalysts.
  • The axis leg extended: FT (1 Sep) — Russia has covertly helped Iran develop advanced cruise-missile technology since ~Nov 2023, alongside the documented Caspian materiel flow; Chinese state shippers have avoided both chokepoints since late July on central guidance.
  • Murrin WW3 119 into the due diligence: “20 Strategic Realities” (18 Aug) graded at Appendix A1 — and the scorecard moves against him this window: WW3 117’s “Iran’s control of the strait remains unchallenged,” corroborated when written, is overtaken by the escort-and-clearance record.
  • Cells move: US “Talks declared over · economic-pain track” → “Economic Outcast launched · strikes resumed inside Iran.” Iran “‘Fully offensive’ declared · missiles reach UAE waters (denied)” → “Rial at 2.02m · strikes five countries.” Israel “Good A/C → regime change” → “Ali al Taher cleared · spoiler channel live.” China “Pushes Resolution” → “Resists isolation · summit constrains both sides.” Russia “Caspian materiel resupply documented” → “Cruise-missile technology aid reported.” Houthis “Fatal strikes at Bab el-Mandeb · Saudi offensive reportedly prepared” → “Strikes reach 950km north · Saudi shields the Red Sea leg.” GCC “UAE cuts all economic ties · the bloc arms wider” → “UAE bases struck a first time · the bloc holds the rupture.” The Resolution tier moves MoU lapsed, channels ruptured → Economic-pressure phase; corridor dead.

Bottom line · the Treasury takes the war; the strait under escort

The scenario set stays bifurcated: Stalemate (modal) and Resolution (economic-pressure phase; corridor dead), with the apex tail held in the long-term allocation below the scenario-modelling threshold. Bessent’s Iran plan landed on 24 Aug as Operation Economic Outcast and became the campaign itself: compliance timelines for every country, “regime collapse” the stated aim, the rial at a record 2.02m and the leadership split on the record. The Iran-Oman corridor died without opening; US strikes inside Iran resumed 30 Aug at the heaviest tempo in a month, while escort and mine clearance moved strait flow back toward pre-war levels — the force leverage Iran built the war on is eroding (its verification channel still authorises ~40% of transits), and ISW reads the hardliners’ answer as escalation timed toward the US midterms. The IDF’s clearing of the Ali al Taher IRGC complex reopened the Israeli front. Brent round-tripped the band floor and re-entered at $92.09, with the widest prompt premiums on record and the strategic reserve at a fresh series low. Murrin’s Article 2 nuclear scenario remains the analytical foundation under structural tail protection. Full scenario stances, drivers, equity and Brent views are in section 03.

01 · Due Diligence on Murrin

Verdict unchanged — cannot rule it out. WW3 117’s call for total war is his own advocacy; his checkable claims hold, with the strait-control call now overtaken by events.

Murrin’s strait-control call — corroborated when written — is overtaken by the mine clearance and the escort regime: the first of his corroborated calls reversed by events. WW3 119 (“20 Strategic Realities,” 18 Aug) grades below. The claim-by-claim tables and the track-record scorecard are in Appendix A1; the full verifiability table sits in the v1 tab.

Murrin’s capabilities case is sound and OSINT-sourced. Timeline sits at the aggressive end of a 6–12 month band that overlaps Roaring Lion’s own assessment. The preemptive-nuclear-use conclusion is his advocacy. The ~440kg 60% HEU stockpile that anchors the capabilities case — the figure the Gallant “440 Kilograms” piece restates — stays inside Iran, physically hardened against seizure, and unmentioned through every window of armed exchange; inspector access stays unresolved, with Grossi expecting entry while Iran ties access to a final deal and sanctions relief, and Iran is not down-blending. The nuclear file itself has gone from deferred to unanchored: Tehran suspended the MoU on 18 Jul, the meeting announced on 2 Aug never convened, and the 60-day term in the signed text lapsed on 17 Aug with the file never opened — Trump declaring talks over the next day; through this window’s strikes and sanctions the file stayed shut, no table for it. On the claims: the axis leg extended again (FT — covert Russian cruise-missile technology aid since ~Nov 2023, beside the documented Caspian flow), while the strait-control claim broke the other way — corroborated when WW3 117 was written, overtaken by mine clearance, the escort regime and a 17m-barrel transit day. “Cannot rule out the nuclear scenario” holds as the analytical foundation; the apex is handled via the long-term allocation rather than modelled scenarios.

02 · Scenario test

Live tail risk on a 6–12 month horizon — below the scenario-modelling threshold.

The conclusion is unchanged; the operational decision is to bear this tail in the long-term allocation rather than model it.

The apex first-use event is paradigm-break, so protection is structural rather than model-derived. As David noted, “in short, I probably don’t need to know what the damage would look like.” Twelve windows of armed exchange since late June have stayed conventional, the ~440kg HEU core unmentioned in any of them. The twelfth (30 Aug – 4 Sep) was the heaviest in over a month and touched no nuclear site; the campaign’s economic turn cuts both ways for this tail, draining the resources a breakout would need while giving a cornered leadership less to lose. The apex window stays open-ended, framed by the war’s midterm-timed trajectory rather than any deal clock; the buffers thinned again (the strategic reserve at a fresh series low, section 05). What stays in the long-term allocation is the nightmare convergence — nuclear Iran + reinvigorated Russia + hedging China + exhausted America + isolated Israel arriving together as oil buffers run dry. Murrin Article 3’s late-stage US-decline thesis sits on the “exhausted America” leg as backdrop conviction. The window-by-window record is in Appendix A4 and the prior tabs.

Verdict

Murrin Article 2 cannot be ruled out and remains a live tail risk on a 6–12 month horizon. The apex probability sits below the threshold where another modelled scenario would change the prescription. Israeli unilateral action remains the most plausible trigger — no unilateral strike on Iran through twelve windows, with the strait and the Lebanon front the live channels an escalation would run through. The Lebanon channel turned kinetic this window with the IDF’s clearing of the Ali al Taher IRGC complex — the detail and ISW’s three response branches are at section 04. Barclays’ flag of a strike risk ahead of Israel’s 27 Oct election stands as the one dated catalyst.

External cross-check — Stavridis’s three paths (4 Aug)
External cross-check — Stavridis’s three paths (4 Aug) · per David, the starting position for the scenario-stress work

Admiral Stavridis (Carlyle Compass, 4 Aug; via Gary, 5 Aug) weights three US paths: significant drawdown ~10%, major escalation ~30%, renewed negotiations backed by measured pressure ~60%. The 60% path lands where this file’s Resolution track sits, and his predicted most-likely outcome — a dual-key reopening with Iran controlling northbound transit and Oman the southbound route — is structurally the US-Qatari corridor design, at the lapse the only drafted text, orphaned: unapproved in Tehran, part-opposed in Washington. The 17–18 Aug record leaned the map toward his 30% escalation path — strikes on economic targets at 300–500+ per 24-hour cycle, an initial ~30,000 ground troops to secure the strait, an all-out Iranian response against Gulf energy — which maps onto the escalation leg this file holds in the $130–160+ band; the 10% drawdown path sits nearest Mearsheimer’s withdrawal expectation. His inputs run close to the file’s own: Iran at ~65% combat-power loss yet retaining the missile, drone, small-craft and mine capability that threatens shipping; Tehran having banked regime survival, $25bn in unfrozen assets and the proposed $300bn fund — his figures for the Articles 11 and 6 terms. One structural read runs beyond the window: strait control as a depreciating asset, the energy system adapting away from the chokepoint — measurable in Japan’s rebuilt import mix (US share ~3% to ~25%, ~200 days of reserve cover; ANRE, 14 Aug). v19 update: the record now runs on a blend his map did not draw — the kinetic tempo of his 30% escalation path beside a Treasury-led economic campaign as the main weapon, his 60% negotiations path dormant with no talks scheduled and the dual-key design dead. The depreciating-asset read gained its strongest data yet: escort-restored flow near pre-war levels, and Bessent asserting the strait will “eventually become irrelevant” as pipelines expand.

ISW weighs three Iranian responses: a large-scale strike, a symbolic one, or none. The Israeli-strike trigger fires for the first time, with the caveat that this is a clearing operation in Lebanon rather than a strike on Iran.
  • The trigger on Iran itself has not fired: no unilateral Israeli strike through twelve windows — Israel is deliberately sitting the campaign out (WSJ, early Aug) while the IDF prepares options; Keane’s on-record description of a plan that “exceeds everything that we did in Epic Fury” is an escalation signal, unexecuted. Barclays flags an Israeli strike as a live if unlikely risk ahead of the 27 Oct election; Papic reads Iran’s own restraint toward Israel as forcing Israeli compliance with the order to stay out.
  • The Lebanon file stays the structural obstacle: a “complete end to the war in Lebanon” is an explicit Iranian red line and Hezbollah’s preservation is Mojtaba’s stated “first condition”; the process track has stalled — talks hung on pilot-zone locations and third-party verifiers, IDF sources reporting LAF gaps in securing the zones (24 Aug), Israel striking Hezbollah targets regularly — and a Turkey-Israel front opened beside it: Netanyahu-ordered strikes in Syria answered by an Ankara arrest warrant and Turkish air defences moving into Syria (TIS Group, 26 Aug).
  • Iran’s conditions run through Israel: Netanyahu rejected the US-backed mediators’ Gaza proposal (9 Aug) — one of the demands Iran attaches to reopening that Washington cannot deliver alone, and Rezaei’s added condition — a region-wide ceasefire including Lebanon and Gaza — widens that dependency.
Ali al Taher cleared ·
spoiler channel live
Iran
Fractured, with the fracture now on the record — and the hardline camp setting policy as the economic floor gives way. The objective is recognised sovereignty over the strait, asserted by force through every window.
detail
  • The economy breaks: the rial at a record 2.02m/USD (24 Aug), depreciation 110% annualised since the 14 Jul reimposition (Brooks), inflation 66% (ISW) to ~80% (CE), a $500m central-bank FX injection (25 Aug), youth unemployment spiking; the UAE rupture severed the hub for ~80% of imported FX and traders shift business to China (ISW, 24 Aug). Khamenei’s office instructs officials to stop highlighting the economy; 30 alleged protest-organiser arrests; the 313,000-personnel “Janfada” exercise reads as a domestic show of force (ISW). The income counterweight stands: Kharg partially reloading from 12 Aug, $7.5bn of oil revenue in four months (Fars, single-sourced), Baghdad’s “special status” ask.
  • The split goes public: Pezeshkian — “it would be better to end [the war] now”; Ghalibaf — Iran cannot endure the war hungry; Hemmati on collapsing exports and FX shortages — against the Vahidi-led anti-concession camp, strengthened by Tehran’s own read that the US subverted the MoU. Zaidan’s Tehran visit and the “economic terrorism” line carry the resistance framing; Fars attacks Pezeshkian’s call as pre-war weakness. Rezaei threatens to treat sanctions compliance as enmity — “not a single drop of oil will be exported” — and Defa Press floats proactive strikes on regional energy infrastructure, publicly opposed by a former VP. The counter-datum stands: Axios’s report that Vahidi told a May US backchannel he fully supported the negotiating team and preferred a negotiated solution.
  • Force against eroding leverage: shore-based rocket mine-laying from Larak after CENTCOM cleared the laid mines — ISW reads the improvised methods, and fast-attack craft used for visual identification in place of destroyed radars, as degraded capability; VLCC strikes on the southern route (the Senegal Prosperity, 31 Aug); strikes on US bases across five countries including first strikes at UAE bases (al Minhad, 3 Sep), the Artesh stating a preemptive-strike doctrine (26 Aug). ISW’s frame: the hardliners are dissatisfied precisely because recognised strait control has not been achieved, and the $200-oil goal set in March has failed — below $100 since May. The command consolidation stands (the armed-forces general-staff merger ordered complete 10 Aug); the Paydari Front stays the rejectionist pole of the factional map.
Rial at 2.02m ·
strikes five countries
China
Now the sanctions campaign’s named target — and the 24 Sep summit constrains both sides.
detail
  • The isolation contest: Bessent names China — buyer of ~90% of Iran’s pre-blockade oil exports — as the campaign’s central target (“no one is above sanctions”) while sparing major Chinese banks; Beijing vows “all necessary measures” and refuses to cut Tehran off without reciprocal concessions; Barclays reads the Xi-Trump summit (24 Sep) as the boundary — only sanctioning a major Chinese bank or SOE would derail it. ISW’s limit stands: Chinese engagement cannot offset a blockade Iran cannot physically ship through.
  • Absorbing the shock: imports abruptly halved (~5mn bpd) at the war’s outset against the ~1.3–1.4bn-barrel reserve with no visible consumption decline — and July crude imports rebounded ~22% to ~8.45mn bpd (desk monitor, 14 Aug); some Hormuz transits reportedly settled in renminbi; Beijing self-arranges Houthi passage for its own tankers (Reuters); COSCO and China Merchants tankers have avoided both Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb since late July on central guidance.
  • Structural de-risking: Qatari LNG to China down ~98% year on year; Sinopec and PetroChina exploring 10+ year non-Gulf supply; BCA adds a feedstock read — the Hormuz crisis is accelerating a petrochemical pivot toward coal (75+ coal-to-chemical projects), a structural headwind for oil-demand growth, too early to trade on BCA’s own account. Beyond the public line: US officials suspect a PRC reconnaissance satellite supports Iranian targeting (WSJ); Iran seeks PRC assistance rebuilding its air defences (ISW).
Resists isolation ·
summit constrains both sides
Russia
Aligned with China publicly; an active supplier privately.
detail
  • The resupply is documented: NBC (18 Aug, citing a European government document verified by a Western official) — drone components, ammunition and TNT delivered to Iran across the Caspian as of July, over two dozen Russian ships to Amirabad Port; US intelligence cites “Russian-enhanced” Shaheds and Russian targeting intelligence used against US forces. The April F-15E downing (disclosed 11 Aug) ran on drone-swarm tactics ISW ties to direct Russian assistance in this war.
  • The technology leg reported: FT (1 Sep) — Russia has covertly helped Iran develop advanced cruise-missile technology since around November 2023; ISW notes it is unclear how far along Iran is. A second axis component moves from hypothesis toward the record; CIA Director Ratcliffe’s Moscow visit (26 Aug, TIS Group) shows the US-Russia back channel open beside it.
  • The HEU custodian pathway: the formal offer to take Iran’s HEU stands (Araghchi: “not currently under discussion”) — the technical route under the Security Guarantee architecture.
Cruise-missile technology
aid reported (FT)
Houthis / Yemen
The second front has an owner, and its reach extended this window.
detail
  • The reach extends: the Saudi tanker AMZAN struck roughly 950km north of Yemen off Yanbu (24 Aug) — the furthest confirmed Houthi strike on a Saudi vessel since their blockade began 20 Jul, possibly indicating an anti-ship ballistic missile range beyond 500km (ISW, open-source unconfirmed).
  • The Saudi shield goes financial: Riyadh in talks to stand up a state-backed fund subsidising commercial war-risk insurance to keep the Red Sea leg running (FT, 24 Aug); Red Sea oil exports hold near 3.5mn bpd against a ~120k pre-war base. Saudi Arabia is reportedly preparing a naval and possible land offensive against the Houthis (ISW, 10 Aug), while the Omani-mediated indirect channel stands with the US privately discouraging retaliation. The blockade on Saudi port calls (declared 20 Jul) holds; the Tihamah (11 Aug, six dead), Mocha Port (9 Aug, seven killed), the MSV Faize Noore Oliya sinking (4 Aug) and the Jizan refinery strike (8 Aug) stand in the fatal-incident record; Barclays judges the risk of a full-scale Saudi-Houthi war increasing on maximalist Houthi revenue demands.
  • The Iranian hand beside their own agenda: ISW — “their own agenda… a key Iranian partner”; the 13 Jul flight carried IRGC commanders, missile equipment and gold; WSJ’s 17 Aug reporting has the IRGC supervising Red Sea missile and drone deployments and passing target lists.
Strikes reach 950km north ·
Saudi shields the Red Sea leg
GCC / Pakistan
Mediation delivered the ceasefire; the bloc’s exposure has widened round by round — and this round Iranian fire reached its bases.
detail
  • The counter-pressure ISW expected arrived: a Supreme Leader’s Office-affiliated outlet published imagery implicitly threatening Emirati fuel storage (23 Aug); the Artesh struck al Minhad Air Base in the UAE and Ahmad al Jaber in Kuwait (3 Sep) — the first strikes at UAE bases, claimed intercepted before entering UAE airspace — and an ADNOC tanker pair was attacked off Fujairah. The UAE holds the rupture; the only Gulf state to have severed financial ties (ex-China it handled ~71% of Iran’s shadow-banking flows, per Barclays).
  • The UAE ruptures: all trade and financial transactions with Iran halted “until further notice” after the UAE-attributed missiles (18 Aug); Rubio and Sheikh Tahnoon coordinate on Hormuz security the same day. ISW reads the move as pressure against any Iran-Oman design granting Iran navigation control, and expects Iranian counter-pressure on the UAE rather than concession.
  • The bloc arms: the Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan joint defence agreement (7 Aug) on top of the 2025 Saudi-Pakistan pact — 8,000 Pakistani troops already in the kingdom; the ripple reaches India, where a retired general calls the alignment a “Sunni NATO” and says India keeps its Iran ties regardless (Jerusalem Post, 20 Aug); GPF’s Friedman reads the pact as raising the odds Iran seeks an off-ramp. The claimed ~50-nation coalition remains uncorroborated by ISW.
  • Iraq becomes a pressure channel: the Jurf al-Sakhr deployment softened to monitoring-only under militia pressure; a militia handed 20 Iranian-made drones to the government before US officials (19 Aug) as Ghalibaf worked Baghdad against disarmament; Iraq asked Iran for “special status” strait exports (19 Aug), a central-bank payment channel discussed 16–17 Aug. The disarmament file tightened toward its 30 Sep deadline: the US rejected a five-militia offer of a two-year operations pause as a “trick” (28 Aug), and ISW assesses Iran running two lines of effort — letting militias covertly retain weapons in depots, and building smaller, more ideological militias under tighter Iranian control (2 Sep).
  • The bypass geography: Yanbu carries ~4mn bpd as the Hormuz bypass with Abqaiq the single upstream node behind it — both inside the Houthi and militia target set; the Saudi–Pakistan airspace cross-promise still binds Israeli unilateral action, deepened by the trilateral pact.
UAE bases struck a first time ·
the bloc holds the rupture
Europe
Aligns with the diplomatic track; constrained from leading any post-war architecture after refusing the US reopening request. The UK and France had offered to lead Hormuz demining — performed instead by CENTCOM (27–28 Aug), allies privately doubting completeness; a NATO contribution to the HEU Security Guarantee would be the test. Capital Economics finds Europe weathering this energy shock far better than 2022 — though European gas keeps printing fresh conflict highs and German inventories enter the winter worse than 2022 (Vanda), with CE’s gas forecast raised to €80/MWh.
Diplomatic backer
Japan / Korea
Lean on the US for Resolution; ~60% of energy via Hormuz — and the adaptation is now measurable. Japan holds ~200 days of reserve cover (ANRE, 14 Aug) with imports rebuilt past 80% of the 2025 average, the US share up from ~3% to ~25%, at a ~$114/bbl premium (CE) feeding the reflation behind 30-year JGBs above 4%. The war has reached the Korean alliance: the premier US-Korea exercise curtailed over Seoul’s refusal to help open the strait (16 Aug, per Bloomberg). The yen leg tightened into a policy squeeze: a BOJ hike ~98–99% priced for 18 Sep under Bessent’s open pressure (the Ueda meeting, 31 Aug), with BCA calling a multi-year yen turn and flagging that a weak yen amplifies Japan’s Hormuz-inflation exposure. Dormant nuclear conversations re-open if the scenario shifts to apex.
Adapting around the strait ·
alliance strain
The map — the leverage question turns

Stalemate stays modal because the US–Iran nuclear divide is wide and the hardliner faction blocks Good A. The structural fault ISW identified — Clause 5 read by Washington as restored passage and by Tehran as affirmed Iranian authority — has run through every variant since, and the sovereignty question is answered in Iran’s favour: every design short of recognised Iranian control with revenue attached has been refused. The flow question that split the counter-reads at v18 has moved toward restoration under escort and clearance (the record and counter-data are at section 05): Iran’s force leverage over the strait is eroding while its economy breaks. Two halves stay open. Barclays describes an interim arrangement operating in practice — ~40% of transits through an Iranian verification channel, Iran having “in effect, ensured all shipping need to obtain authorisation” — so the power to stop traffic erodes while the claim to authorise it is conceded in practice. And whether the pressure can force capitulation is unresolved: Barclays judges regime change “doubtful” on forty years of sanctions endurance, ISW reads the strengthened hardline camp as answering lost leverage with midterm-timed force, and Citrinowicz’s read stands: a cornered Iran escalates. The version-by-version map is in the prior tabs.

What it confirms: the sovereignty read carried since v3 — and its consequence: with recognised control refused and the strait now flowing under US escort, Iran’s remaining leverage is what its forces can hit and the verification channel it still runs, and the hardliners have taken the war to the first. What it does not change: the bifurcated architecture, the apex held in the long-term allocation, the Murrin due diligence, the Brent bands. Watch-list:
  • Trigger status: Iran-formal-response fires a sixth time (Ghalibaf, Rezaei, Araghchi on the record); Mediation-breakdown a third (the corridor never opened, mediators “ferrying unchanged viewpoints”); Israeli-strike fires for the first time (Ali al Taher); Signed-deal held (the IRGC fee-share claim stays unconfirmed); Saudi-Pakistan airspace stays listed, the pact deepened again.
  • The September calendar: US CPI 11 Sep → FOMC 15–16 Sep (a hike roughly even-odds, Vanda 5 Sep) → BOJ 17–18 Sep (~98–99% priced) → Xi-Trump summit 24 Sep, Barclays’ boundary on China sanctions → Iraq’s militia-disarmament deadline 30 Sep.
  • The Ali al Taher response: ISW’s three branches — large-scale strike on Israel, symbolic, or none; the stalled pilot-zone talks run under its shadow (a September Rome round was set; no convening recorded on the desk through 4 Sep), with Israel’s 27 Oct election Barclays’ dated strike-risk marker.
  • The infrastructure-strike debate in Tehran: Defa Press floats proactive strikes on regional energy targets, unresolved in the regime’s own media; the ~2% hit rate on escorted ships is the operational reason fixed targets beckon.
  • The pressure track’s next moves: the promised “major financial institution” designation and the compliance timelines running out (Brooks names Turkey next); the reported Saudi offensive preparation against the Houthis beside Barclays’ rising odds of a full Saudi-Houthi war.
  • The SPR floor: the contracted release runs out within weeks, leaving the sub-300 debate with no programme behind it.

The escalation timeline is in Appendix A4; the print and session record in Appendix A5.

05 · Market & thematic implications

Scenario views across equities, Brent, rates, and rotation.

Views only. Brent bands unchanged from v12.

ScenarioEquitiesBrentRatesRotation
Stalemate
Modal		 Mid-teens downside; the modal outcome flat, the skew down (Vanda). Tight, elevated, drawing inventory — back inside the band at $92.09 (2 Sep) after the round trip. Yields up; the long end draws policy defence (the buyback doubling); oil the dominant 30Y driver (Vanda); a Warsh-led hike live for 15–16 Sep. Iran-axis exposure screens unattractive; rare earths, security and infrastructure favoured.
Resolution
Economic-pressure phase; corridor dead		 Mid-single-digit upside. Declines toward $90–110 over months on a realised reopening. Yields ease as the energy premium unwinds. Screens better selectively; the China sleeve recalibrates on a firmer Hormuz-access outcome.

Equities — the two-sided tape

Mid-teens downside under Stalemate, with EPS holding until ~2027 demand destruction. The oil-to-equity transmission has compressed — roughly 1.5% S&P downside per 10% oil rise — and the war and the AI cycle are pulling equities in opposite directions. August closed +2.6% on the S&P (NDR), Nvidia’s $96.2bn quarter carrying the AI side; the resumed exchange took the index 7,712 (28 Aug) → 7,631 (1 Sep) → 7,667 (2 Sep) as yields eased. Rate sensitivity explains roughly half of US sector moves (Vanda), putting the 30-year — and through it, oil — at the centre of the equity question; Vanda expects a moderate September drawdown, recovering toward ~7,950 by late November. The bubble question moved to the centre of the firm’s own reading: David’s 18–19 Aug strategy updates place markets at the neighbourhood of a bubble — made bigger or nearer its end if the oil-inflation shock lands — with Yardeni’s vigilantes stirring at a 5–6% 30-year range, NDR uneasy at 25x against 5.5%, and Dudley (20 Aug) putting the burst before end-2027 on CAPE 41 and a 240% Buffett Indicator. The AI financing is the flagged fault line: WSJ counts ~$3tn of off-balance-sheet commitments across nine companies against ~$600bn of trailing capex. CE notes the Shiller CAPE ending August near its dotcom high.

Brent — the physical ledger

The floor traded from both sides: $92.67 (21 Aug) faded to $86.30 (27 Aug) on the sanctions-pivot de-escalation read, then the resumed strikes took the front month to $92.09 (2 Sep, +5.9% on the week) and ~$97 intraday; WTI crossed $90 on 1 Sep. Structure moved harder than price: Brent’s prompt basis inverted to −$3.54 and Dubai’s to −$10.08 in two sessions, the widest prompt premiums the benchmarks have printed; transit cost ~$20m per supertanker, roughly $10/bbl (TotalEnergies). The re-closure scenario the market prices as a ~$150 shock remains the near-term, non-nuclear face of the escalation leg.

The live flags — inventory, flow, print divergences, external calls
  • Inventory: SPR 286.6m barrels (week to 28 Aug) — a fourth consecutive taper, ~4.7m contracted barrels left: the release engine is nearly out, with 86.6m above the desk monitor’s ~200m operational-floor estimate (its last cushion estimate: 20–24 weeks, at the 89.7m print). The floor debate stands — Hochstein: “I don’t know anyone who believes we can go below 300,” against DOE’s cavern rebuttal, with the reserve already below it. Commercial crude drew faster than the SPR this window (424.5m); IEA counts global inventories down 410m barrels since the war began.
  • Flow, resolved toward restoration: mines cleared from the traffic separation scheme (27–28 Aug; allies privately doubt all of an estimated 80–150 are gone), 500+ escorted ships in 30 days with ~2% hit, 20–30 tankers a night on the southern route; 17m barrels transited 31 Aug against ~21.6m bpd pre-war, ~40 vessels on 1 Sep. The counter-data keep it short of complete: Axios’s own summary metric has escorted transits restoring shipping to about half pre-war levels (28 Aug), EIA’s Q2 average was 4.9m bpd, Barclays counts ~60% of pre-war flow across both chokepoints — and ~40% of transits run through Iran’s verification channel, the procedural leverage the escort regime has not touched. The gas complex stays the unshielded leg: European gas at post-Jan-2023 highs.
  • Print divergences: the desk series remains primary (the 23 Jul peak ~$94 against the AP $100.69 settle); the gasoline series stays split — the desk monitor has $4.79 (18 Aug), grinding higher — and distillates are the sharper strain: stocks ~13% below the five-year average with diesel margins at records; the monitor flags a diesel-crisis risk as the likelier near-term break; diesel printed $5.78/gal near the record $5.81 (Barclays, ~4 Sep), and BCA’s commodities desk opened a short crack-spread position on rising dark transits — the refined-product strain now trades as its own leg.
  • External calls: Barclays $65–80 (28 Jul) sits below our floor — its ~4 Sep note trades the spot at $90–95, with no revised forward range on the desk’s record — BCA $70–100 and Papic’s $85–100 (12 Aug) straddle it, and Papic pairs his range with “oil prices are unlikely to decline much.” All flagged, not adopted; EIA raised its 2026 Brent forecast to $87 (11 Aug). This window the external set moved toward the band: CE raised its end-2026 forecast to $100 on a Hormuz crisis it now assumes runs into next year; NDR moved crude bearish → neutral; Papic holds Brent averaging at least $80–100 into next year with forward curves underpricing the risk; the below-floor side keeps BCA’s commodities desk, floating a ~$70 near-term floor (25 Aug); Murrin’s $150+ logged in Appendix A1.

Rates & FX — the curve, the buyback turn and the yen

Fiscal pressure lifts yields and the war’s oil pressure feeds the curve. The 11–20 Aug window took it systemic: the 10-year auction at 4.683% (12 Aug) and the 30-year at 5.216% (13 Aug) — the highest since 2007 and 2001 — then a 5.31% 30-year close (17 Aug) with the debt through $40tn and July’s $432bn deficit the largest monthly shortfall since early 2021. Treasury answered on 19 Aug by at least doubling long-end liquidity-support buybacks — the 30-year fell to 5.18%, the dollar to a three-month low — and Bessent followed: possibly more than $4bn per issue, “part of it is signaling,” a fiscal-consolidation announcement due within days — the Iran plan landed 24 Aug; no fiscal plan reached the desk in this window. Per David’s 19 Aug note, the doubling reads as a reach toward yield-curve control (“Bessent blinks”), funded at the short end; his conclusion is gold above $4,500, on the confidence channel. Saravelos: “soft-form financial repression.” The structural bid thins underneath — June TIC has the weakest foreign long-term buying since February (China’s YTD sales $40.3bn; JPM’s 2026 foreign-demand forecast cut to $450bn) just as hyperscaler issuance competes for the long end (~$2tn expected in 2026). Warsh’s first Jackson Hole keynote (28 Aug) drew the sharpest reaction of any Jackson Hole — 2s30s flattened 10bp (most since 1989), gold fell 3%, a September hike ~55–60% priced; Waller keyed a hold to a soft CPI (11 Sep), and August payrolls beat at +162k. The doubled buybacks run 9 Sep – 4 Nov, opposed on the record by Druckenmiller (“price management, not liquidity management”), Dalio, Slok and Brooks filling in the fiscal frame David’s monetary-order reading pack circulates. NBIM proposed cutting government bonds to 50% of its bond portfolio (~$75bn less in Treasuries) — reallocation rather than exodus on Papic’s read. The yen/JGB leg is tracked at firm level as a scenario-stress item (per David’s 6 Aug note) and tightened through mid-August: 30-year JGBs above 4% for the first time, Japan’s PPI at 8% against CPI and wages near 3%, Eurizon calling the joint intervention “a watershed” with an eventual 125 target against BCA’s ~130 fair value. The BOJ decision (17–18 Sep) is now ~98–99% priced for a hike under open Treasury pressure (Bessent’s “strong support” at the Ueda meeting, 31 Aug), with BCA calling a multi-year yen turn on un-anchored Japanese inflation. Gold holds the other side of the same logic — above $4,250 for the first time since June (UBS, 7 Aug; central banks bought 289 tonnes in Q2), UBS targeting $5,000 by H1 2027, and David’s own studies framing gold as a question about global debt rather than a price call. The Jackson Hole day’s 3% gold drop reads on Vanda’s account as crowded positioning rather than a thesis change; Brooks argues a September hike would be performative and gold-bullish via the Treasury-Fed accord frame.

Rotation — the thematic screen
  • Realised target set: Gulf civilian utilities and energy infrastructure (Kuwaiti power and desalination, the KPC facility, Aramco’s Jizan refinery); Saudi oil infrastructure and the Red Sea leg; the Mediterranean port vector (Damietta); UAE state shipping — and now UAE waters on the Emirati account (18 Aug), with the rupture putting UAE-Iran trade exposure (a third of Iran’s imports) into the screen; this window added US bases in the UAE and Kuwait (al Minhad, Ahmad al Jaber, 3 Sep) and VLCCs on the southern route (the Senegal Prosperity), with the Tehran infrastructure-strike debate pointing at fixed Gulf energy targets next.
  • A third chokepoint vector: Suez-adjacent drone strikes attributed to pro-Iranian Iraqi militias (Straits Times synthesis, primary corroboration outstanding). The second chokepoint’s record turned fatal at the Tihamah (11 Aug).
  • Screened, unstruck vectors: UAE data centres, regional fintech, Gulf cable-dependent payments, the undersea-cables / SWIFT non-oil vector — the cables vector moved from screened toward planned: WSJ’s 17 Aug reporting has preemptive strikes on Gulf internet cables inside the IRGC’s drawn-up options.
  • Thematic stances: the China sleeve re-rates on the Beijing read of US weakness; the energy-paradigm shift favours rare earths, security and infrastructure, defensive on regional refining; Japan’s rebuilt import mix (US share ~25%) is the adaptation trade in practice; the supply-side answer widened with the Venezuelan concession (17 fields, ~65bn barrels claimed, 28 Aug) — BCA grades it a paper tiger near term (~0.2m bpd today, the 320k b/d uplift not before 2031) with Middle East disruption still the dominant crude driver; BCA’s defense-stocks read pairs the structural buildup with post-ceasefire cyclical risk, neutral large-cap A&D, overweight drone makers.
  • Context series: the AI-financing series (WSJ’s ~$3tn off-balance-sheet count; Nvidia backing up to $105bn of financing for a data-centre campus leased by OpenAI; SK Hynix’s $29bn buyback); CSIS interceptor inventories behind the munitions-depletion read.

Apex / tail: escalation toward $130–160+ Brent is held in the long-term allocation; first-use ($200+, SPX ~3,500) sits below the scenario-modelling threshold as structural tail protection. The deal’s re-timing of this tail ended with the text itself: the 60-day term lapsed on 17 Aug, so the window is open-ended; the HEU stays in Iran, hardened, and unmentioned in every exchange to date. The war’s trajectory now frames the tail: midterm-timed escalation on ISW’s read, a post-midterm flare-up on BCA’s, and the twelfth window’s exchanges again leaving the nuclear file untouched. BCA’s proliferation read runs the other way from Murrin’s — the next nuclear step comes from US allies (Japan, Korea, the Gulf) rather than an Iranian breakout. The proliferation-adjacent log is carried in the prior tabs; the reported US-Saudi enrichment agreement stays single-sourced, the Signed-deal watch item provisional. The Taiwan-war and US-default extrapolations are held as backdrop only, outside the modelled set.

The $300bn in the signed terms is external Gulf investment funded by sanctions relief — not a US Treasury outlay — which reconciles the terms with Iran’s frozen-asset demand; the relief flows through GCC capital.

A1 · Murrin due diligence — claim-by-claim tables and track record

WW3 119 — the twenty strategic realities, graded

“WW3 119: 20 Strategic Realities of Our Age” (18 Aug; reached the desk 21 Aug via Gary) is Murrin’s widest frame yet — ten “strategic realities” and five numbered predictions placing the Iran war as one of three fronts (Ukraine, Iran, Taiwan) in an existential struggle against an “Axis of Autocracy,” with a wartime-economy and rearmament prescription attached. The piece pre-dates the escort-and-clearance turn, so its Iran cost-imposition framing describes the record through mid-August; its five numbered predictions are structural rearmament calls carrying no dated Iran forecast, so no new scorecard row enters. It moves nothing in the architecture, the bands or the verdict; the Iran-relevant claims grade as follows.

ClaimTierChecked againstOur read
“The IRGC seeks nothing less than the strategic submission of America” and refuses a negotiated peace. Partly ISW’s factional map (21 Aug on): a Vahidi-led anti-concession camp seeking full US surrender likely guides policy — but against a realist camp (Pezeshkian, Ghalibaf, Hemmati) publicly arguing to end the war, and Araghchi keeping a Qatar channel open (“isn’t impossible,” 28 Aug). Washington has also declared talks over on its side. The camp he describes does hold policy, but Iran is not the monolith he assumes — and the refusal of peace runs through both capitals this window, which his one-sided framing does not carry.
The central prediction. Ukraine, Iran and the Taiwan confrontation are “stages of a wider conflict rather than disconnected wars” — the piece’s own label for its central geopolitical prediction. Interpretive The same frame graded at WW3 117: BCA’s Gertken models the wars staying separate as his base case — US political-will limits, Russia’s two-front aversion, China’s external constraints — with a Hormuz oil shock the tail that merges them. The couplings themselves are documented on this desk: shared munitions strain, the Caspian materiel flow, the reported cruise-missile aid, PRC support short of direct involvement. Unchanged from the WW3 117 treatment: the file carries the wars as coupled through observable channels without adopting the single-war thesis. His stated escalation marker — weakening Western deterrence raising the risk of direct confrontation with China — carries no date or threshold and cannot be graded.
Axis enablement. China and Russia’s economic, technological and strategic support sustains Iran’s war. Components corroborated NBC’s documented Caspian materiel flow (18 Aug); FT on covert Russian cruise-missile technology assistance since ~Nov 2023 (1 Sep); the suspected PRC targeting satellite (WSJ); Chinese purchases of ~90% of pre-blockade Iranian oil exports. The components keep verifying — two more entered the record this window; the single-war frame they feed is graded in the row above.
US deterrence and munitions are draining across fronts. Corroborated CSIS interceptor counts (Patriot 2,330 → ~759–827; THAAD 452 → ~234–278 by late Jul); the curtailed US-Korea exercise over strait tasking; the lone Asia-based carrier redeployed to the Gulf; 5th Fleet resupplying via Diego Garcia (Barclays). Corroborated from primary trackers this file already holds — consistent with the munitions-depletion read carried since v3.
The prescription: a wartime economy, private-capital rearmament, layered air defence. Advocacy — His policy conclusion, kept in quotation as with WW3 117’s total-war call. No forecast content to grade.

WW3 117 — the total-war call, graded

“WW3 117: Trump's Watershed Moment in Recognising a Common Autocratic Enemy” (28 Jul; reached the desk an hour after the v14 send) is Murrin's escalation call. The frame is a single integrated struggle — Ukraine, the Middle East and a coming Indo-Pacific theatre against one autocratic axis — hung on Senator Graham's funeral as the catalyst, and it concludes that Trump “has only one choice” — total war with Iran alongside Israel. It moves nothing in the architecture, the bands or the verdict.

ClaimTierChecked againstOur read

Track record — prior calls against the 20 May to 4 Sep record

The capability, structure and chokepoint calls have held — with the strait-control call now overtaken by the escort record — and three of them are working assumptions in this file. Timing and agency are where he fails, consistently and across every piece. The rows below are not independent trials — the Israel-trigger thesis recurs in four pieces and is entered once, and several draw on the same escalation sequence — so this reads as a map of where he is reliable rather than a hit rate. Unfalsifiable framing and advocacy carrying no forecast content are excluded, as is a 2024 Lebanon ground-campaign piece re-stamped 29 May 2026 and circulated as current with its body text never revised.

WW3 116 moves nothing in the scenario architecture, the Brent bands or the verdict. The two claims in it that carry weight are corroborated from outside the piece: CSIS puts PAC-3 and THAAD replenishment on a three-plus-year queue with FY2027 deliveries starting in 2029, supplying the numbers behind an interceptor mechanism he asserts without any, and ISW's Clause 5 finding vindicates the MoU read he made on signing day. The claims nothing here tests are the al-Shabaab coordination and drone transfer, the persistent-armed-ISR doctrine shift, and the Bear Island and Japan-Okinawa passages; the assassination-plot row is no longer untested — two of its legs hardened at v18 (the Ankara MANPADS disclosure). The Bab el-Mandeb vector is the one genuinely new watch item, and the account of agency behind it is not his: Reuters has Iran instructing the Houthis conditional on US strikes against Iranian power plants, while Bremmer and Barclays both attribute Houthi behaviour to a payments dispute with Riyadh. The capability, structure and chokepoint reads are the durable part of his work (the strait-control read now overtaken — see the track-record table), and three of them are working assumptions in this file. His quantities do not travel into our text without independent confirmation. His timelines and his assignment of agency to Israel have failed repeatedly across the file.

Essential Lessons Part I — the retrospective, graded

“Essential Lessons from the Iran Conflict — Part I: Strategic Realities” (Murrinations, 21 Jul; reached the desk 26 Jul via Gary) is Murrin grading the war he has covered since WW3 112. It is doctrine — seven lessons and five predictions, one of them dated only as “inevitable.” The checkable lessons land close to sources this file already holds. It moves nothing in the architecture, the bands or the verdict. A Part II on operational lessons is flagged and will be read when it arrives.

Corroborated by the primary source this file weights most, in the same week he published. The Vietnam and Kosovo parallels and the JCS air-power-bias counterfactual are his framing; the operative claim stands on ISW alone.

Corroborated in the v14 window — the pause v14 wrote into the file is the mechanism he describes. It cuts both ways for the diplomatic track: the pause that enables the table also lets Iran reconstitute (ISW, 27 Jul).
